evidence_items.summary: The proposed road-surface dataset was developed for automated road-surface condition assessment, road-damage classification, and computer vision applications for infrastructure monitoring. It contains three classes: Major Damage, Minor Damage, and Normal, representing different levels of road-surface conditions. The images were collected in Barishal district, Bangladesh, under natural road and weather conditions. They capture diverse surface textures, lighting conditions, viewpoints, and road surroundings. Each image was visually inspected and labeled according to the dominant road-surface condition. Major Damage includes severe potholes, significant cracks, deformation, and extensive surface loss. Minor Damage contains small holes, local cracks, surface imperfections, and minor deformations. Normal represents road surfaces without significant visible damage. The dataset contains 2,855 original images, comprising 1,907 Major Damage, 354 Minor Damage, and 594 Normal images. Before augmentation, the images were split into training, validation, and test sets in a 7:1:2 ratio, resulting in 1,996, 290, and 569 images, respectively. Splitting was performed before augmentation to prevent data leakage across subsets. To address class imbalance, 2,504 additional training images were generated using random rotation, brightness and contrast adjustment, Gaussian blurring, and hue and saturation shifts. These included 166 Major Damage, 1,253 Minor Damage, and 1,085 Normal images. Consequently, the final training set contains 4,500 balanced images, with 1,500 images per class, comprising 1,996 original and 2,504 augmented images. The dataset contains 5,359 unique original and augmented images across all subsets. Images were standardized to 1024 × 1024 pixels while preserving their original aspect ratios through black padding where necessary, avoiding geometric distortion of road features. For model training and evaluation, images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels.
evidence_items.title: PavementSense: A benchmark dataset for road surface damage severity classification

The record has one ZIP archive per model: SGN v1.zip (490 MB): SGN segmentation. 48 (40 for training, 8 for validation) 3D crops from light-sheet microscopy volumes of cleared mouse cochleae, with the parvalbumin (PV) stain. Each crop has an instance annotation of the SGNs (2887 SGNs in total). Format: TIFF. Model: CochleaNet SGN Segmentation, version 1, on BioImage.io as knowledgeable-mouse. IHC v1.zip (3.3 GB): IHC segmentation. 89 (75 for training, 14 for validation) 3D crops from light-sheet microscopy volumes of cleared mouse and gerbil cochleae, with the Vglut3 stain. Each crop has an instance annotation of the IHCs (1726 IHCs in total). Format: TIFF. Each crop has a point annotation of the synapses (3996 synapses in total). Format: Zarr for the images, CSV for the points. Model: CochleaNet Ribbon Synapse Detection, version 1, on BioImage.io as loyal-ant. SGN-lowres v1.zip (741 MB): SGN segmentation in lower-resolution, anisotropic data. 18 (15 for training, 3 for validation) 3D crops from light-sheet microscopy volumes (LaVision UltraMicroscope) of cleared mouse and marmoset cochleae, with the PV stain. Each crop has an instance annotation of the SGNs (1416 SGNs in total). Format: TIFF. Model: CochleaNet Low-Resolution SGN Segmentation, version 1, on BioImage.io as nervous-shark. evidence_items.summary: Decision models support routing, guardrails, and output verification in LLM systems. However, item accuracy alone cannot establish whether models make correct decisions across controlled variations or assign reliable confidence to their predictions. We introduce DecisionPivot, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 48 tasks and 40,033 items across seven decision roles. Its core track contains 7,800 items from 13 generated task families, organized into contrast groups with computed answers verified by independently implemented solvers. The complementary reference track contains 32,233 items from 35 public test sets, preserving their original evaluation metrics. We evaluate 40 decision models and 14 general models using documented, model-specific protocols, assessing item and contrast-group accuracy, probability ordering, calibration, and empirical selective coverage. Our results reveal substantial differences obscured by aggregate scores: two 27B models separated by only 2.6 points on the reference track achieve contrast-group accuracies of 70.1% and 44.2%. Across 2,400 binary contrast pairs, Perplexity Decider correctly ranks the positive member above the negative member in 92.3% of pairs but answers both members correctly in only 74.1%, exposing a gap between probability ordering and decision correctness. Models with similar item accuracy also differ in the reliability of their high-confidence predictions. On a separate 1,296-item subset, GLM-5.3 achieves 93.5\% contrast-group accuracy at a higher reasoning setting, compared with 81.5% at its lowest effort. By linking errors to pivotal details and difficulty levels, DecisionPivot provides fine-grained diagnostics of decision failures that aggregate evaluation alone cannot reveal.
evidence_items.title: DecisionPivot: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Decision Models in LLM Systems

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains 25 long-duration time-series experiments collected from a laboratory two-tank water pumping plant. The experiments were performed under three operating conditions: Steady-State Baseline (Minimal Outflow) Steady-State With Constant Passive Outflow Dynamic Disturbance Rejection (High and Low Outflow Transients) Each experiment lasts approximately 8.5 hours, sampled at 1 Hz, and is provided as an individual CSV file. Disturbance experiments include an additional binary flag indicating externally induced outflow changes. This dataset serves as a real world benchmark for system identification, adaptive control, disturbance rejection, and anomaly detection, capturing essential nonlinearities such as turbulence, actuator saturation, and abrupt hydraulic transitions. Associated article: Gómez-González, P.-P. et al. Multi-scenario datasets for system identification and adaptive control of a nonlinear two tank system. Scientific Data 13, 1465 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-026-07686-2 . Code: https://github.com/pedropgg/TwoTank-Dataset-Code . What's new in version 2.0 Version 2.0 was verified against the acquisition code and the raw data. All measured signals, the RLS parameters (b1, a1, a2) and Kp are identical to version 1.0. Full details are in CHANGELOG.md inside the archive. Ki and Kd corrected. In v1 the logged gains had Ti and Td swapped (Ki = Kp/Td, Kd = Kp·Ti). The control action applied to the plant was not affected. The correct gains are recovered exactly from the v1 values. Valve metadata. New column Valve Opening pct (= 100 − Valve Closure pct). The closure of the HighOutflow runs is restored to the originally logged values. In every file name, X in Xpct.csv is now the electrovalve opening.

evidence_items.summary: Omni LLMs can naturally locate key audio and visual evidence and integrate information across modalities for audiovisual reasoning. Existing audio-visual reasoning benchmarks that mainly rely on multiple-choice questions usually score models solely based on answer correctness, making it difficult to assess whether a model truly forms a reasoning chain from evidence to the correct answer. In addition, textual or unimodal shortcuts may allow models to answer correctly without analyzing the necessary audio-visual evidence, further weakening the reliability of evaluation benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce EvaOmni, an evidence-grounded benchmark containing 392 videos and 1,027 purely human-annotated question-answer pairs, covering 15 capabilities and three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. We design a series of rigorous annotation procedures in which experts annotate audio and visual evidence and construct video-based distractors; humans review whether questions meet strict inspection criteria, and finally models filter textual and unimodal shortcuts. Beyond high-quality question-answer pairs, we require models to simultaneously return the answer and supporting evidence intervals in order to evaluate the complete reasoning chain. We propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies, and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality; both are incorporated into answer correctness. Across 7 open-weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs, Gemini3.7-Flash achieved the highest overall accuracy (79.4%), C.G. (70.8%), and B.G. (35.1%). At Level 3, it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. These results show that even the most advanced models still have room for development in grounded audio-visual reasoning.
evidence_items.title: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Identifying recipe entities and linking them to ontology concepts is fundamental for semantic recipe understanding. However, food mentions in recipes are often ambiguous, context-dependent, and lexically diverse, making ontology entity linking (EL) challenging. We propose SCODEL, a streamlined, model-agnostic approach based on a central idea: contextual food mentions and ontology concepts that refer to the same entity should learn the same canonical ontology-oriented definition. SCODEL uses these shared definitions as a semantic normalisation layer, providing complementary semantic information to existing EL models without requiring a new linking architecture. We further introduce ReciLinkD, the first benchmark for contextual food ontology entity linking in recipes. Experiments show that SCODEL consistently improves three modular EL models (ReFinED, GSM-EL, and BLINK): SCODEL x BLINK achieves the highest Hit@1 on seen concepts (88.33%), while SCODEL x GSM-EL achieves the highest Hit@1 on unseen concepts (83.15%), outperforming the strongest large language model (LLM) based EL baseline in each setting. Experiments on a biomedical ontology benchmark further demonstrate that SCODEL generalises beyond the food domain. Finally, we use SCODEL to ground food mentions at scale and construct an ontology-grounded recipe knowledge graph, demonstrating its utility for ontology-aware recipe retrieval and corpus-level food analysis.
evidence_items.title: SCODEL: Shared Canonical Ontology Definitions for Food Entity Linking and Ontology-Grounded Recipe Knowledge Graphs

evidence_items.summary: Despite advances in photorealism, semantic fidelity, and aesthetics, text-to-image generation and image editing remain understudied in a human-centered dimension: whether their outputs feel psychologically comforting. Grounded in cognitive evaluation theory, we define psychological comfort as an affective response shaped by viewers' appraisal of restorative and emotionally supportive visual cues. We introduce HealBench, a fine-grained benchmark of 30,000 high-quality image-text pairs spanning 19 categories and 92 subcategories, selected from 100,000 candidates through a human- and expert-in-the-loop pipeline combining vision-language model matching, human preference models, expert filtering, and exemplar-guided augmentation. We also construct HealBench-Eval, a feature-clustered evaluation set of 1,095 instances. Using HealBench-Eval, we conduct objective and subjective evaluations of 14 representative image generation models and prompt-rewriting strategies. Results reveal a gap between conventional visual quality and perceived comfort: strong semantic alignment and aesthetics do not guarantee emotionally restorative images. Reinforcement learning experiments further show that HealScorer can serve as a reward signal for assessing and improving the emotional and restorative quality of generated images. These findings establish psychological comfort as a distinct dimension of human-centered image generation and position HealBench as a foundation for affect-aware generative models.
evidence_items.title: HealBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Evaluating Psychological Comfort in Text-to-Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving beyond reactive responses toward proactive assistance that anticipates user needs without explicit requests. However, existing proactive agents primarily address immediate needs, while many everyday situations involve delayed intentions that can only be acted on hours or days later. Humans handle such intentions through prospective memory, the ability to remember to act on an intention when the right moment arises. In this paper, we introduce ProMemAgent, the first proactive agent to incorporate prospective memory over everyday sensory contexts for long-horizon proactive assistance. ProMemAgent organizes past sensory perceptions (e.g., egocentric video and audio) into context-aware memory, generating prospective cues and linking earlier events with subsequent developments for future retrieval. Given the current context, it retrieves relevant past events and performs memory-augmented proactive reasoning to determine whether assistance is needed. We further introduce CPMBench, the first benchmark for evaluating long-horizon proactive assistance over sensory contexts, comprising 1,000 instances across eight everyday categories. Extensive experiments show that ProMemAgent achieves the best memory retrieval performance and consistently outperforms all baselines on long-horizon proactive assistance.
evidence_items.title: ProMemAgent: Long-Horizon Proactive Assistance with Context-Aware Prospective Memory from Sensory Perceptions

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have advanced rapidly in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain limited on tasks requiring fine-grained understanding of small or easily overlooked image regions. Recent thinking with images approaches mitigate this limitation by allowing models to inspect images through operations such as zooming, cropping, or code execution. While effective, their multi-turn interactions with VLMs introduce redundant token computation and slow inference, and separate region inspection from the reasoning step that depends on it. To address these issues, we propose Look Before You Reason (LoRe), an implicit visual thinking framework for efficient visual reasoning within a single-turn VLM interaction. Given an image and a question, LoRe predicts the most relevant image region, aligns it with the corresponding image patch features, and strengthens the associated key-value (KV) cache entries, enabling subsequent decoding to directly exploit the selected visual cues without additional visual inputs or explicit tool calls. We further employ reinforcement learning to guide the VLM toward identifying informative image regions and leveraging them during reasoning. To support fine-grained evaluation of multimodal reasoning, we introduce COCO-ObjQA, a large-scale benchmark for object-centric multimodal reasoning. Experiments on three challenging multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that LoRe consistently improves VLM reasoning performance with low additional inference overhead.
evidence_items.title: Look Before You Reason: Implicit Visual Thinking for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Scientific method figures often provide researchers with a clear visual entry point into a paper's methodology and core contributions, yet their dense layouts and complex information flows are difficult for Vision Language Models (VLMs) to interpret. Existing benchmarks predominantly focus on coarse-grained tasks, such as context-based retrieval or holistic comprehension, overlooking the fine-grained content and inter-module relations within complex methodological diagrams. To address these overlooked aspects, we introduce Scientific Figure Benchmark (SciFigBench), a benchmark for evaluating core capabilities required for scientific method figure understanding. Specifically, it targets three capabilities: dense content perception, visual relation comprehension, and information-flow tracing. For this purpose, we curate 4,352 scientific method figures from real-world research papers and construct 40,670 QA pairs to operationalize these capabilities as measurable question-answering tasks. All annotations are generated by dedicated pipelines and then manually verified. We further propose SciFigCue, a training-free visual prompting module that externalizes arrow-induced dependencies as visual relational evidence for method-figure reasoning. Experiments across open-source and proprietary VLMs show that even strong models remain substantially limited in visual relation comprehension, while SciFigCue improves performance across several tasks without parameter updates. The code and related resources are available at https://github.com/LeNcyer/SciFigBench.
evidence_items.title: SciFigBench: A Benchmark for Scientific Method Figure Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Despite advancements in automatic speech recognition systems (ASR), current systems exhibit speaker-attribute bias, i.e., their speech recognition performance is biased against certain speakers based on their demographic attributes such as gender, accents, and speaker type. However, accurately assessing speaker attribute bias in a given ASR system requires the availability of a bias evaluation dataset with comparable speech across subgroups of a speaker attribute. In this paper, we introduce African speech Bias Evaluation Dataset (AfriBED), a novel speech recognition bias evaluation dataset for two low resource African languages, Bemba and Nyanja, to detect and estimate gender and speaker-type bias for ASR systems. The dataset comprises 9 hours of speech with 3928 utterances recorded by 80 speakers for Bemba, while the Nyanja set includes 6260 utterances with approximately 18 hours of speech recorded by 127 speakers. The results of our baseline experiments demonstrate that the datasets are useful for examining gender and speaker-type attribute bias in the target languages.
evidence_items.title: AfriBED: a Speech Recognition Bias Evaluation Dataset for Low Resource African Languages

evidence_items.summary: Conversational AI systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) require routing mechanisms that balance answer quality and response latency at scale. However, existing LLM routing benchmarks assume full observability of all candidate model outcomes, under-emphasize latency as a first-class metric, and fragment evaluation across heterogeneous protocols misaligned with real-world settings. We introduce RouterWorld, a comprehensive benchmark for LLM routing in conversational GenAI. RouterWorld unifies 371k single-turn responses and 76k multi-turn agentic trajectories, adopts natural user interactions with a standardized LLM-as-a-judge protocol, and decouples efficiency from transient pricing via hardware-grounded latency annotations. Crucially, RouterWorld formalizes routing under partial observability through two setups: Cold-Start, which restricts learning to sparse, static logs, and Voyager, which models continuous data streams where routing decisions shape future training distributions. Evaluating 13 routing baselines, we find that most routers over-emphasize accuracy while ignoring latency under partial observability. Code and benchmark data are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: RouterWorld: Scaling Conversational AI with Latency-Aware LLM Routing

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) trains policies for open-ended generation with natural-language criteria as rewards, but these rewards can become ineffective as training progresses. We identify two failure modes. Under non-discriminative rewards, scores collapse to uniformly low or high values due to insufficient exploration or a mismatch between task difficulty and policy capability. Under spurious rewards, higher scores do not correspond to better responses. Both reflect a training configuration whose task sampling, exploration, and evaluation stay fixed as the policy evolves. We introduce HarnessRL, a training-time harness that co-evolves with the policy through three interfaces for task sampling, rollout guidance, and rubric criteria. HarnessRL maintains a training-time memory from which a harness evolver retrieves within-task history and cross-task evidence. Using this evidence, the evolver attributes each reward failure to the interface whose update can address it. It then runs a proposer and just-in-time critic loop in which the critic accepts a candidate update only after measuring its effect on the current frozen policy, returning rejected candidates for revision. We also curate Rubric-Mix-10k, a five-domain training and evaluation suite for open-ended RL across medical, science, writing, role-play, and instruction-following tasks. On Rubric-Mix-10k, HarnessRL outperforms the strongest baselines by 2.8 to 3.1 points across both 4B and 9B model scales and nearly halves the training steps to its best checkpoint. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Tongyi-ConvAI/Qwen-Character/tree/main/HarnessRL.
evidence_items.title: HarnessRL: Co-Evolving Policies with a Just-in-Time Training Harness for Open-Ended RL

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in unfamiliar and evolving environments, requiring them to proactively explore, understand, and adapt to environmental dynamics. However, existing benchmarks rarely test whether agents can proactively discover how an environment works and adapt as it evolves. To address this gap, we introduce AdaExploreBench, a benchmark for proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments. By instantiating environmental dynamics as hidden rules, AdaExploreBench requires agents to actively acquire evidence and infer the rules. Under implicit rule drift, the latent rule changes without announcement, requiring agents to detect from degraded performance that prior knowledge is stale and re-explore. Experiments on eight leading LLMs show that proactive and adaptive exploration remain challenging: GPT-6 Sol achieves only 61.9% calibrated accuracy, while providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance significantly by close to 10%. These results reveal a critical bottleneck in current LLM agents: they can often reason effectively from informative evidence once it is available, but struggle to actively acquire the right evidence and recognize when previously acquired evidence is no longer valid.
evidence_items.title: AdaExploreBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Proactive Exploration and Test-time Adaptation in Evolving Environments

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.
evidence_items.title: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model

evidence_items.summary: Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three-dimensional world. Yet spatial question answering offers limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language model (VLM) agents on active object-level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, camera calibration, and camera poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. The task requires coordinating viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage through object-scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets exceeding an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 and only 3.25% exceeding 0.9. These results reveal a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at https://github.com/JesseZZZZZ/SpatialScout.
evidence_items.title: SpatialScout: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore and Map 3D Scenes?

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Evaluating software agents on a full benchmark is expensive. A small task subset can preserve agent rankings while yielding inaccurate scores. Historical responses provide useful structure, but tasks with identical source responses can have different outcomes for a new target agent. We introduce Hierarchical Score Posterior Recovery (HSPR), which combines source-fitted response factors with uncertain group success rates. Observed target outcomes update the posteriors over the target latent state and group rates; posterior-guided acquisition selects subsequent tasks. Its score-based criterion equals the expected one-step reduction in full-score posterior variance. Observed successes and posterior-predictive counts for unqueried tasks yield a full-score posterior. The final estimate uses its median with source-selected calibration. At a 10% task budget on four task banks from the SWE-bench family, HSPR achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on three banks and the lowest maximum absolute error (MaxErr) on all four among the methods compared. Removing group uncertainty or replacing adaptive queries increases macro MAE in the respective controls. Macro MAE decreases across 5-20% budgets. Code and project resources are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: HSPR: Recovering Software-Agent Benchmark Scores via Hierarchical Posterior Inference

evidence_items.summary: Performing accurate protein-glycan docking is critical to understanding protein-glycan interactions which govern many biological processes. However, this important task is hampered by the lack of tailored datasets, benchmarks and models for protein-glycan docking. To fill this blank, we first curate a standard benchmark ProtGlycanDock for training and evaluating protein-glycan docking models under both protein and glycan generalization settings. On this benchmark, we evaluate ten models in three categories, physics-based docking methods, machine-learning-based docking models and molecular structure prediction models. To obtain more precise binding poses, we further propose two finetuning techniques to inject the knowledge of glycan conformations into a general-purpose molecular structure prediction model. These two techniques respectively augment model inputs with glycan topological features and refine glycan binding pose with a glycan energy loss. Benchmark results show the superiority of AlphaFold 3 among existing methods, and the two proposed finetuning techniques can be well combined to achieve a state-of-the-art model for protein-glycan docking. Also, we perform stratified benchmark analysis and case studies to better understand the strengths and weaknesses of current models, providing insights for future model improvements. We maintain datasets at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ProtGlycanDock/ProtGlycanDock and source codes at https://github.com/kasawa1234/ProtGlycanDock
evidence_items.title: ProtGlycanDock: Towards Accurate Protein-Glycan Docking with Tailored Dataset, Benchmark and Model

evidence_items.summary: Tool-using language agents increasingly perform regulated customer-service workflows, where a correct final state is insufficient: agents must also provide disclosures, obtain consent, and follow required procedures. Existing tool-agent benchmarks largely score final business states, accepting trajectories that reach correct outcomes through non-compliant processes. We introduce cxbench, a benchmark that evaluates outcome and process compliance separately across six regulated domains. Each task combines a customer request, a tool-based environment, and explicit process requirements. Rule cards link cited regulatory obligations to observable trace evidence. A hybrid grader combines deterministic checks for ordering and authority with an LLM judge for semantic requirements. We define a false-pass as an outcome-pass run that fails process checks. Across seven models and 120 tasks, 55.5% of the 840 retained executions are false-passes, representing 80.1% of outcome-passing runs; only 13.8% pass both checks. Process-inclusive evaluation changes the observed model ordering and exposes differences hidden by outcome-only scoring. cxbench makes these failures inspectable through trace-linked criteria.
evidence_items.title: CXBench: A Benchmark for Process-Compliant LLM Agents in Regulated Customer-Experience Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Conversational large language models can respond with warmth and reassurance while failing to advance the user's stated goal. We conceptualize this failure as $\textbf{goal displacement}$, the substitution of persona-maintenance content for goal-relevant substance. To measure it, we introduce $\textbf{GDB}$ (Goal Displacement Benchmark), comprising 230 scenarios across nine domains and $4{,}134$ human-scored responses from 18 models. A $2 \times 2$ taxonomy crosses hard constraints with emotional distress, distinguishing failures to confront infeasible goals or combine empathy with practical guidance from reverse displacement, where unsolicited problem-solving replaces requested emotional support. A deletion-test rubric assesses whether substantive help remains after purely supportive sentences are removed. Independent raters achieve weighted $κ= 0.82$ against author scores for displacement severity. Trap displacement ranges from $0.0\%$ to $37.7\%$ and is strongly negatively correlated with Chatbot Arena Elo ($ρ= -0.706$, $n = 15$). Reverse displacement reaches $41.9\%$, including substantial rates in models with negligible trap displacement. A factorial probe supports a distinction from social sycophancy. Human-scored responses in the high-complexity, low-pressure condition exhibit $35.0\%$ sycophancy but $7.5\%$ displacement, with little association between the constructs. Matched OLMo-2 checkpoints show that mixed empathy-with-constraints displacement remains at $52.3\%$ after supervised fine-tuning and falls to $13.8\%$ after direct preference optimization. GDB provides a reproducible diagnostic of whether responses advance the operationalized user goal, supporting model comparison, post-training evaluation, and regression testing. We release the dataset, annotations, and rubric under CC-BY-4.0 and the evaluation code under MIT.
evidence_items.title: When Empathy Misses the Goal: A Benchmark for Goal Displacement in LLM Advice

evidence_items.summary: We test whether Javo, a sales agent fine-tuned on 4.6 million consented, de-identified commercial conversations, sells better than a frontier general-purpose model and better than human sales associates. The evaluation has four parts. Study 1 scores the agent on two public sales benchmarks, SalesLLM and SmartSalesBench, against 10 frontier and open-weight models. Study 2 is a randomized controlled trial on 100 live websites in 14 industries (e-commerce, travel and hospitality, and high-consideration services), run from 1 May to 30 September 2026, in which 14.8 million visitors were randomized to no agent, Javo, or a frontier-model agent with an identical interface, catalog tools and guardrails. Study 3 isolates the effect of the model by comparing those two agent arms. Study 4 compares Javo with each site's own human associates on 20 sites with staffed live chat. Relative to no agent, Javo changed revenue per visitor by +10.0% (95% CI +5.1 to +14.9). Among engaged visitors, it changed conversion by +21.6% relative to the frontier-model agent (95% CI +16.9 to +26.3). Against human associates, its engaged conversion was 11.26% versus 11.20% (non-inferior, margin -7%, one-sided p = 0.004; no significant superiority), at 1.8% of the cost per conversation. Return rates, unsupported product claims and complaint rates met the prespecified safety guardrails.
evidence_items.title: Selling in the Wild: Benchmark and Randomized Field Evidence for a Sales Agent Trained on Commercial Conversations

evidence_items.summary: Comparing the predictive performance and computational cost of flow-based intrusion detection experiments requires both quantities to be available for each run. GreenNIDS connects benchmark execution on public NetFlow datasets to a reusable analysis dataset. Model implementations write a common set of outputs, which are ingested into a run-level table with companion tables for model configuration, feature importance, and training history. The run-level table combines predictive metrics with timing, throughput, memory use, and energy estimates based on thermal design power. A CPU-only demonstration comprises 216 runs across four dataset families, three versions, and binary and multiclass tasks. Ingestion produces a 216 x 96 analysis table with no duplicate run identifiers and complete Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and F1 coverage. Multiclass ROC-AUC is missing for 36 PyTorch runs, making metric availability an explicit part of subsequent comparisons. The stored records support grouped performance and training-time plots, as well as resource screening after execution. Combining task-specific MCC thresholds with limits on training time, peak RAM, and estimated training energy retains 25.0% of the full run collection. These results establish compatibility within the evaluated collection and support comparisons after execution, subject to the recorded preprocessing, execution profile, and approximate energy accounting.
evidence_items.title: GreenNIDS: A Benchmark Workflow and Analysis Dataset for NetFlow Intrusion Detection Experiments

evidence_items.summary: Reliable radio-based indoor localization is essential for industrial automation, yet existing methods are often evaluated in environments that do not fully reflect the severe multipath and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions encountered in real deployments. This limits our understanding of how AI, i.e., modern geometric, unsupervised, and semi-supervised localization methods generalize to industrial 5G settings. We present RAIL-5G, a public real-world 5G NR channel impulse response (CIR) benchmark recorded in an operational railway maintenance facility. RAIL-5G covers an 811m$^2$ indoor area with eight distributed radio units, robot-mounted user equipment (UE) trajectories, high-accuracy iGPS reference positions, and severe metal-induced multipath caused by train compartments and maintenance infrastructure. We benchmark geometric time-difference of arrival (TDoA), supervised fingerprinting, unsupervised channel charting, and self-supervised wireless pretraining methods. Our results highlight the difficulty of RAIL-5G: on the full dataset, TDoA reaches 7.02m mean average error (MAE), the best unsupervised method reaches 2.46m, and supervised fingerprinting achieves 0.52m. Self-supervised pretraining reduces the labeling effort by up to one order of magnitude, but the remaining gap to supervised learning shows that robust AI-based localization under severe multipath remains an open challenge. The dataset and code are available at https://iis.fraunhofer.de/rail-5g.
evidence_items.title: RAIL-5G: A Challenging Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for AI-Based 5G Indoor Localization

evidence_items.summary: Despite advancements in visible-thermal face recognition, where thermal probe (query) face images are matched against visible enrollment templates, existing benchmarks are currently limited by small gallery sizes (N $\approx$ 100 subjects). This limitation inhibits the ability to accurately evaluate visible-thermal facial recognition at scale and to report significant recognition performance metrics, which have better operational relevance. Therefore, we introduce VTF900, a large-scale visible-thermal face recognition benchmark with 900 subjects and paired imagery that includes expression, pose, and occlusion variations. VTF900 is designed to support large-scale (i.e., large gallery) evaluations across verification (1:1 matching) and closed-set identification (1:N matching) for visible-thermal face recognition. Furthermore, VTF900 specifically addresses the challenging combination of cross-spectral and cross-dataset analysis. In this paper, after training models on the ARL-VTF dataset, we provide benchmark analyses across convolutional (baseline), vision transformers, and domain-adaptive neural network architectures to assess how these methods scale. At full gallery scale (N = 900), transformer models achieve strong discriminative performance under frontal conditions (e.g., ViT-B: 97.68% AUC, 51.10% TAR@1%FAR), while domain-adaptive methods such as DPIT-ResNet50 demonstrate greater robustness under off-pose conditions (94.68%AUC, 36.08% TAR@1%FAR). Our results show that high AUC at small scale does not translate to reliable performance at deployment scale, and that pose variation significantly amplifies performance degradation. VTF900 exposes these limitations, enabling more rigorous evaluation of cross-spectral face recognition systems.
evidence_items.title: VTF900: A 900-Subject Visible-Thermal Face Recognition Dataset and Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Public leaderboards and pricing catalogues offer complementary but hard-to-combine views of the large language model ecosystem. We analyse three linked public sources: an archived Open LLM Leaderboard v2 sample of 4,565 open-weight evaluation records with complete six-benchmark scores; an 89-snapshot human-preference panel of 279 models (June 2024–August 2025); and 2,685 priced chat endpoints (October 2026). Principal component analysis identifies a dominant common component (74% of benchmark variance), retained by parallel analysis and robust to family deduplication. Benchmark performance rises with parameter count (13.6 points per tenfold) and with submission date at constant size and type (10.5 points per year) under family-clustered inference. A documented change of the default rating on 20 May 2025 shifted all listed scores by about 18 points; within the stable period the preference frontier rose by about 187 points per year relative to a fixed reference set through 17 leaders with median spells of 12 days, top-20 slots concentrated among fewer organisations, and ratings did not drift within models. Among 201 models listed by three or more providers, the median maximum-to-minimum price ratio is 1.38 (1.27 under version-strict identifiers). A hedonic model adjusting for time since first listing attributes multipliers of about 3.1 to one standard deviation of arena score and 0.18 to open-weight status, robust to version-exact matching. Preference ratings and benchmark averages agree strongly for 69 matched models. Temporal mismatch, selective coverage, and related model families preclude causal interpretation.
evidence_items.title: Capability, ranking dynamics, and inference pricing in the large language model ecosystem: evidence from linked public data

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning benchmarks act as guideposts for model development and spur the creation of training datasets intended to improve benchmark scores. We introduce BenchDoor, a family of data poisoning attacks that exploits this incentive. Beyond preserving benign performance, BenchDoor requires benchmark gains that encourage adoption of data that also implants a backdoor. The adversary either manipulates a benchmark's training or test data, creating an adversarial benchmark, or supplies an independent training dataset while leaving the benchmark unchanged. We formalize five attack scenarios, including training on rewritten test examples and applying similarity-based decontamination. Across multiple-choice Q&A, text classification, and open-ended Q&A with Qwen and Gemma models, BenchDoor achieves positive benchmark gains for all 30 evaluated configurations, with held-out attack success rates of 82.33% to 100.00% at poisoning rates of 2% to 10%. Both objectives remain achievable after synthetic data generation and similarity-based decontamination, with attack success rates of at least 90.33%. These findings show how benchmarks can serve as attack vectors both through their own data and through training resources that deliver improvements on them.
evidence_items.title: Adversarial Benchmarks and BenchDoor Attacks: Exploiting Benchmark Incentives for Backdoor Attacks

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Introduction Skin cancer is a growing global cause of morbidity and mortality. Rural populations are at an increased risk due to greater ultraviolet exposure and limited access to dermatology services. Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health information, their ability to accurately diagnose and triage skin lesions remains uncertain. Objectives To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy, triage safety and reproducibility of multimodal LLMs in interpreting skin lesions representative of rural clinical practice. Methods Seven multimodal LLMs from three developers (OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic) were evaluated using 34 histopathologically confirmed skin lesions from a rural Canadian practice. The dataset comprised paired macroscopic and dermoscopic images of both malignant and non-malignant lesions. Each image was assessed independently a total of five times by each model using a standardized prompt. Results A total of 2,380 model outputs were generated. Diagnostic accuracy varied widely across models (39.4%-72.1%). Claude Opus 4.8 achieved the highest accuracy (72.1%) and the best overall balance of sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility. GPT-5.5 Instant had the lowest specificity and highest over-triage rate, whereas Gemini 3.5 Flash had the lowest sensitivity and highest misclassification rate. Safe triage of malignant lesions ranged from 36% to 87%. Dermoscopic images significantly improved AI performance compared with macroscopic images (OR, 1.65; 95% Cl, 1.30–2.10; p < 0.001). Self-reported diagnostic confidence correlated poorly with model performance, and diagnostic reproducibility across repeated runs was moderate to almost perfect for most models. Conclusions Multimodal LLMs can interpret skin lesion images but are not yet accurate, consistent, or safe for independent diagnosis or triage.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating large language models for skin lesion diagnosis and triage in rural settings

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare relies on diverse mathematical frameworks, yet their contributions to model development, evaluation, interpretability, and clinical translation remain fragmented. This systematic review synthesized the classical and emerging mathematical foundations underpinning healthcare AI and examined major methodological and application trends. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, studies published between January 2016 and June 30, 2026, were identified through systematic searches of Scopus, Google Scholar, and PubMed/MEDLINE, with searches conducted using Harzing’s Publish or Perish v8 where applicable. Bibliometric analysis was performed using VOSviewer, while methodological quality was assessed using an adapted JBI-based framework and AMSTAR-2 for systematic reviews. Of 653 records identified, 147 studies met the eligibility criteria. Non-mutually exclusive mathematical-domain coding identified linear algebra in 100/147 studies (68.0%), calculus and optimization in 91/147 (61.9%), and probability and statistics in 79/147 (53.7%), highlighting their roles in data representation, learning, optimization, inference, uncertainty quantification, and validation. A separate mutually exclusive classification of dominant methodological themes identified explainable and trustworthy AI in 24/147 studies (16.3%), statistics and learning theory in 23/147 (15.6%), probability and Bayesian methods in 23/147 (15.6%), calculus and optimization in 19/147 (12.9%), and linear algebra in 15/147 (10.2%). Radiology and medical imaging were the leading healthcare application (24.3%), while classification and diagnosis were the most frequent clinical task (17.1%). Overall, healthcare AI is supported by an interconnected mathematical ecosystem. Emerging approaches, including graph neural networks, Transformers, and quantum machine learning, require stronger external validation, standardized benchmarking, and rigorous evaluation for reliable clinical translation.
evidence_items.title: Mathematical foundations of artificial intelligence in healthcare: a systematic review

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The heterogeneity of Point of Interest (POI) taxonomies is a persistent challenge for the integration of urban datasets and the development of location-based services. OpenStreetMap (OSM) adopts a flexible, community-driven tagging system, while Foursquare (FS) relies on a curated hierarchical structure. Here we release an openly available, manually validated benchmark dataset that links 1,205 OSM tags to full FS category paths, from broad thematic groups down to fine-grained labels. By making these two widely used but previously unconnected sources interoperable, the dataset enables consistent, multi-scale analyses of urban functions and can be downloaded and reused as a high-precision resource. The dataset is complemented by an automatic alignment procedure, combining text embeddings with LLM-based refinement, whose code we release to support scalable updates of the benchmark as OSM evolves. Together, these elements provide both a robust reference resource and a practical tool for the community. The benchmark is manually curated and validated to serve as a high-quality gold-standard reference, with direct applications to urban analytics, mobility studies, and smart city services.
evidence_items.title: An openly available OpenStreetMap-to-Foursquare category benchmark for points of interest

evidence_items.summary: As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important. We introduce StreamEval, a unified benchmark for interactive streaming video generation spanning five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing. StreamEval comprises 300 scripted test cases lasting 15-300s, each specifying initial assets, incrementally arriving multimodal requests, and explicit requirements for state changes and content preservation. Performance is assessed along four evaluation dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination, instantiated through ten task-specific metrics on a 0-100 scale. Evaluating 37 distinct models across 300 test cases, we find that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. In particular, request execution remains challenging: the highest task-specific scores are 36.90 for Following among seven avatar-performance models, 25.93 for Following in text-conditioned world generation, and 15.00 for Edit Success among three reported reference-editing models. These findings identify reliable request execution under timing and preservation constraints as a central challenge for advancing omni-modal real-time interactive systems. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai
evidence_items.title: StreamEval: Evaluating Interactive Streaming Video Generation Models

evidence_items.summary: A growing body of work proposes dynamic expert-skipping methods for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that adjust the number of experts activated per token during inference, aiming to preserve model quality while further reducing the number of active parameters. These methods have added calibrated importance scores, inter-expert similarity metrics, or learned per-token allocators in order to identify experts to skip. However, different calibration regimes, different reductions in the effective number of experts, and evaluation suites make comparisons difficult. We classify four representative prior methods into a unified taxonomy and benchmark them against a natural, simple baseline: statically reducing the number of experts $k$ (i.e., same reduced $k$ across all layers and tokens). We provide a fair comparison of these methods at matched expert-compute budget, on two modern MoEs (Gemma4-26B-A4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B) in a text-only setting and a contemporary vision-language model (Qwen3-VL) in a multimodal setting. Surprisingly, we find that the simple baseline is hard to outperform consistently across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings. The methods we benchmark often underperform the baseline and achieved gains, when present, are minor. We further find that the effective $k$ achieved (or optimized for) in calibration can diverge from the effective $k$ in testing, resulting in over- or under-estimating the compute at inference time. Based on these findings, we recommend a calibration-free per-modality static $k$ reduction and validate this on a held-out model and modality. We further argue that a static control at matched measured compute is the baseline any dynamic skipping method must beat.
evidence_items.title: Don't Skip the Baseline: A Controlled Comparison of Dynamic Expert Skipping in MoEs

The revised release includes five-seed model evaluation, bootstrap uncertainty estimation and a 2,000-replicate group-aware bootstrap analysis that accounts for observations sharing identical normalised texts. The archive also contains saved predictions, machine-readable statistical results, figure files, software requirements and instructions for reproducing the analyses. Original third-party datasets are not redistributed. Data-source information and input-file checksums are provided to support independent verification.

evidence_items.summary: As LLM-based agents are deployed with increasing autonomy in real-world environments, a critical failure mode emerges: agentic misalignment, where agents choose harmful actions over failure. However, existing safety benchmarks primarily evaluate whether agents comply with explicitly harmful instructions, leaving the conditions that cause agents to choose harmful actions poorly understood. To address this limitation, we propose AM-Bench, a unified taxonomy and 35 scenario evaluation benchmark spanning seven industries for agentic misalignment grounded in the fraud triangle, a well-established criminological framework explaining goal-directed misconduct. We adapt this framework to agentic environments and construct our evaluation suite and detection systems along three dimensions: perceived threat, perceived opportunity, and reasoning. We operationalize each dimension into structured subcategories rooted in prior theory: five threat categories derived from the instrumental convergence thesis, seven opportunity categories drawn from the Emergent Strategic Reasoning Risks (ESRR) taxonomy, and a novel four-question binary reasoning framework synthesized from prior literature. Our evaluation of 10 frontier models reveals a 62-percentage-point gap in misalignment across scenarios, with Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro exhibiting the highest levels of agentic misalignment while Claude Sonnet 4.6 displays near-zero rates across all conditions. Our reasoning framework further reveals that models may exhibit harmful behaviours without explicit situational awareness or explanation, complicating both mitigation and detection. AM-Bench scenarios and code are available at https://github.com/AI4Collaboration/Agentic-Misalignment-Bench
evidence_items.title: AM-Bench: A Unified Taxonomy and Evaluation Suite for Agentic Misalignment

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language processing; however, their direct application to food safety remains limited by insufficient domain knowledge, inadequate reasoning over regulatory documents, and the tendency to generate factual hallucinations. To address these challenges, this study proposes FSLLM, a domain-specific LLM designed for food safety applications. A high-quality domain corpus was constructed from diverse sources, including food safety incidents, regulatory documents, inspection reports, and industry-related materials. It initially comprised approximately 150 million tokens, of which 45,024 documents and approximately 121 million tokens were retained after decontamination. Based on the Qwen3-8B foundation model, FSLLM was developed through a two-stage training framework consisting of continual pre-training for domain knowledge adaptation and supervised fine-tuning for task alignment. Furthermore, a comprehensive benchmark covering 10 representative food safety tasks, including named entity recognition, text classification, text generation, factual verification, regulatory compliance analysis, and public health question answering, was established for systematic evaluation. Experimental results show that FSLLM outperforms the base model across multiple food safety tasks. Specifically, FSLLM achieved a Micro-F1 score of 0.5286 in named entity recognition and an accuracy of 85.21% in food safety event classification, demonstrating improvements over the base model. These findings indicate that domain-specific corpus and continual pre-training with fine-tuning enhance LLM expertise and reasoning, offering a viable solution for intelligent food safety supervision and risk analysis.
evidence_items.title: Data Engineering and Large Language Model Construction for the Food Safety Domain

evidence_items.summary: Forecasting the seasonal dynamics of Aedes albopictus, a highly invasive arbovirus vector now established across much of Europe, is a growing public health priority. Numerous mechanistic and correlative models have been developed over the last two decades, but largely in isolation, each calibrated and validated against its own data, which has prevented any assessment of where predictive capacity is genuinely limited. Rather than ranking models, which were built for different purposes and cannot be reduced to a single skill score, we establish common ground: a shared evaluation framework in which six mechanistic models, one correlative machine learning model, and two naive baseline predictors are driven by identical ERA5-Land forcing and assessed against the harmonised VectAbundance ovitrap dataset (Albania, Italy, Switzerland) using a single protocol, with robustness quantified by bootstrap resampling. We additionally combine the models into a weighted ensemble via approximate Bayesian computation. Both naive baselines outperformed every process-based and machine learning model, and the ensemble matched but did not exceed the best individual models. Predictive skill varied markedly in space, with all model classes, including the uncalibrated baselines, performing best in intensively monitored regions and worst at sparsely sampled sites. This pattern suggests that geographic variation in skill reflects the density and consistency of surveillance data more than differences in model complexity. We present this benchmark not as a league table but as shared infrastructure, common evaluation data, covariates, and protocol, on which comparable, policy-relevant forecasting tools can be built, and we argue that sustained, harmonised surveillance is the principal precondition for operational Ae. albopictus prediction.
evidence_items.title: A common benchmark for Aedes albopictus phenological models reveals surveillance data, not model complexity, as the limiting factor

evidence_items.summary: Object-detection benchmark scores are often transferred across settings without restating the evaluation target that gives a metric its meaning. This focused interpretive review examines how that target changes along a scale-centered path from regular-scale to small-object detection, with point-based targets treated as a representation-dependent branch. Orientation-aware and temporal evaluation are treated as selected extensions when geometric representation or sequence-level evaluation targets require criteria beyond scale alone. Across these settings, the review distinguishes reporting protocols, matching and localization measures, and loss-derived formulations used mainly for optimization. An intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold can determine whether a prediction is matched to a target, while precision and recall describe an operating point and average precision, mean average precision, and average recall summarize behavior under a specified benchmark protocol. The same metric label can therefore support different claims when thresholds, annotation granularity, prediction structure, or temporal targets differ. A four-slot evaluation contract makes the prediction target, matching primitive, reporting endpoint, and metric role explicit. A cross-setting guide links those slots to protocol selection. Reassessments of Common Objects in Context (COCO), Dataset for Object Detection in Aerial Images (DOTA), and multi-object tracking (MOT) predictions connect scale-conditioned reporting, geometric matching, and identity continuity to concrete interpretation decisions. The review synthesizes these findings into a practical guide for reading benchmark evidence and choosing evaluation protocols.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation Protocols and Benchmark Interpretation for Deep Learning-Based Object Detection: A Scale-Centered Review

evidence_items.summary: Chinese short-form dramas (duanju) drive a growing demand for automated Japanese dubbing that preserves each character’s voice. The decisive component is zero-shot cross-lingual voice cloning: synthesising Japanese speech from a short Chinese reference clip. We benchmark four neural text-to-speech systems—GPT-SoVITS v3, F5-TTS, CosyVoice2-0.5B, and the non-cloning commercial baseline EdgeTTS—on an annotated short-drama corpus (79 episodes, 3692 segments, 12 speakers) with native-speaker-verified Japanese references, combining automatic intelligibility (Whisper re-transcription) and speaker-embedding similarity with a blind listening study by five JLPT-N1 raters. Among cloning systems, only GPT-SoVITS attains usable intelligibility (character error rate 0.215, against 1.152 for F5-TTS and 4.603 for CosyVoice2), while EdgeTTS is most intelligible overall (0.030). Critically, the automatic and perceptual measures dissociate: F5-TTS scores marginally higher on embedding similarity (0.729 vs. 0.722), yet raters preferr GPT-SoVITS three to one. Naturalness shows no detectable gap between GPT-SoVITS and EdgeTTS (mean opinion score 3.08 versus 3.12, p=0.93), a null result at a resolution of about 0.6 points. In a single-speaker probe, speaker similarity rises from 0.64 to 0.71 as the reference lengthens from 3 to 10 s. Embedding similarity alone is therefore an unreliable proxy for perceived speaker identity.
evidence_items.title: Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Japanese Voice Cloning to Dub Chinese Short Dramas: A Four-System Benchmark with Human Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) affects social interaction and communication, and automatically recognizing emotions from the facial expressions of children with ASD remains challenging. A key barrier to facial emotion recognition (FER) in children with ASD is the absence of ASD-specific datasets with proper emotion-level annotations. To address this, we present ASD-FER , a benchmark of 2,779 facial images of children with ASD annotated across six emotion categories by three independent annotators using majority voting. We evaluate nine models — CNN, SVM, AlexNet, ResNet34, ResNet50, MobileNetV2, and three backbone configurations of our proposed task-specific architecture, EQFormer : ViT, Swin-T, and a compact Hybrid CNN-Transformer (HybridT) — under stratified 10-fold cross-validation and a held-out 90/10 evaluation. ResNet50 led conventional models at 84.89% mean cross-validation accuracy; among transformer-based models, ViT led with 88.27%, followed by Swin-T at 88.02% and HybridT at 86.58%. On the held-out set, ViT achieved the highest overall accuracy (91.01%), while Swin-T obtained the best balanced accuracy (74.47%) and macro-F1 (0.7078); HybridT remained competitive at 89.57% accuracy with a fraction of the parameters. To support explainability, Grad-CAM visualizations highlighted attention on emotion-relevant facial regions — eyes, eyebrows, and mouth — with Swin-T the most spatially focused and the HybridT the most parameter-efficient (2.66M). Class imbalance and cross-dataset generalization remain open challenges.
evidence_items.title: ASD-FER: An Annotated Multi-Class Benchmark and Comparative Study for Facial Emotion Recognition in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder

evidence_items.summary: Background Clinical trial data pipelines must follow Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium (CDISC) standards, including the study data tabulation model (SDTM) and analysis data model (ADaM). General-purpose large language models (LLMs) can produce plausible artifacts that omit required variables, misuse terminology, or invent derivation logic. Curated context may reduce these errors, but the value of organizing that context by workflow topology has not been separated from corpus access alone. Objective This study aimed to examine when workflow topology–guided skill loading adds value beyond a domain prompt, nonrouted curated context, or lexical retrieval, and whether bounded scheduling retains quality with less injected context. Methods A 45-node, 7-layer directed acyclic workflow graph was linked to 59 modular rule files (SKILL.md). A sequential exploratory evaluation examined 4 evidence regimes spanning domain-context, component isolation, lexically reachable, and topology-dependent conditions (10 tasks, 90 runs; 10 tasks, 180 and 120 runs; 24 tasks, 288 runs; and 18 tasks, 324 runs; the task, not the agent run, was the inferential unit). End points included LLM rubric scores, deterministic atomic criteria, required-evidence recall, and manifest checks. A blinded practicing statistical programmer independently rescored 60 outputs. Task-level paired inference used bootstrap 95% CIs, exact sign-flip tests, and Holm adjustment. Results Routed context scored 4.63 versus 4.20 for prompt-only (difference 0.43 on a 1-5 scale; 95% CI 0.25-0.63; Holm-adjusted P=.01) but did not exceed flat or random loading. The lower-context scheduler used 28.82% less context while retaining quality; all 559 injected fragments had recorded sources, and all 120 manifests were reproduced exactly.
evidence_items.title: Workflow Topology–Guided Skill Loading for Agentic AI in Clinical Trial Data Pipelines: Sequential Exploratory Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed where tools fail, objectives change, and constraints tighten while a task is in progress. Prevailing benchmarks score only static end-task accuracy and therefore miss mid-episode responsiveness, which is the ability to adapt and recover after a controlled change. We present a responsiveness evaluation framework that pairs three agent architectures (ReAct, Reflexion, and Plan-and-Execute) with three deterministic synthetic environments (tool planning, debugging, and constraint planning) and injects tool denial, goal modification, or constraint injection at graded severity. Across two matched factorial grids of 4,320 episodes each—one with an explicit perturbation notice and one silent. ReAct attains the highest pooled reward (0.544), yet Plan-and-Execute leads on tool planning (0.711 vs. 0.532) while collapsing on constraint planning (0.114). Tool denial uniquely depresses behavioural recovery, and severity within [0.1, 0.9] yields no monotone dose–response. Explicit notices do not improve mean reward for any architecture. Code, logs, and analysis pipelines are released for extension.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking the responsiveness of LLM-based agentic systems under controlled mid-task perturbations

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer knowledge from large-scale pretraining into robot control, but their manipulation performance remains sensitive to changes in observation conditions, which recent work addresses by fine-tuning the visual module on target-domain data. However, it remains unclear how such adaptation affects robustness beyond the target condition, as existing robustness benchmarks only evaluate models without fine-tuning and adaptation studies only report the target gain. Measuring this cross-dimension effect requires separating target gains from off-target changes, isolating adaptation effects from architectural differences, ruling out generic forgetting, and comparing tuning choices. Therefore, we introduce VLA-Retain, a benchmark that compares five open VLA models, tuned on Camera-view or Sensor-noise data, with their own base checkpoints on LIBERO-Plus dataset spanning seven perturbation dimensions. Our study reveals four findings. First, targeted vision tuning is not local, and its target gain does not predict retention. Mean off-target gain is negative in 8 of 10 model--domain configurations. Under Camera-view tuning, X-VLA gains $69.4$ percentage points on the target but loses $4.6$ points on average elsewhere, whereas OpenVLA-OFT gains $39.3$ and $1.4$ points, respectively. Second, these regressions are not explained only by performance loss on the same tasks without perturbations. Third, broader training coverage raises overall gain over target-specific training but does not eliminate dimension-level regressions. Fourth, tuning strategies are model-dependent, as DELTA-style feature preservation raises X-VLA's mean off-target gain to $+1.2$ points but lowers OpenVLA-OFT's to $-23.1$. Overall, these findings show that target-domain success alone is insufficient and highlight cross-dimensional retention as a key criterion for targeted VLA adaptation.
evidence_items.title: VLA-Retain: Benchmarking Cross-Dimension Effects of Vision Tuning in VLAs

evidence_items.summary: Visual manuals communicate procedural knowledge through stepwise diagrams, but translating these instructions into reliable long-horizon robotic execution remains challenging. We introduce JARVIS, a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous visual-manual-guided execution without additional language instructions. JARVIS comprises 236,679 LEGO assembly tasks across 8,987 scenes, with a carefully curated JARVIS-v1 suite of 50 tasks for interactive robotic evaluation. Tasks span varying initial structural complexities and assembly horizons, requiring agents to interpret manuals, ground actions in an evolving workspace, and execute the intended procedure. A structure-aware evaluation protocol captures geometric accuracy, structural relations, construction order, partial progress, and completion. We further introduce JARVIS-agentic, a tool-grounded embodied agent that composes robot primitives into executable programs and uses execution feedback for verification and recovery, without task-specific action trajectories or model parameter updates. Across nine multimodal and reasoning models, task-oriented primitives increase the average assembly score. Performance nevertheless declines sharply with assembly horizon, and execution errors remain difficult to correct. Prior-task experience improves initial performance, while repeated reflection provides inconsistent benefits, highlighting persistent limitations in connecting visual procedural reasoning with reliable physical execution.
evidence_items.title: JARVIS: From Visual Manuals to Autonomous Robotic Assembly
