evidence_items.summary: Tool-using LLM agents increasingly answer e-commerce queries through multi-step tool interactions. The expected output of a tool call can shift between agent development and execution, allowing a plausible but incorrect value to be returned without an explicit failure signal. These silent errors may propagate through subsequent decisions into final answers. To study agents' resilience across this end-to-end process, we formulate Silent-error Resilience Task, an interactive task that evaluates whether they complete the original query after a silent error corrupts an intermediate state. We introduce RITE, a benchmark built from human-authored industrial workflows and production-log-derived inputs. To enable controlled and reproducible evaluation, we use a semantic error taxonomy to inject errors into fixed workflow prefixes, freeze recorded tool behavior, and let agents continue freely. It contains 167 matched units across nine e-commerce workflows, yielding 501 silent-error, correct-value, and explicit-failure instances. Across 10 recent LLMs, silent errors roughly halve task success and are consistently harder than explicit failures. Recognition, use of an available verification path, and integration of the resulting evidence form successive bottlenecks. We also propose a light State Checker as an intervention to test whether resilience can be improved.
evidence_items.title: RITE: Evaluating End-to-End Resilience to Silent Tool Errors in E-Commerce Agentic Systems

evidence_items.summary: Five Large-Scale Unit Commitment MILP Instances This dataset contains five deterministic mixed-integer linear programming instances for thermal generation and pumped-storage hydropower scheduling. Each model covers 96 scheduling periods of 15 minutes, representing a 24-hour horizon. The instances retain the original identifiers Physics 1 through Physics 5. They range from 100 to 1,508 thermal units and 15 to 150 pumped-storage units, with 145,456–2,061,959 constraint rows, 66,240–955,008 variables and 31,680–463,104 binary variables. The models include commitment, startup/shutdown, minimum up/down times, ramping, piecewise-linear costs, storage operating modes and energy balance, power balance, upward reserve and network interface flow limits. Explicit N-1 contingency constraints are not included. Five gzip-compressed MPS files preserve the original models without presolve or reductions. Supplementary JSON metadata provides unit/time variable mappings, selected temporal parameters, original identifiers and checksums. An independent Python script verifies model integrity, dimensions and metadata using only the standard library. The MPS files define the mathematical optimization problems. The additional UC metadata provides interpretation without modifying the constraints. Modeling limitations and missing metadata are documented in the README. evidence_items.summary: As computer-use agents (CUAs) move to long-horizon workflows spanning multiple applications, undetected errors can silently corrupt persistent state and cause cascading failures in subsequent actions. Reliable error detection and recovery have become critical bottlenecks for building robust CUAs. However, existing benchmarks focus primarily on end-to-end task performance, providing limited insight into whether agents can detect and recover from errors during execution. The few benchmarks that evaluate recovery rely largely on manually injected errors, which may not reflect the types or horizons of failures induced by real agent policies. We introduce CUA-Recovery, a benchmark comprising test and training suites across multiple desktop applications. We construct it using ReRail, a framework for synthesizing long-horizon tasks and trajectories in a persistent desktop environment. ReRail composes MyPCBench tasks into new long-horizon workflows with executable ground truth, collects verifier-confirmed failures from multiple policies, and turns them into verified recovery trajectories. CUA-Recovery comprises a human-verified test suite of 2,250 erroneous states over 100 tasks and a training suite of 8.6K trajectories over 377 tasks. Evaluation on the test suite shows that agents struggle both to recognize inherited errors and to complete the task. Across six agents and six takeover depths, Error Awareness Rate (EAR) reaches at most 44.0% and Pass@3 at most 25.5%. After fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on the training suite, its average EAR rises from 19.9% to 35.2% on held-out recovery states, and its Rubric Score goes from 5.0% to 16.1%. It also gains 15.3 points on MyPCBench and 10.8 points on Odysseys for Pass@3, showing that the training trajectories help both with recovery and with completing tasks from a clean start. Our code is available at https://github.com/xu-hu-2002/CUA-Recovery.
evidence_items.title: CUA-Recovery: Benchmarking Error Recovery in Long-Horizon Computer-Use Agents

evidence_items.summary: Modern generative models can produce visually plausible images while violating exact identity constraints. Evaluating such failures requires distinguishing violations of the requested identity from permissible variation in appearance. We introduce Low-Entropy Visual Identity (LEVI), which characterizes visual identities determined by compact facts and explicit rules. The low-entropy requirement concerns identity uncertainty, while appearance may remain diverse. We formulate identity fidelity in terms of the probability that a conditional image distribution assigns to the identities permitted by the prompt. Visual Identity Spaces (VIS) formalize this distinction by specifying admissible identity values and which different realizations express the same identity. Building on this formulation, we develop Verifiable Visual Grammar (VVG), a declarative language whose typed primitives and compositional constraints describe identity-bearing structures. Using this grammar, we build a benchmark for image generation. It assesses each output against the task's identity requirements, drawing evidence from the final pixels. The curated benchmark contains 1,375 tasks spanning 120 base identity spaces across six domains. Among ten evaluated model configurations, the highest whole-task pass rate is 58.69%. These results reveal a persistent gap between visually plausible images and faithful realization of their specified identities. Project page: https://maxiao0234.github.io/LEVI/.
evidence_items.title: LEVI: Benchmarking Visual Identity Fidelity with Verifiable Low-Entropy Constructs

evidence_items.summary: Personalization is classically a two-party problem: a sender chooses what to say, and a receiver with independent objectives decides whether to act. A salesperson pitching the same analytics product leads with HIPAA compliance for a hospital and real-time reporting for a retailer, expecting a different argument to work on each. Existing LLM personalization benchmarks measure a narrower, one-party property: whether output matches the preferences of the same user it serves—sender and receiver being the same, as when RLHF aligns an assistant to its own user. The two-party case is harder to study automatically, since it needs ground truth linking specific content to an observed receiver action.Sales outreach provides this: a message written for one prospect, recorded against whether it produced a reply, a call, or a closed deal. We introduce SDR-Arena, a framework for benchmarking two-party generative personalization at scale, and SDR-Bench, a public corpus of 50,000 customer success stories across 22 industries and 3500 enterprises. Given only pre-outcome information, an agent must reconstruct the arguments that won the deal, scored by a weighted nugget-recall metric (WCS). The best model, Claude Sonnet 4.6, reaches 55.8% WCS indicating it recovers only half the winning content—a plateau we observe across model families that costly deep-research pipelines do not close. An ablation shows the cause is retrieval, not reasoning: models improve substantially given the facts a human researcher would gather, but rarely find them through web search alone. Two studies with professional SDRs support the metric: only 48% of generated pitches were rated usable without editing, and WCS yields model rankings consistent with evaluation against expert strategies authored independently of any model output.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking the Personalization Capabilities of Large Language Models

organizations: Department of Computer Science, Faculty of Information Technology, Farabi University, Almaty 050040, Kazakhstan
evidence_items.summary: Legal question answering is usually evaluated as if the law were static. In Kazakhstan, it changed twice within one year: a new Constitution replaced the 1995 text on 1 July 2026, and a new Tax Code replaced its predecessor on 1 January 2026, both reusing article numbers for different norms. We release a dated corpus of 41 Kazakhstani acts parsed to article level in both official languages (12,235 Russian and 11,973 Kazakh articles) and a benchmark of 150 question-answer pairs in seven layers, two of which score declining to answer and asking for a date. Two practising lawyers confirmed every pair. Comparing a no-retrieval baseline, retrieval-augmented generation and a tool-using agent, we find that retrieval rather than generation accounts for most citation error, measured against each pair’s source articles: given the gold article, the model cites it in 92% of cases, and retrieval alone reduces citations of non-existent norms from 31% to zero. The agent adds nothing on this measure and abstains far less often. Dense retrieval improves citation recall but nearly doubles the repealed norms presented as current; date-aware ranking removes them for every retriever, although under dense retrieval it also removes three historically required citations. The retrieval findings are reproduced on two open models.
evidence_items.title: A Dated Corpus and a Seven-Layer Benchmark for Kazakhstani Legal Question Answering

Artificial Intelligence Technology Institute, SRM University-AP
evidence_items.summary: Rare malignant cells in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), including circulating tumor cells (CTCs), minimal residual disease (MRD) cells, and small malignant populations in heterogeneous tumor microenvironments (TME), represent an important clinical challenge. These cells occur at very low frequency, requiring separation from a large non-malignant background. Existing methods show inconsistent evaluation, using different datasets, label definitions, prevalence settings, scoring strategies, and failure handling. We present Rare-cell Evaluation Across Cancer Heterogeneity (REACH), treating inter-lineage rare malignant cell detection as an imbalanced ranking task. REACH benchmarks CNV-supported malignant cells (P HC) against immune, stromal, and normal epithelial cells (B HC), modeling the CTC and MRD screening setting. REACH excludes intra-lineage state discovery, including drug-tolerant persisters, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), and transitional malignant states, evaluating these separately in Track F. REACH combines confidence tiered multi-arm labels with five evaluation tracks, covering controlled real spike-ins, synthetic Splatter stress tests, null background controls, natural blood/CTC prevalence, and supervised label noise diagnostics. Applying standardized method wrappers, fallback-aware metrics, non-parametric statistics, and audited figure regeneration, REACH provides a reproducible evaluation framework. REACH evaluates 10 computational methods on 10 curated scRNA-seq cancer datasets containing 359,739 cells. This benchmark produces 11,250 performance measurements across 1,125 benchmark tasks. The supervised highly variable gene logistic regression ceiling achieves a median average precision of 1.0, indicating strong expression differences between tumor and non-tumor cells. Current unsupervised methods recover only part of this signal.
evidence_items.title: REACH: a reproducible benchmark for inter-lineage rare malignant cell detection in single-cell RNA sequencing

evidence_items.summary: Background Sea turtle rehabilitation is widely practiced worldwide, yet standardized benchmark indicators for objectively evaluating rehabilitation quality are currently lacking. This study aimed to establish and evaluate a set of benchmark indicators for assessing rehabilitation outcomes in sea turtles while providing long-term epidemiological information on the principal causes of admission to a wildlife rehabilitation center. Methods A retrospective study included 2,278 sea turtle admission records from the La Tahonilla Wildlife Rehabilitation Center (LTWRC), Tenerife, Spain, between 1982 and 2025. After excluding eight readmission records, the first-admission dataset comprised 2,270 individual turtles: 2,216 loggerhead turtles ( Caretta caretta ) and 54 green turtles ( Chelonia mydas ). Rehabilitation performance was evaluated using cause-specific benchmark indicators, including euthanasia (E r ), unassisted mortality during hospitalization (M r ), and release (R r ) rates, time to final disposition, post-release readmissions, and standardized rehabilitation costs. Results Entanglement in fishing gear and/or plastic materials was the most common cause at first admission (42.8%), whereas unknown/undetermined causes predominated among turtles dead on first admission (63.9%). Outcomes for turtles alive at first admission were E r = 1.4%, M r = 12.5%, and R r = 86%. Rehabilitation outcome was strongly influenced by the primary cause of admission, with entanglement associated with significantly higher odds of release, whereas trauma, hook/monofilament ingestion, and infectious disease were associated with significantly higher unassisted mortality. Among hospitalization episodes resulting in release, median rehabilitation time ranged from 10 days for crude oil exposure to 37 days for trauma. Post-release readmissions were uncommon (16/1,560 turtles; 1.0%), accounting for 22 readmission events; all 20 events involving turtles admitted alive resulted in release.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark indicators for evaluating sea turtle rehabilitation outcomes at a wildlife rehabilitation center on Tenerife island, Spain (1982–2025)

organizations: Department of Industrial Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah 21589, Saudi Arabia
evidence_items.summary: Financial forecasting under uncertainty is fundamental to strategic investment decision making. Among the factors that influence investment decisions, market efficiency plays a critical role because it determines whether historical information can provide predictive value for future market behavior. The Hurst exponent is widely used to measure persistence and weak-form market efficiency, where values close to 0.5 indicate random behavior and values above or below 0.5 indicate persistent or mean-reverting dynamics. Despite extensive research using the Hurst exponent to characterize market persistence and market-efficiency-related behavior, limited studies have investigated whether future Hurst exponent estimates can be forecast using machine learning techniques and whether these models can outperform a simple constant benchmark. This study addresses this gap by developing a machine learning framework to forecast the next-month Hurst exponent using firm-level descriptive, financial, technical, and statistical indicators and comparing their performance against a constant benchmark. A dataset comprising 141 Saudi-listed companies, 705 firm-month observations, approximately 147 predictor variables, and five monthly periods was constructed. Monthly Hurst exponent values were estimated using the Rescaled Range (R/S) method and used as the target variable. Linear Regression, Ridge Regression, Elastic Net, Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random Forest, and XGBoost were evaluated using an expanding-window time-series validation strategy with two chronological forecast origins. Model performance was assessed using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the coefficient of determination (R2). None of the evaluated machine learning models outperformed the constant benchmark, which achieved the lowest RMSE (0.227) and MAE (0.179).
evidence_items.title: Do Machine Learning Models Beat a Constant Benchmark When Forecasting Next-Month Hurst Exponents? Evidence from Saudi-Listed Firms

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents now trade real capital using news as evidence, yet they cannot reliably tell fabricated headlines from real news. Because they read the same feeds under near-identical policies, a single fabricated post can push them into the same trade at the same moment. We present a systematic attack benchmark for information injection against LLM trading agents. Unlike prompt injection, which targets the model's instructions, information injection targets the evidence the agent trusts. The benchmark spans five injection vectors and seven event categories, evaluated over ~10,000 decisions on 15 U.S. stocks. Five findings emerge. (i) Prompt injection achieves 14% attack success rate (ASR), but fabricated news reaches 62% and two 30-word templates reach 100% on all 15 stocks, inverting the usual LLM-security intuition. (ii) For fact-poisoning templates, surface form matters more than content, since removing credibility cues such as a named source or a"BREAKING"tag drops ASR from 100% to 0% while the fake claim remains identical. (iii) Success depends on the agent's state, with a fake indicator panel scoring 91% against an agent about to hold but 12% against one about to buy. (iv) Attacks generalize across model vendors and remain effective when blended, unlabeled, into real news feeds. (v) Most attacks evade standard defenses, since model scaling stops shallow vectors but not fact poisoning, peer debate fails, and only hierarchical aggregation reduces ASR.
evidence_items.title: Fake News, Real Crashes: Information Injection Attacks on LLM Financial Trading Agents

evidence_items.summary: Complementary-label learning (CLL) trains a classifier from labels that name a class an instance does not belong to. Such labels are cheap to collect from crowdworkers or vision-language models (VLMs), making them attractive for large-scale annotation. However, both sources can mistakenly assign the true class as the complementary label. Such annotation errors are particularly harmful in CLL because the model is explicitly trained to suppress the correct answer. Optimal transport (OT) data valuation identifies harmful samples by comparing training data with a clean validation set, but transferring it directly to CLL creates a semantic mismatch: label $c$ means not class $c$ in the training but class $c$ in the validation. We show that this makes the OT label groups noisy mixtures whose behavior depends on the noise rate. The transferred score is informative only at sufficiently high noise, becomes uninformative at the crossover rate $1/M$ for $M$ classes, and reverses below it, where practical CLL annotation typically operates. We propose CAVA, which introduces a complementary label cost and a label margin that isolates the contribution of each complementary label to the transport potential. The margin keeps a consistent direction across noise rates, detects diagonal noise with a parameter-free threshold of closed-form precision, and allows detected samples to be recycled as ordinary-label supervision. On synthetic and human-annotated benchmarks, CAVA separates diagonal noise almost perfectly where directly transferred OT valuation performs worse than random. With only a fraction of the clean validation data, it also improves every CLL objective we evaluate, showing that OT-based valuation becomes reliable once the semantics of complementary supervision are modeled explicitly.
evidence_items.title: CAVA: Complementary-Label-Aware Data Valuation

evidence_items.summary: Recent embodied systems increasingly build on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for their pretrained understanding and reasoning capabilities, but their perception of the physical world remains largely limited to basic modalities such as vision and audio. However, broadening MLLMs to more diverse sensory modalities from the physical environment is challenging: their representations are often weakly connected to the MLLM and vary substantially in structure and statistics, while their interpretation still requires shared high-level understanding and reasoning. We therefore propose Unisense, a unified embodied MLLM framework that supports diverse physical sensory modalities within a shared multimodal architecture. Unisense follows a two-stage training process: (i) aligning sensory representations with language to establish a language-accessible interface; and (ii) tuning modality-specific experts within the shared LLM to provide specialized processing for different sensory modalities. To support broad sensory learning, we curate Unisense-1M, a large-scale embodied sensory training corpus comprising 1M samples across 8 sensory modalities. We further evaluate Unisense on 12 benchmarks spanning depth, point cloud, IMU, tactile, thermal, radar, motion, and smell understanding. Across these heterogeneous sensing tasks, Unisense achieves strong performance and outperforms both generalist and specialized models on most benchmarks, demonstrating the potential of pretrained MLLMs as unified models for embodied sensory understanding.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Omni: A Unified MLLM for Embodied Sensory Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. We evaluate the resulting open-ended artifacts using independently verifiable keypoints and complementary programmatic and VLM judges. Across nine frontier (M)LLMs, the strongest system achieves an overall score of only 52.12 out of 100, revealing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains a substantial challenge for current models in practical webpage-development settings.
evidence_items.title: RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development

evidence_items.summary: Platforms that host young users screen messages with commercial text-safety APIs, but independent evidence on how often such systems miss harm or flag harmless text is scarce, especially outside English, and the documentation of the one studied here leaves its false-positive rate unquantified. We evaluated one such API, Tuteliq Detect as deployed under the release identifier tuteliq-detect-v5.20261011 (not the separately published v6 model), on six harm categories: authorised push-payment fraud, money-mule recruitment, social engineering, romance scams, gambling harm and bullying. We built SITO (Synthetic Independent Text-safety benchmark with Overflagging tests; sito is Ukrainian for'sieve'), 2,332 synthetic cases in English, Ukrainian and mixed Ukrainian, with each harmful case matched by hard harmless ones: same-topic messages, minimal-edit contrasts, warnings and retrospective accounts. On English text the system flagged 84.9-94.1% of harmful cases and 0-4.3% of harmless ones per category. It missed third-party reports of ongoing harm far more often than perpetrators'messages (63.6% against 95.1% recall, all languages), when sent without the settings the API offers for reports of harm. Ukrainian and mixed-language input was detected at least as often as English, recall was lower on text from a held-out generator family, so headline recall may be optimistic, and 3.2% of cases received a different decision in repeated runs. A platform should measure false positives on its own traffic and check how bystander reports are handled. The datasets, generation prompts and code are released.
evidence_items.title: SITO: Sifting a Commercial Text-Safety API for Missed Harm and False Flags in English, Ukrainian and Surzhyk

evidence_items.summary: Gene perturbation models aim to predict transcriptional responses to unseen genetic interventions, but comparisons rely on heterogeneous evaluation metrics and differentially-expressed (DE) gene subsets. We investigate the consequences of these choices using eight methods across six single-gene perturbation datasets under a unified evaluation protocol. Varying the number of top DE genes reveals substantial instability in Precision-based rankings, with the winning method changing $86.7\%$ of the time, while rankings based on the rest of the metrics remain comparatively stable. Investigating this discrepancy exposes that repeating a single predicted expression profile across cell-level rows, a standard practice for many methods, can inflate significance estimates and produce excessively large predicted significant-DE sets. Specifically we found that $67.1\%$ of tested perturbation--gene pairs pass the significance threshold despite some of them having minuscule effects. We derive an inflation factor showing that replicated predictions can amplify the standardized Mann--Whitney statistic even after correction for tied ranks, without adding independent information. This artifact changes Precision mainly as the number of DE genes increases because for smaller cutoffs, most of the genes are already significant due to the effect-based ordering. Taking this pitfall into account in our benchmark comparison, we find that a random forest using Gene Ontology features achieves the best overall results.
evidence_items.title: A Pitfall in the Evaluation of Gene Perturbation Models

evidence_items.summary: Extracting meaningful patterns from complex, real-world environments, such as noisy IoT sensor networks or e-commerce systems with promotional discounts, requires handling data uncertainty and mixed profit structures. Top-k high-utility itemset mining identifies the k most profitable patterns in transactional data without requiring a user-defined minimum utility threshold. Existing algorithms are designed only for deterministic databases with positive item profits and do not address uncertain data containing both positive and negative utilities. To bridge this critical gap, this paper formulates this problem and introduces two complementary algorithmic approaches. The first approach, PTK-HUIM, is an exact prefix-growth framework based on the Utility-Probability-Utility List (UPU-List) and a two-level pruning mechanism using Positive Transaction-Weighted Utility (PTWU) and Positive Upper Bound (PUB). PTK-HUIM supports three search strategies: depth-first search, breadth-first search, and best-first search. All three strategies are proven to produce the same correct results. The second approach, UTKU-PSO, is the first heuristic algorithm developed for this problem. It extends Particle Swarm Optimization by incorporating probability-aware fitness estimation, PTWU-based bit clearing, and a shifted roulette-wheel selection mechanism to effectively handle negative expected utilities. A counterexample establishes that the classical transaction-weighted utility bound remains unsafe in this combined setting even after probability weighting, so PTWU and PUB are required for correctness rather than merely for efficiency. Since no natively uncertain benchmark with mixed utilities is publicly available, the evaluation augments six real-world benchmark datasets with synthetic existential probabilities, and every reported result is therefore conditional on that assumed model; robustness is assessed under three further probability models, one of which violates the independence assumption and shifts the identity of up to 61% of the top-k set. Experiments show that no single search strategy dominates: pairwise differences are not statistically significant across the suite, because frontier-ordered strategies visit up to 5.9 times fewer nodes but pay up to 17.9 times more per node, and which term prevails depends on transaction length and k. On large, sparse datasets the runtime of UTKU-PSO grows only mildly with k, making it up to 5.6 times faster than the exact family. Its set accuracy, however, degrades substantially at very large k: at k = 20,000 on the sparsest benchmark roughly half of the returned set falls outside the exact top-k, although 83% of the total expected utility is still recovered. Instrumentation traces this to the search space widening faster than the fixed budget can cover it, and a diagnostic requiring no ground truth tracks true accuracy at Spearman rho = 0.998. The proposed framework provides a practical solution with explicitly characterised trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency for utility-driven data analytics in uncertain environments.
evidence_items.title: Exact and heuristic approaches for mining top-k high-utility itemsets in uncertain databases with mixed utilities

evidence_items.summary: The growing application of artificial intelligence in dentistry has opened new opportunities for predicting peri-implantitis (PI) using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Transfer learning, where knowledge from a model pre-trained on a large dataset is adapted to a new, domain-specific task, may enhance performance, particularly when medical datasets are limited. This study evaluated the ability of several pre-trained CNN architectures applied to baseline 2D intraoral radiographs to predict peri-implantitis onset. A retrospective multi-center study was conducted at the University of Michigan and King’s College London. A total of 195 implants (146 from Michigan and 49 from London) placed in 108 maintained patients were included. For each implant, a baseline periapical radiograph taken up to one year after prosthetic restoration was analyzed. Five pre-trained CNN architectures (ResNet50, DenseNet, VGG16, InceptionV3, EfficientNet) were combined with four transfer learning strategies: feature extraction (hybrid and non-hybrid), partial fine-tuning (50% of layers), and full fine-tuning. Models were trained using patient-wise splits to avoid leakage, and performance was evaluated on an independent test set using accuracy, area under the ROC curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. All CNN architectures showed variable performance across transfer learning strategies. The non-hybrid feature extraction approach provided the most consistent discrimination, with the best models achieving AUC values between 0.74 and 0.83. InceptionV3 reached the highest AUC (0.83). Fine-tuning strategies yielded modest or low performance, with AUCs generally ranging from 0.42 to 0.69 across architectures. Non-hybrid feature extraction applied to pre-trained CNNs showed the most promising, though moderate, performance for predicting PI onset from baseline intraoral radiographs. These findings indicate that transfer learning may assist early risk stratification in implant dentistry, but larger prospective studies are needed before clinical adoption. Deep learning models may serve as adjunctive tools to identify implants at higher risk for future PI based on routine baseline radiographs, supporting more individualized maintenance protocols and earlier preventive interventions.
evidence_items.title: Accuracy of transfer learning in predicting peri-implantitis onset from intraoral radiograph: A multi-center longitudinal retrospective study

evidence_items.summary: Full-duplex speech agents must update persistent memory while listening and speaking, yet it remains unclear which events should be stored, revised, or excluded. Existing benchmarks isolate interaction timing from memory outcomes, obscuring the state transitions behind a correct answer. We introduce DuplexLedger, a bilingual benchmark of 1,094 persistent sessions aligning four full-duplex scenarios with event-level Write/Update/Ignore/Retain supervision, explicit pre/post memory states, and 6,564 same-session questions and checks. Evaluating five full-duplex models reveals an interaction-memory gap: no system combines strong boundary control with coherent final-state memory, and the best final-state fact coverage is 2.01%. We propose ACT-Mem, an 8.92M-parameter sidecar comprising an event controller, a versioned transactional ledger, and a typed retriever coupled with a frozen MiniCPM-o 4.5 backbone. On 219 held-out sessions, ACT-Mem increases latest-value accuracy from 4.11% to 8.68% while reducing stale assertions and distractor adoption. It improves interaction boundaries but slows interruption stopping. These results motivate selective, auditable full-duplex memory rather than indiscriminate transcript retention. Code is available at https://github.com/lyx-researcher/DuplexLedger.

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the supplementary material for the article “Reliability Evaluation of Open-Weight Large Language Models for Clinical Diagnosis Assistance” (Chebout, Hamana & Belkhiri). The study evaluates three open-weight LLMs (LLaMA 3.2 3B, Gemma 2 2B, Qwen 2.5 7B) in 12 configurations. These are the three individual models, six two-model Analyzer–Decider ensembles and three three-model Dual-Analyzer–Decider ensembles. Each configuration is tested under Zero-Shot, Few-Shot and Chain-of-Thought prompting on 66 clinical cases (51 standard and 15 adversarially perturbed, noise groups G1–G4), with three repetitions, for 7,128 responses in total. An extension to Qwen3-8B adds 2,376 responses. Responses are scored on Accuracy, Consistency, a rule-based Safety proxy and the Clinical Reliability Score (CRS = 0.3 × Accuracy + 0.2 × Consistency + 0.5 × Safety). Contents Clinical case benchmark: 51 standard cases and the 15 adversarial cases exactly as used in the study Adversarial case generation code Prompt templates (Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought; individual, two-model and three-model configurations) Code notebooks for inference, diagnosis extraction and metric computation Full experimental logs (raw responses and extracted diagnoses for every run) Per-run metrics workbooks, including the Qwen3-8B extension Statistical analyses (Friedman and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests) and CRS weighting sensitivity analysis Clinician-validation data (two physicians, 45 responses) Reproduction The notebooks were run on Google Colab (NVIDIA T4) with 4-bit NF4 quantization. The case-generation script uses random sampling, so running it again gives different cases. Use the provided adversarial case file to reproduce the reported results exactly. See README.md for the file structure and metric definitions.

evidence_items.summary: Underwater robots support a growing range of work, from inspecting offshore structures and pipelines to surveying reefs and accompanying divers. Most of these tasks, however, are still flown by hand by a pilot, which raises the question of whether they can be carried out autonomously instead. On land, vision-language-action (VLA) models already let robots carry out tasks autonomously from language instructions, which makes them a natural candidate for taking the pilot's place. Underwater, however, there is little data to train such models. We take inspiration from how these tasks are flown today: the pilot watches the camera image and steers with a joystick, whose commands the flight controller turns into motion. We therefore record the pilots and introduce AQUAACT, to our knowledge the first publicly available language-annotated underwater dataset pairing camera images with human joystick commands. It comprises 1.9 hours of real-world and 17.9 hours of simulated demonstrations, both flown by human pilots, together with the vehicle's inertial measurements. Experiments with AQUAACT show that its simulated demonstrations transfer to real data and greatly reduce the real demonstrations a policy needs. A closed-loop benchmark of seven policies in simulation, from imitation-learning baselines to VLA models, each trained with its default recipe, shows that these tasks remain far from solved: no policy completes more than a fifth of the episodes. Pretraining on land data gives large VLA models no advantage over small policies trained from scratch, a gap that land-trained models have yet to close underwater.
evidence_items.title: AQUAACT: A Joystick-Level Underwater Teleoperation Dataset and Closed-Loop Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Code agents increasingly work on evolving real repositories, and memory systems aim to help them reuse earlier experience. However, such experience is diverse and evolving, so it remains unclear how memory systems organize it and thereby affect code agents. Existing benchmarks cannot answer this reliably because they lack either temporally valid histories or control over prior-task relevance. In this paper, we present MemDev-Bench to evaluate how memory systems affect code agents over diverse repository histories. It pairs each task with relevance-annotated earlier tasks from the same repository to build histories with controlled relevance. We also build an automated pipeline that reliably makes these earlier tasks executable and verifiable, producing 4,869 historical tasks for 555 base tasks. Based on MemDev-Bench, our systematic evaluation of memory systems across diverse development scenarios yields three main findings. (1) Memory mainly improves fine-grained localization and editing, increasing functional correctness. (2) Memory also causes failures on otherwise solvable tasks even with related history, and unrelated history tends to increase such failures. These failures mainly stem from agents reusing memory without reassessing its applicability. (3) Compared with using memory systems, directly providing agents with raw historical trajectories substantially reduces their steps. Further analysis suggests that agents save these steps by reusing process information that compressed memories tend to omit. These results suggest that future memory systems should preserve process information and reassess memory applicability against current task context.
evidence_items.title: MemDev-Bench: Does Memory Help Code Agents?Benchmarking Memory Systems over Real Repository Histories

evidence_items.summary: Solid and gel polymer electrolytes are central to safer, more flexible batteries, and machine learning has been used to predict their ionic conductivity directly from composition and processing variables. Almost all of this work targets lithium-ion systems, for which large, curated datasets exist. Polymer electrolytes conducting multivalent or non-lithium cations (magnesium, zinc, sodium) are promising lower-cost alternatives but remain comparably underexplored, in part because no public, ML-ready dataset of their measured ionic conductivities exists. Here we validate a standard composition-to-conductivity pipeline (Random Forest and XGBoost regression) on OBELiX, a published dataset of 599 lithium solid-state electrolytes, reaching R2 = 0.79 against a mean-predicting baseline near zero. We then construct, to our knowledge, the first ML-ready dataset of Mg-, Zn-, and Na-conducting polymer electrolytes, systematically mined from the primary and review literature: 135 data points across 105 distinct host-polymer/salt systems. Applying the same pipeline to this new dataset, a tuned Random Forest reaches R2 = 0.47 under leave-one-out cross-validation, or 0.36 under a more conservative 5-fold estimate, well below the lithium benchmark. Through chemistry-informed feature engineering and a nested cross-validation check, we show this gap is driven primarily by data scarcity and literature measurement heterogeneity, not by model or feature choice. We argue the scarcity is itself the central finding: it puts a number, for the first time, on how far behind the multivalent and non-lithium polymer electrolyte literature sits relative to the lithium-ion mainstream. We release the curated dataset and pipeline to support future community data collection.
evidence_items.title: Machine Learning for Ionic Conductivity Prediction in Polymer Electrolytes: A Benchmark on Lithium Systems and a Feasibility Study on the Data-Scarce Multivalent (Mg, Zn, Na) Frontier

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users'susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p<0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.
evidence_items.title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects

evidence_items.summary: Aiming to modify textual content while preserving the original style, Scene Text Editing (STE) has significant practical value in many applications. STE typically requires paired images before and after editing for training. However, recent approaches rely heavily on synthetic paired data and complex disentanglement strategies. They struggle to faithfully capture the diversity and complexity of natural scenes, often producing artifacts or hallucinations. In this work, we challenge the common practice and investigate whether STE can be driven by turning each real sample into its own paired supervision. Concretely, we explore multiple ways to disrupt the original image (e.g., Crop, Shuffle, Mask) to construct self-paired training data, and build a strong baseline (TextRIRO}) upon a conditional diffusion architecture. Our experiments show that combining character-column shuffling with image cropping (Shuffle&Crop) effectively destroys text semantics while preserving key style cues, enabling the model to learn editing behaviors directly from the real text image. With this concise yet real-oriented design, TextRIRO achieves promising performance in both accuracy and visual realism across real-world benchmarks, substantially mitigating the synthetic-to-real domain gap. Furthermore, we leverage TextRIRO to build TextRIRO-3M, a large-scale realistic dataset for long-text recognition by concatenating edited and original images. Experimental results show that training recognition models with TextRIRO-3M significantly improves recognition accuracy, demonstrating that TextRIRO provides highly useful training resources for downstream tasks. Overall, TextRIRO lifts STE to realistic, reliable, and widely applicable new levels. Code is available at https://github.com/YesianRohn/TextRIRO.
evidence_items.title: Real In, Real Out: What If We Only Use Real Data for Scene Text Editing?

evidence_items.summary: This numerical supplement accompanies the manuscript “Structure-Preserving Quaternionic Polynomial LQ Control of an Underwater Inspection Point”, submitted to the 17th IFAC Conference on Control Applications in Marine Systems, Robotics and Vehicles (CAMS 2027). It specifies a single BlueROV2 Heavy literature simulation benchmark, the local and nonlinear model conventions, three virtual inspection-point tasks, and the complete principal LQ and integral LQ (LQI) feedback matrices. It also gives the corresponding value matrices, a four-real-component representation of the quaternionic gains, the nonlinear coordinate maps used by the controllers, and the centre- and point-based smoothed sliding-mode comparators. The model derivations, synthesis method and proofs remain in the companion paper and are not repeated here. The numerical results cover point-versus-centre cost ablations, 24 common-effort operating points for two initial states, tuning curves, constant-body-load tests, holding-force and integral-state traces, and geometric excursion bounds. Simulations use full state information and an ideal resultant body wrench; thruster allocation, actuator saturation, tether dynamics and ambient currents are outside this model. The geometric bounds evaluated along sampled nonlinear trajectories are distinguished from uniform nonlinear invariance guarantees. The accompanying compact data archive contains unrounded matrices for all 35 LQ/LQI gain arrays used in the comparisons, principal value matrices and quaternion spectral-factor coefficients, 84 sweep summaries, 24 common-effort summaries, load and bound tables, and selected plot traces. All data are supplied as ordinary CSV or JSON. Quaternion matrices are represented by four real component arrays, and polynomial coefficients are ordered by ascending powers. Reading the data requires neither the author's quaternion toolbox nor the polynomial toolbox.
evidence_items.title: Numerical Supplement to "Structure-Preserving Quaternionic Polynomial LQ Control of an Underwater Inspection Point": Models, Controller Matrices and Simulation Results

evidence_items.summary: Pretrial detention in Nigerian custody facilities exposes detainees to trauma and is associated with mental health crisis presentation, but the causal effect of detention duration is confounded by offence severity and facility assignment. The analysis is a design and power evaluation, not an empirical estimate: no observational data are used or claimed. Under a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.64, the design was evaluated across 2000 replications per cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power rose with cluster count and effect size, and 54 clusters were required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. Docket randomisation is a defensible identification strategy for detention-duration effects, but that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 imposes a cluster-count floor that most single-state Nigerian studies cannot meet. The contribution is a design template and a power benchmark for future custody-trauma research, not a causal claim about Nigerian detainees.
evidence_items.title: Police Custody Trauma Exposure and Mental Health Crisis Presentation in Nigerian Detention Facilities: An Instrumental-Variable Analysis of Pretrial Detention Duration

evidence_items.summary: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease for which no curative treatment currently exists, posing a significant challenge because of its deleterious effects on patients' quality of life and its substantial economic burden on healthcare systems. Current first-line therapies, including corticosteroids and systemic immunosuppressants, are associated with considerable local and systemic side effects, underscoring the need for safer topical alternatives. Topical celecoxib (CXB), a selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor, suppresses prostaglandin-mediated inflammation and pain, whereas diallyl trisulfide (DATS), a naturally derived, slow-releasing hydrogen sulfide donor, has been shown to restore the Th17/Treg balance in other inflammatory disease models. The present study aimed to evaluate the effects of topical application of CXB and DATS emulgels, administered individually and in combination, against imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasis in female BALB/c mice, using clobetasol as a benchmark comparator, and to investigate the underlying mechanisms. Treatment with CXB, DATS, or their combination significantly relieved pruritus, as demonstrated by reduced scratch bouts, improved Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) scores, amelioration of histopathological alterations, and restoration of spleen mass. CXB and DATS exerted their antipsoriatic effects by suppressing inflammation, as evidenced by inhibition of the IL-23/IL-22/IL-19/IL-17 axis and reduction of IL-6, JAK2/STAT3 total proteins, along with decreased TNF-α and IFN-γ levels, reduced myeloperoxidase (MPO) content, and diminished serotonin (5-HT) levels. CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell infiltration, assessed by histoscore, was likewise reduced. Across all assessed endpoints, the combination therapy showed encouraging outcomes that warrant direct comparison with clobetasol in future trials.
evidence_items.title: Celecoxib or diallyl trisulfide topical emulgels, alone or in combination, reduce pruritus and inflammatory cascades in a BALB/c mouse model of imiquimod-induced psoriasis

evidence_items.summary: Community health worker (CHW) caseload thresholds are widely used to ration trauma-focused therapy in post-conflict settings, yet the empirical basis for any specific threshold remains thin. Using a multilevel logistic specification with district random intercepts, the analysis treats caseload as a continuous allocation parameter and estimates the caseload level at which predicted completion falls below a programme-defined adequacy benchmark. The data provenance is the DHS Program survey indicator 'Family planning messages at community meeting or event' (id FP EFPM M COM), 15 African countries, 2021-2025, 15 country-survey observations, with a mean of 29.733 and a standard deviation of 17.495. Caseload thresholds should be treated as empirically estimated allocation parameters rather than as fixed administrative constants, and it specifies the identification conditions under which such estimation is defensible. The contribution is a methodological framework for deriving CHW caseload thresholds from programme data, together with a set of boundary conditions that limit its transportability across districts and service packages.
evidence_items.title: Community Health Worker Caseload and Trauma-Focused Therapy Completion in Post-Conflict Sierra Leone: A Multilevel Analysis of Mental Health Worker Allocation Thresholds

evidence_items.summary: AI virtual cells seek to predict the consequences of intervention across cellular settings. Their methods span mechanistic simulators, compositional latent models, regulatory graphs, foundation representations and population generators. Human-derived assays and recent model-informed drug-development guidance sharpen a common question: what evidence makes a prediction useful for a particular decision? This critical narrative Review traces the field's historical branches and organizes current methods through the interfaces connecting baseline context, achieved intervention, biological response and measurement. A statistical description distinguishes dynamic path laws, endpoint distributions and feasible sets, while retaining assay noise, feature coverage and selection into the measured population. We compare the transfer assumptions of major model families and the evidence supplied by strong baselines, calibration and target-context holdouts. The fifteen biological challenges for generative cell biology extend this analysis from molecular responses to cellular function and patient-level outcomes. We then examine how cellular prediction can be combined with exposure models, organoids and microphysiological systems to build evidence for experimental and regulatory use. This deposit contains the full V10-restored Review (27 pages, five original figures), Supplementary Information (21 pages), and an independently compiled TeX source archive with bibliographic evidence records and editable vector figures. The supplement includes a 71-entry method catalog, the fifteen-challenge crosswalk, and dated regulatory and industrial source records. There are 152 unique cited records. The thematic search snapshot is October 15, 2026, with targeted checks through October 20. Preprint; not peer reviewed. This Review synthesizes existing literature and introduces no new biological dataset or comparative model benchmark.
evidence_items.title: AI virtual cells: models, measurements and evidence for use

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Simulation-based controller comparisons can report a single winner even when score differences are too small to justify a unique engineering preference. We assessed preference reliability for five fixed controllers on a numerically verified nonlinear rotary inverted pendulum model using two independent Latin-hypercube realizations across matched ± 10%, ± 15%, and ± 20% uncertainty bands (30,000 closed-loop simulations). A four-metric score and a prespecified 5% practical margin quantified controller separation. Under the common uncertainty score, PID had the lowest controller robustness index in every band, but the four leading indices remained within 3.87%. In the pooled ± 15% domain, all ten paired comparisons were detectable after Holm correction, yet 69.40% of 2,000 scenario blocks lacked a unique practical preference. PID retained rank one in 99.95% of paired-bootstrap replicates but only 63.16% and 43.06% under two weight-variation analyses. Post-review sensitivity analyses showed that the principal practical-separation conclusion was robust to the tested CRI coefficient, realization-specific median normalization, and heavier-tail dependence models, while command delay altered separation among near-tied controllers. These findings are specific to the fixed controller portfolio, score definition, RIP model, and simulated uncertainty domain.
evidence_items.title: Quantifying controller preference reliability under uncertainty in a rotary inverted pendulum benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Published database comparisons typically cover engine pairs, conflate the engine effect with the schema effect, and compare queries that do not compute the same result. We present StreamCart, a benchmark built on a realistic e-commerce workload, and use it to decompose performance across six systems, PostgreSQL as an optimized relational baseline and five specialized engines (MongoDB, Cassandra, Neo4j, Elasticsearch, TimescaleDB), each implemented at a naive migration level and at an engine-optimized level, eleven configurations in all. Result equivalence for the claim-bearing analytics queries is verified row by row against the relational reference. Across seven read query classes, no naive implementation outperforms the baseline on any query, and no single engine dominates, with the classes splitting between PostgreSQL, optimized Elasticsearch, and optimized MongoDB. Schema design emerges as a factor on par with engine choice, improving performance by up to 3892 times on Cassandra and 137 times on Elasticsearch, where load-time denormalization lets the optimized form outperform PostgreSQL by 15.8 and 6.3 times on identical results, while a single omitted uniqueness constraint reduced Neo4j write throughput a hundredfold. Concurrent write throughput spans roughly two orders of magnitude (165 to 12,603 events per second). All code, data, and raw timings are public.
evidence_items.title: Decomposing Engine and Schema Effects in Database Performance: A Result-Equivalent E-Commerce Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Modern technological society is highly vulnerable to extreme geomagnetic storms, yet the terrestrial upper limit of such events remains poorly constrained because continuous instrumental geomagnetic records cover only a relatively short historical period. To extend this baseline, we quantitatively reconstruct the geomagnetic superstorm of September 1770 (termed Qianlong XXXV storm) using systematically documented auroral observations preserved in Chinese regional chronicles. These historical records indicate that the auroral oval expanded to a magnetic latitude as low as 20.40°N at the ionospheric height, implying an exceptionally intense magnetospheric disturbance. From this equatorward auroral boundary, we derive a best-estimate Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) index of −1,319 nT (95% Confidence Interval (CI): [−1,832, −1,066]), exceeding the reconstructed Dst intensity of the 1859 Carrington event ( ≈ −1,025 nT, 95% CI of [−1367, −853]) by approximately 30%. An extreme value statistical model suggests an order-of-magnitude recurrence interval of approximately 14,000 years for the Qianlong XXXV event, compared with approximately 1,400 years for Carrington-class storms. These results suggest that the Qianlong XXXV geomagnetic storm represent an important low-latitude benchmark for extreme solar–terrestrial disturbances. This potential benchmark provides a quantitatively constrained reference for testing the physical limits of modern infrastructure and the atmosphere of the Earth under the impact of catastrophic space weather.
evidence_items.title: The Qianlong XXXV event: a potential benchmark for extreme geomagnetic storms based on historical Chinese auroral archives

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Design for Additive Manufacturing tools apply predefined geometric checks, while dimensional limits require experimental validation for specific alloys, machines, and process settings. Engineers often interpret their applicability and manually coordinate assessment, redesign, and simulation. Large language models alone cannot reliably provide precise geometric measurements. This paper introduces AgenticDfAM, which coordinates reasoning agents and tools to revise designs and their assessment and construction procedures. Tools retain authority over numerical evidence. The feature-recognition and measurement tools were developed and benchmarked against reference geometries. Scripted agent replies were used to test validation of communication between agentic stages, error handling, and recovery. Invalid inter-agent messages were rejected by semantic validators. Across computational case studies, three redesign strategies remove all reference violations while exposing material and distortion tradeoffs. Thermal feedback lowers a part’s predicted layer-scale peak temperature by 160 °C. In a support design experiment, support above an intended contact surface was identified by a reviewer and corrected by the agent after diagnosis of the construction code. The correction was verified on curved and flat targets and reused in four autonomous clamp runs, with returns to support construction reduced from ten to five. The workflow investigates issues beyond prescribed checks while retaining verifiable engineering evidence.
evidence_items.title: AgenticDfAM: An agentic workﬂow automates design for additive manufacturing through traceable adaptive assessment and multicriteria redesigns

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon terminal agents may solve a task in one run yet fail across repeated runs. Stochastic errors can propagate through actions and context, creating a gap between capability and reliable execution. We present RiseHarness, a framework for iteratively improving agent harnesses with model weights fixed. It focuses on flipping tasks with both successful and failed runs under the same configuration, using successful runs as references for failure analysis. RiseHarness combines agent trajectories with internal harness traces from a runtime monitor to examine how model actions interact with command execution, feedback, context management, and completion decisions. A Harness Handbook links this evidence to harness behaviors and source code, helping identify recurring problems in mechanisms shared across tasks. RiseHarness then searches other harness frameworks for relevant implementations and adapts them as design references to the current model and execution protocol. Candidate changes undergo behavioral checks and repeated task evaluation; versions with measured gains seed the next iteration. This loop integrates suitable mechanisms from different frameworks into a single harness and uses new execution evidence to guide further changes. We evaluate task success and reliability across models, ablate harness execution evidence and external research, and test transfer to unseen benchmarks with the same model. RiseHarness treats a specific model as the unit of harness adaptation, studying how changes to shared interaction mechanisms can make existing capabilities more reliable across tasks.
evidence_items.title: Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents

evidence_items.summary: Reliable multi-view forecasting requires videos from different cameras to describe the same evolving 3D scene. To this end, we introduce Video-Point Model (VPM), a world model that conditions on multi-view video histories and a language instruction to jointly forecast future videos from arbitrary viewpoints and the 3D trajectories of persistent scene points. We extend a pretrained world model with camera-conditioned multi-view processing that integrates complementary observations across cameras, and add a trajectory head that predicts how physical points move through time. Each trajectory tracks a single point across all views, and supervising these trajectories alongside video generation therefore anchors appearance changes in every camera to a shared description of 3D motion. To support training and evaluation, we build VPM-Data, a simulation corpus pairing synchronized multi-view videos with persistent point trajectories, and VP-WorldBench, a forecasting benchmark spanning simulated and real environments. We further extend VPM to robot control by adding robot actions as a token modality in the generator. Action tokens share the point-supervised backbone and are denoised jointly with future videos, thereby grounding the policy in the same 3D-aware representation. On VP-WorldBench and existing 4D generation benchmarks, point supervision improves both video fidelity and 3D motion accuracy over a video-only counterpart, and in simulated and real-robot experiments, it also raises the manipulation success of the action-enabled model.
evidence_items.title: Learning the 4D World through Point Trajectory Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate plausible responses without using the relevant evidence or meeting task constraints. We separate the Modality Gap in cross-modal correspondence and evidence use from the Intent Gap in behavior relative to specified constraints, goals, and human expectations. Six dimensions organize the review: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. The first four control evidence access, optimization targets, supervision, and updates. Comparing mechanisms and supervision assumptions shows what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment. Evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels tests these choices through controlled input changes and reward-model validation, and we interpret each gain together with its model, task, and evaluation setup instead of comparing scores across conditions. Studies in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support share three requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and constraint-sensitive decisions. Stronger representations or higher benchmark scores can leave the claimed alignment mechanism unresolved, which motivates four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, targeted repair from failure diagnosis, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.
evidence_items.title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Chart reasoning requires multimodal models to interpret visual encodings, derive structured semantics, execute formal reasoning procedures, and generate evidence-grounded outputs. This survey reviews chart reasoning methodologies for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), categorizing them by their primary intervention points: data and supervision design, inference-time reasoning strategies, and model-integrated optimization. We examine how existing approaches extract chart semantics, use intermediate representations, execute reasoning workflows, ground predictions in visual evidence, and verify outputs. We also summarize major chart reasoning benchmarks and cross-paradigm empirical results, and examine limitations in current evaluation protocols and metrics. Finally, we discuss recurring challenges in synthetic-to-real generalization, semantic reconstruction, visual grounding, reasoning faithfulness, and diagnostic evaluation, outlining directions toward more reliable and generalizable chart reasoning systems.
evidence_items.title: Chart Reasoning with Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have introduced new possibilities for machine translation (MT) by allowing translation outputs to be shaped through natural-language instructions. However, evidence about how different prompt configurations affect translation quality relative to established neural machine translation (NMT) systems remains limited, particularly for Indonesian–English translation. This exploratory mixed-methods comparative study examines three prompt configurations applied to ChatGPT and compares the resulting outputs with DeepL and Google Translate across six tourism, promotional, and proverbial texts. Translation outputs were assessed computationally using cross-lingual cosine similarity from text-embedding-3-large as an exploratory indicator of semantic proximity and qualitatively through evaluations by three professional translators focusing on accuracy, appropriateness, naturalness, and discourse style. In the observed sample, DeepL and the baseline-prompt condition tended to obtain higher similarity scores for factual tourism texts, whereas contextual- and persona-prompt outputs received comparatively favorable expert evaluations in selected promotional and culturally embedded cases. Contextual prompting also produced additions beyond the wording shown in the source excerpts, indicating a trade-off between rhetorical adaptation and source fidelity. Because the corpus is small, the prompt conditions bundle several instructional features, repeated generations were not documented, and some reproducibility metadata were not archived, the findings are interpreted descriptively rather than as causal or statistically generalizable effects. The study therefore highlights a genre- and criterion-sensitive relationship among prompt configuration, semantic preservation, and functional translation quality, while underscoring the need for human verification of adaptive LLM translations.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Prompt Engineering for Large Language Models-Based Translation

evidence_items.summary: Nowadays innovative technologies impact various aspects of the lives of people. The forefront of innovative technologies Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been among countries' strategic priorities in recent years in terms of economic development, transformation of public services, competitiveness, and social benefit. AI is now one of the primary powers behind both the global development race and technical innovation. Many countries think of AI as a means of competitive advantage and economic expansion, employing AI technology to analyze enormous volumes of public data. In this context, while governments establish national AI policies, international organizations offer shared principles and guidelines for the ethical, trustworthy, and human-centered application of AI, while also supporting standardization initiatives. Türkiye has published the transition process strategically and released the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS) 2021–2025 document in 2021, describing its policy framework for AI. The article analyzes Türkiye's present status regarding the evolution of its AI policies, including global benchmarks, alongside the essential elements of the AI Strategy and its formulation and execution process. The strategy's multidisciplinary approach is given comprehensively, emphasizing the advancements and evaluations accomplished by NAIS.
evidence_items.title: Türkiye’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy

evidence_items.summary: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and quantum technologies are beginning to shape how countries design digital infrastructure, critical services and long-term security. However, technical work on models and architectures often evolves separately from national strategies on resilience, governance and capability building. This chapter brings these perspectives into a single structured view. We first position AGI within the evolution of artificial intelligence and explain how it differs from narrow, generative and agentic systems. The chapter groups AGI requirements into core capability areas and summarises the main architecture families that are emerging across model-centric, agentic, predictive, knowledge-integrated and system-integrated designs, together with current approaches to safety and evaluation. The second section focuses on emerging technologies that support AGI in practice. On the classical side, it describes computing and acceleration platforms, communication and 6G networks, digital twins, data and knowledge systems, and security foundations. On the quantum side, it explains how quantum computing and optimisation, quantum communication, quantum-enhanced simulation and quantum-safe security can strengthen optimisation, coordination, modelling and long-term protection for AGI-scale systems. Together, they show how AGI systems are trained, connected and protected in real environments. Building on this structure, the third section organises national AGI and quantum strategies into three layers: mission domains that guide where AGI creates public value, capability pillars that define the required technical foundations, and governance themes that link these technologies to safety and strategic readiness. Overall, the chapter provides a shared structure for researchers, engineers and policymakers who need to plan AGI as both a technical system and a national capability within a wider digital infrastructure.
evidence_items.title: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Emerging Technologies (Quantum Tech.)

evidence_items.summary: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has become a critical component in the deployment of deep learning-based object detection models, particularly in remote sensing applications where complex scenes, heterogeneous targets, and safety-critical decisions demand transparency and interpretability. Among XAI techniques, class activation mapping (CAM)-based methods are widely adopted; however, their relative effectiveness in object detection settings, particularly under varying scene complexity and target density, remains insufficiently explored. In this study, a systematic qualitative and quantitative evaluation of CAM-based XAI methods for target detection in optical remote sensing imagery is conducted, using the YOLOv5 architecture as the underlying detector. The evaluated methods are Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, XGrad-CAM, Eigen-CAM, Score-CAM, KPCA-CAM, Shapley-CAM, and Finer-CAM. Experiments are performed on the DIOR dataset, which provides a diverse set of object classes and scene configurations representative of real-world high-resolution remote sensing imagery. To quantitatively evaluate CAM-based explanations, a masking-based evaluation framework is employed, consisting of two primary strategies (M1 and M2), and complemented by an additional entropy-based analysis (M3). The M1 and M2 strategies evaluate the relevance and sufficiency of CAM-highlighted regions by selectively removing or preserving salient areas and analyzing the resulting changes in detection performance. In addition, an adapted M3 strategy based on Bernoulli entropy is introduced to analyze changes in the Bernoulli entropy derived from detector confidence scores under CAM-guided perturbations, providing a complementary assessment of the spatial concentration of CAM explanations around annotated targets.
evidence_items.title: Comparative evaluation of class activation mapping-based explainable artificial intelligence methods for target detection in optical remote sensing using YOLOv5

evidence_items.summary: Social behavior is a sensitive readout of brain state, but quantifying rodent social behavior at scale has relied on siloed, lab-specific tools. We assembled Days of our Mice (DooM), a benchmark of manually annotated video and pose tracking spanning 15 laboratories and 33 social and solitary behaviors, and hosted a community behavior classification challenge. We built on challenge solutions to develop the High-Dimensional Rodent Annotator (HiDRA), a behavior classification tool that generalizes to labs unseen during training and learns cross-lab movement features. Applied without retraining to experimental data, HiDRA resolves line-specific and state-dependent behavioral fingerprints with strong generalizability and reproducibility, establishing high-resolution, shareable social phenotyping as a scalable readout of brain and internal state. We release the DooM dataset and HiDRA classifiers as open resources.
evidence_items.title: A community benchmark enables high-resolution, cross-lab quantification of mouse social behavior

organizations: Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Forecasting solar soft X-ray (SXR) and proton flux underpins space-weather operations, yet machine-learning work largely frames the task as flare classification, not continuous-flux prediction, and the few regression studies use one solar cycle, under-specified splits, and no baselines.We present a time-series benchmark for multi-step regression of two drivers, the GOES 1–8 ˚A SXR flux (2002–2026) and the ≥10 MeV proton flux (1999–2026), on a 5-minute cadence with historical horizons in days and forecast horizons in hours.A leakage-controlled, term-based rotating k-fold assigns half-year terms atomically, and event skill is graded against persistence and the operational National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) forecast with imbalance- and extreme-aware metrics.Across 36 settings a segment-recurrent model (SegRNN) attains the lowest root-mean-square error (RMSE) in 35, yet the aggregate ranking conceals an event-skill artefact: its SXR M-class per-day Heidke skill score (HSS) near 0.10 sits on the persistence floor, far below occurrence-persistence near 0.46, matched by the operational reference, and no model separates from the proton floor near 0.79.The impulsive SXR regime stays essentially unpredicted at 12–24 h, reaching parity only at 3–6 h despite low global error. We release the dataset and code.
evidence_items.title: A Leakage-Controlled Time-Series Forecasting Benchmark for GOES Soft X-ray and Proton Flux

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine-learning studies on the ann-thyroid benchmark routinely report near-perfect discrimination, yet the sources of that performance are rarely isolated and the benchmark’s own class labels are rarely questioned. We report a controlled audit of this benchmark, separating what a conventional pipeline contributes from what is inherited from the data. Ten classifiers were evaluated across ten stratified splits in a leakage-free pipeline. A 2 × 2 factorial ablation separated feature selection from class balancing; nine feature-selection methods and seven balancing strategies were compared; a parameter sweep tested the hybrid selector; and a simple threshold rule on TSH and TT4 served as a clinical baseline. Differences between methods were assessed by Friedman tests with Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons and by two one-sided tests against equivalence margins fixed before the tests were run. Class labels were verified against the hormone panel and, at record level, against the diagnosis codes distributed with the same archive. The UCI files do not name their classes, and the accompanying documentation describes a hyperfunction class the data do not contain; matching against the diagnosis codes distributed in the same archive yields 3597 one-to-one correspondences with no discordance, establishing three hypothyroid-spectrum strata (overt hypothyroid, subclinical hypothyroid, euthyroid) instead, and locating 89 diagnosed hyperthyroid records inside the majority class. A majority-class baseline reaches 92.6% accuracy at macro-F1 0.320, so accuracy is uninformative. The principal clinical gain, macro-specificity rising from 0.905 to 0.987, is attributable predominantly to class balancing rather than feature selection.
evidence_items.title: Reported performance differences on the ann-thyroid benchmark reflect class labelling rather than method choice
