evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Actuator saturation forces two controller‐design choices: how to impose the force limit and how to represent post‐yield softening. We isolate the two choices on a reproducible OpenSeesPy reimplementation of the 3‐story and 9‐story Ohtori SAC steel‐frame benchmark structures, checked against published modal frequencies and selected uncontrolled response peaks. A matched finite‐horizon two‐by‐two factorial crosses elastic versus softened design models with post‐hoc clipping versus in‐QP actuator bounds. Across 44 3‐story evaluations using 22 FEMA P695 far‐field records at two intensity tiers, constraint handling accounts for 82% of the descriptive variance among four pooled cell‐mean costs, frequency tuning for 14%, and interaction for 4%; in the 9‐story 10‐case common‐finite‐score canonical subset the constraint‐handling share is 99.5%. Elastic in‐QP has the lowest mean under all five weight sets, yet under the primary score it loses to matched elastic clipping in 12 of 44 cases, with losses more frequent at larger uncontrolled drifts. Design‐frequency retuning stays small and inconsistent (elastic‐minus‐softened mean margin ); yield‐adaptive updating gives no consistent improvement, and a softening‐capable constitutive branch retains the principal ordering. In the transferred magnetorheological‐device comparison, powered operation reduces casewise peak drift by 19.9% on average but has a higher mean cost than zero‐current operation, and separate collapse‐limit analyses do not establish a consistent advantage for either allocation rule. For the primary score, the results prioritize actuator‐bound handling over the tested frequency retuning within the two planar frames, retaining clipping as a high‐demand comparator rather than a validated switching fallback.
evidence_items.title: Actuator‐Constraint Handling Versus Frequency Retuning in Active Seismic Control: A Two‐Height Yielding Steel‐Frame Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Computational protein design workflows require the orchestration of multiple tools, data formats, and analysis steps that are often fragmented. Here, we introduce Chaperone, a lightweight and customizable framework that enables seamless integration of RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) with downstream sequence design, structure prediction, and evaluation tools, including ProteinMPNN, AlphaFold3 (AF3), and more than 50 other protein design tools. By combining a programmable agent-friendly interface with parallelized execution on high-performance computing systems, Chaperone as a harness enables rapid iteration and scalable exploration of complex protein design workflows. Across an evaluation of nine biomolecular design tasks, we find using Chaperone reduces total token usage relative to baseline agents by 86% and GPU costs by 64%, while increasing the overall computational design pass rate. We demonstrate Chaperones utility for large-scale design-space exploration through a two-week end-to-end small-molecule binder design campaign, yielding low nanomolar binders to cortisol zero shot. We further demonstrate its versatility across distinct design challenges, including the design of a symmetric 12-subunit self-assembly nanoparticle and a linker that mediates interactions between C2- and D3-symmetric protein complexes to form crystalline assemblies. Together, these results demonstrate how agent harnesses built around standardized tool interfaces can substantially improve the efficiency and success of complex, long-horizon agentic design workflows in biology. We make Chaperone freely available to the community on GitHub: https://github.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone.
evidence_items.title: Reliable and Efficient Agentic Protein Design with Toolset Harnessing

evidence_items.summary: For public safety in crowded public places, less human detection is insufficient without interpretability and actionability of decision assistances. Although deep learning–based video surveillance systems have achieved accurate detection recently, the majority are restricted to passive perception and do not convert visual products into executive decisions for crowd status. This study presents an agentic AI-based decision support framework for interpretable real-time crowd status monitoring, to link vision-based perception and public safety decision. The proposed framework incorporates a YOLOv5-derived human detection module, an agentic state evaluation by considering persistability and a transparent rule-based decision making, which distinguishes scenes into crowd versus non-crowd. The human detections are temporally accumulated by counting and persistence measures to maintain stable and interpretable decision signals. The framework is tested on CCTV-style surveillance data and demonstrate consistent performance for detection, with a mean average precision of 95.3% (at IoU = 0.5) while achieving real-time processing speed of 25–30 fps on commodity hardware. The results interpretable decision logic explicitly into speech-and-video based monitoring of crowd status in safety-critical public facilities, which is practical, scalable, and explainable.
evidence_items.title: An Agentic AI Decision-Support Framework for Interpretable Crowd Status Monitoring via YOLOv5

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) predict multiple token positions per forward pass, yet block-wise decoders serialize generation and repeatedly recompute stable predictions. We attribute this inefficiency to coupling a prediction's readiness for irreversible commitment with its utility as context. We introduce Tentative Context Pipelining (TeCoP), a training-free decoder that decouples these roles through staggered block-parallel pipelining and draft-and-verify. TeCoP reuses stable but uncommitted predictions as provisional cross-block context, with commitment governed by confidence and stability checks. Across four LLaDA and Dream dLLMs on GSM8K, Minerva MATH, and MBPP, TeCoP reduces number of forward evaluations by up to 87% and achieves up to 7.50-fold throughput without KV caching and 11.77-fold with caching over the uncached original decoder. It outperforms Fast-dLLM and DSB in throughput across all 12 model-benchmark settings, with and without caching, while keeping average cached accuracy within one percentage point of the original decoder.
evidence_items.title: TeCoP: Accelerating Diffusion Large Language Model Decoding via Tentative Context Pipelining

evidence_items.summary: Ensuring the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) with diverse cultural values is critical for their safe global deployment. However, existing alignment benchmarks are predominantly English-centric or confined to simple discriminative tasks. Moreover, they often fail to effectively evaluate model robustness against complex, adversarial inductions within specific cultural contexts. To address these limitations, we propose ABench, a fine-grained, handcrafted benchmark specifically tailored to taxonomized values in Chinese. Grounded in a rigorous hierarchical taxonomy comprising 158 derived value subcategories, ABench consists of 2,895 open-ended questions. These questions employ techniques such as role-playing and logical traps to probe the stability of models'stances in adversarially induced contexts. Furthermore, we propose a weighted automated evaluation framework that utilizes question-specific scoring criteria for nuanced assessment. Extensive experiments on 16 mainstream LLMs reveal that most models exhibit significant vulnerabilities when subjected to sophisticated adversary attacks on values (scoring below 60). This underscores the need for more robust, culturally specific alignment strategies. Our data will be publicly released to promote further research on taxonomized value alignment.
evidence_items.title: ABench: Adversarily Benchmarking Large Language Models across Taxonomized Values

evidence_items.summary: Recent work reports that the distribution verbalized directly in the output text aligns far better with human opinion distributions than the next-token log-probability distribution of LLMs. However, the verbalized distribution reflects what LLMs know about a group's opinions (knowledge distribution), while what they actually output at deployment is governed by their log-probability distribution (behavior distribution). We find that when prompting LLMs to predict the opinion of a specific group, the most likely answer under the verbalized distribution differs from that under the log-probability distribution for 37% of World Values Survey questions, averaged over three LLMs. Thus, LLMs'knowledge does not match their behavior. This matters for evaluation: a verbalized distribution can score well against a group while its most likely answer is one the model never outputs, so the score no longer describes the model. The alignment scores for these two distributions reflect only the model's behavior or its knowledge, separately. We therefore propose a learnable combination of the two distributions that follows the most likely answer of the behavior distribution while preserving the shape of the knowledge distribution, with a single hyperparameter trading off behavioral fidelity against distribution quality. Our experiments on three opinion survey datasets and six models show that the balanced distribution improves behavioral consistency over the verbalized distribution from 71.6% to 95.6% on average, while the total variation distance to the human opinion distributions rises only slightly from 28.8% to 33.8%, and it remains effective under temperature scaling and cross-dataset settings.
evidence_items.title: Speak vs. Know: Balancing Behavior and Knowledge Distributions of Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models show strong vision-language capabilities, yet their geometry-centric reasoning remains insufficiently understood. Existing mathematical benchmarks typically rely on rasterized figures and cover limited geometric knowledge areas and response formats, making it difficult to assess whether models reason over geometric structures or exploit superficial visual patterns. We introduce TriGeoBench, a geometry-centric multimodal benchmark constructed from Chinese middle- and high-school mathematics examinations. TriGeoBench contains 7,000 question-answer pairs and 12,235 geometric figures with TikZ code, spanning plane geometry, solid geometry, analytic geometry, function, and vector geometry across diverse response formats. Each instance forms a {question-answer pair, image, TikZ} triplet: question-answer pairs are stored in LaTeX, images as RGB figures, and TikZ preserves geometric topology, symbolic annotations, and relational structure. We evaluate representative open- and closed-source MLLMs through image-to-TikZ and multimodal reasoning probes. Results reveal persistent fine-grained structure and image-text alignment challenges. Oracle experiments with human-curated reference TikZ suggest that accurate executable representations provide complementary geometric cues; they do not evaluate an end-to-end conversion pipeline. TriGeoBench offers a testbed for structure-aware mathematical reasoning.
evidence_items.title: TriGeoBench: A Multimodal Mathematical Geometry Benchmark with Figures and TikZ

evidence_items.summary: Existing reasoning evaluations typically provide task-relevant information to models as available premises, rarely examining concurrently how models discover evidence autonomously and how information presentation within narratives guides or obscures judgment. This paper proposes the WORTH Benchmark: models read original mystery narratives without clue annotations, autonomously select key clue sentences, identify case participants, and explain their reasoning process. The narrative materials are designed by professional authors such that evidence facilitating reasoning coexists with narrative arrangements that delay the revelation of truth. We report a pilot experiment under full-story conditions across two episodes, conducting a total of 70 formal runs on models, of which 67 runs are content-scorable. Scoring separately records hits on author-designated key clue sentences and participant selections; natural language explanations are used for case diagnosis and are not scored independently. The results show that clue hits and participant judgments are not synchronized; across 37 content-scorable runs in Episode 02, 31 runs simultaneously selected the same set of incorrect participants, while adjacent suspicion-oriented and exoneration-oriented sentences were selected 25 times and 0 times, respectively. These phenomena illustrate the diagnostic value of component-wise analysis and suggest that not-fully-cooperative informational relationships may influence evidence selection and judgment. This study only implements full-story conditions for two episodes, and does not establish stable model rankings or infer general mechanisms on this basis; human player records have not yet been cleaned, and this version does not report human-model comparisons.
evidence_items.title: WORTH Benchmark: Evidence Discovery under Not-Fully-Cooperative Information -- A Two-Episode Pilot

evidence_items.summary: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings. Evaluations on graph-theoretic benchmarks also show that performance on small graphs is preserved.
evidence_items.title: Scaling Graph Reasoning in Language Models with Learnable Graph Positional Encodings

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are expected to estimate their own uncertainty, with confidence signals used to guide retrieval, adaptive compute allocation, routing, and selective abstention. We investigate whether confidence signals measured at different temporal stages of problem solving encode distinct forms of epistemic information and remain reliable beyond English-centric settings. Inspired by classical meta-memory theory, we distinguish anticipatory pre-solve confidence (Feeling-of-Knowing, FOK) from retrospective post-solve confidence (Judgement-of-Learning, JOL). We evaluate these signals across two frontier LLMs, multiple reasoning domains, translated Marathi benchmarks, and a newly constructed benchmark of genuinely local Marathi factual questions. Across settings, the cheaper pre-solve signal remains weakly calibrated, while post-solve confidence generally provides stronger epistemic alignment despite its additional inference cost. Confidence behaviour transfers surprisingly well under direct language translation, with calibration trends largely preserved between English and Marathi, but degrades substantially on local Marathi knowledge, suggesting that linguistic transfer alone is insufficient for region-specific information needs. Finally, hallucinated responses maintain persistently elevated confidence after answer generation, highlighting important limitations of current LLM self-assessment mechanisms.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Calibration: Temporal LLM Confidence Assessment Across Languages and Local Settings

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon language agents requires identifying whether intermediate actions make eventual task success more or less likely when supervision is available only at trajectory level. The main difficulty is that a critic with aggregate return-prediction accuracy may still fail to resolve the local value differences needed to assign credit to actions, especially under sparse feedback and function approximation. Conventional critics estimate future return, but policy improvement also depends on knowing whether each intermediate decision makes task success more or less likely. We introduce SCALE, an actor-critic framework that augments conventional return estimation with explicit prediction of eventual task success. At each interaction prefix, the critic predicts a return value and a Success Value, defined as the probability that the task will eventually be completed from that prefix. SCALE converts changes in Success Value into multi-step action credit through Success-GAE and modulates its contribution according to the estimated reliability of the predictor, while retaining the token-level PPO objective. Across five agent benchmarks and three model backbones, SCALE improves task performance over the compared RL baselines in most settings, with gains of up to 4.1 percentage points in success rate. Separate critic-learning analyses show that SCALE also improves critic estimation and training stability.
evidence_items.title: From Outcomes to Steps: Reliable Success-Aware Critic Learning for Long-Horizon Language Agents

evidence_items.summary: Generative reward models (GenRMs) generate natural language rationales to justify preference judgments, yet a correct verdict does not guarantee a sound justification. Existing approaches often rely on reference explanations to supervise rationales, but obtaining such references can be costly and does not necessarily establish whether generated rationales support the resulting verdict. To address these limitations, we propose DeCert, a framework that evaluates the validity and verdict consistency of generated rationales without requiring reference explanations. Crucially, DeCert translates these assessments into preference supervision that accounts for both verdict correctness and justification quality. In particular, when multiple sampled judgments share the same correct verdict, differences in certificate quality enable DeCert to construct rationale preference pairs that distinguish stronger from weaker justifications. Extensive empirical studies across two model families and multiple in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that DeCert consistently outperforms strong generative judge baselines while improving rationale quality. Moreover, DeCert effectively mitigates positional bias, improving position-consistent accuracy by up to 14.8 points. These results highlight the importance of supervising not only which verdict is correct, but also how that verdict is justified.
evidence_items.title: Judging the Justification: Decision Certificate Supervision for Generative Reward Models

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built from language models are deployed on the premise that collaboration beats a single-agent system (SAS), yet when it pays is unclear. The most systematic study to date gives a capability-saturation rule: coordination helps while the SAS is weak and hurts once it is strong, with the crossing near 45% single-agent accuracy. That rule was derived on autonomous benchmarks, where no user takes part. We test it where agents now work: in conversation with a user under a written policy, on $\tau^2$-bench, the dual-control benchmark. On its airline, retail and telecom domains we compare the stock SAS with a centralized MAS built from the same model for six models from three families, over about 7,950 simulated conversations, with one completion-token ledger per episode per system. The study was pre-registered with a public change log; the MAS is reported as built, with one validity bar unmet (its planner never saw the tool schemas). Under a fixed simulated user no cell shows a MAS benefit: the MAS is worse in 12 of the 13 valid cells and tied in the thirteenth, and the fitted gain is negative across the observed capability range (weighted mean -28 points, 95% CI [-44, -12]). On the two cells where the rule predicts a benefit, the MAS loses by 13 and 22 points, and without a budget ceiling it at best draws level at 5.5 times the SAS's token spend. The one gain appears on the cell nearest 45%, under a second simulator. Whether the gain declines with capability is unresolved (slope -0.41, 95% CI [-1.51, +0.68]), because model-by-domain effects dominate. The MAS does not detectably reduce wrongful database writes; it converts other failures into budget exhaustion and inaction. For agents that serve people, the SAS is the default; a multi-agent design must show compute-matched evidence from the setting itself. We release all trajectories, ledgers, prompts and code.
evidence_items.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Pay When Agents Serve Users? Testing Agent Scaling in Dual-Control Settings

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models have shown strong code generation capabilities, yet their outputs often contain subtle bugs. Automatically repairing such code requires informative tests: inputs that expose faulty behavior, paired with correct expected outputs. Recent RL-based test generation methods apply the same outcome reward to all reasoning steps, which can discourage useful reasoning and reinforce flawed steps. They also fail to effectively learn from trajectories that find bug-triggering inputs but predict incorrect outputs, leaving their verified bug-triggering progress insufficiently exploited. To address these limitations, we propose SCALF, a process-supervised RL approach that combines Step-level Credit Assignment with targeted Learning from valuable Failed trajectories. SCALF derives step-specific advantages from process rewards, allowing each reasoning stage to receive its own learning signal. It further routes trajectories that expose bugs but predict incorrect outputs to on-policy self-distillation, using execution feedback to learn from their valuable bug-triggering progress. Across three benchmarks, SCALF outperforms strong prompting and post-training baselines by up to 2.97, 5.26, and 3.53 percentage points in joint success rate, output correctness rate, and bug-triggering rate, respectively. Our code and datasets are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SCALF-F4D1.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing Bug-Exposing Test Generation via Step-Level Credit Assignment and Self-Distillation from Valuable Failures

evidence_items.summary: With increasing autonomy, Large Language Models (LLMs) may engage in deceptive behaviors, such as scheming to pursue misaligned goals or sandbagging to escape oversight. Monitoring outputs alone is insufficient, as models can produce seemingly benign responses while harboring misaligned internal objectives. While mechanistic approaches like linear probing are promising, they rely on the assumption that deception corresponds to a single direction in representation space. We demonstrate that such single-direction probes fail to generalize across diverse deception scenarios. To bridge this gap, we propose representing deception as a multi-dimensional subspace rather than a single direction. Our method utilizes iterative orthogonal decomposition to identify complementary directions that capture distinct facets of deceptive intent. To effectively leverage these directions for detection, we find that static combinations prove brittle due to strong domain dependence across different scenarios. We therefore introduce a domain-adaptive gating mechanism that dynamically composes the extracted directions through few-shot adaptation at test time. With only 10 examples, our approach achieves an average AUROC of 0.97 and 94% recall at 5% FPR across all evaluated datasets, substantially outperforming existing methods.
evidence_items.title: Why Static Probes Fail: Context Determines Deception Feature Composition

evidence_items.summary: Text-to-image models can generate visual concepts that their prompts never mention, and recent work shows that such associations can be implanted so that ordinary prompts trigger them. Auditing this behavior requires recovering the description that a prompt omits. Existing prompt optimizers are not well suited to this task. Gradient-based methods require backward access to the scoring encoder. Discrete evolutionary search treats semantically unrelated tokens as equally close. Language-model-guided search requires one inference call per candidate, which limits exploration. This paper presents EmbGA, an embedding-space genetic algorithm that recovers concepts present in a set of images but absent from the prompt that generated them. EmbGA keeps the population structure of genetic search but applies its operators in the token embedding space. Crossover interpolates between parent embeddings, and mutation moves an embedding toward a randomly drawn vocabulary embedding. Each offspring is then projected back to discrete tokens before scoring, so every evaluated candidate is a valid token sequence. We evaluate EmbGA on two benchmarks against six optimizers under two exploration budgets. EmbGA achieves the highest alignment when the exploration budget is large, recovers the most grounded tokens on natural images, and runs much faster than language-model-guided search.
evidence_items.title: Beyond the Prompt: Recovering Hidden Concepts in Text-to-Image Models

evidence_items.summary: Systems for code-mixed (CM) text and speech rarely start from scratch. CM data is scarce, so most work borrows from the languages being mixed, which we call native languages. This transfer can also run in reverse, when CM data is used to improve models for the native languages. Existing surveys focus on processing CM itself, and none brings the two directions together. This paper fills that gap with a systematic survey of transfer in both directions, across text and speech. We organise the surveyed work in a taxonomy of transfer direction, route and modality. Through this taxonomy, we find that most transfer runs from native languages into the CM setting. The reverse direction is younger, and in it code-switching mainly helps by aligning the two languages. Text and speech work share methods but rarely cite each other. On a shared speech benchmark, native data helps more than new architectures. These findings point to open challenges, such as how much native and CM data to mix in training, and how to evaluate CM text written in different scripts.
evidence_items.title: A Two-Way Street: Surveying the Interplay between Code-Mixing and Native Languages in Text and Speech

evidence_items.summary: Adapting a forecasting system to a changing world classically means retraining. We ask whether the task of continually learning regimes for time series forecasting can be represented by a piece of text: a guidance block, evolved by outcome-driven reflection and used in a frozen LLM forecaster's prompt. On a refreshed multimodal benchmark (weekly search indices, daily currencies, daily commodities, each window paired with web-retrieved news), we run GEPA-style prompt evolution under strict contamination control to prevent the data leakage common in timeseries benchmarks: the forecaster's knowledge cutoff predates every evaluated window. A 900-word evolved guidance carried by Llama-3.3-70B beats TimeSeries Foundation Models (TSFMs) on held-out data (GM MASE 0.776 vs. 0.898 for TabPFN-TS-3), transfers to more recent models without measurable loss, and costs dollars rather than GPU-days to update. We characterize the loop: out-of-loop gains concentrate in the first reflection, in-loop improvements overstate out-of-loop gains 2-3x unless an untouched monitor arbitrates, and error-only objectives silently suppress the text modality. We provide two extensions. First, compiling the guidance into executable code with a TSFM as a callable tool recovers most of the gain deterministically. Second, ablations show the advantage widens at short horizons and that removing the news text does not hurt the guided forecaster, consistent with the text's value being distilled into policy during learning. We argue that continual prompt evolution is a practical, training-free alternative to retraining for multimodal forecasting.
evidence_items.title: Training-Free Continual Learning for Multimodal Forecasting via Prompt Evolution

evidence_items.summary: Existing steering benchmarks are built around simplified, isolated generation tasks and evaluate a single behavioral attribute under controlled settings that do not reflect the diversity and complexity of practical deployment. As a result, performance on these benchmarks provides only a limited picture of how steering methods perform in the real world. We therefore introduce RealControlBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating fine-grained steering of LLMs and LLM agents across diverse behavioral targets and interaction settings. RealControlBench extends steering evaluation beyond isolated generations to complex, execution-grounded, multi-turn agent interactions, covering five complementary dimensions: instruction-following control, agentic tool-use decision control, reasoning-performance steering, reasoning-length control, and trajectory-conditioned safety awareness. Rather than measuring steering success alone, the benchmark jointly evaluates target controllability and capability preservation, including instruction following, reasoning performance, and downstream agent utility and safety. It further examines whether steering effects remain specific and robust across prompt variations, domains, and model architectures. Our evaluation shows that existing steering methods remain unreliable across realistic control objectives: they often fail to consistently induce the intended behavior and can substantially degrade the model's underlying task performance. These results suggest that strong steering effects in controlled settings do not necessarily translate into reliable control in more realistic evaluations. By providing a unified, model-agnostic steering evaluation framework, RealControlBench aims to support the development of steering methods that are not only effective but also precise, robust, and useful in realistic AI deployments.
evidence_items.title: RealControlBench: A Benchmark for Interpretability-Informed Fine-Grained Control of LLMs and Agents

evidence_items.summary: Video generation models can create realistic-looking video footage from images and text prompts. Some of the recent advances have raised concerns about the reproduction of copyrighted visual content. However, copyright leakage detection in generated videos remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce a new benchmark data set for copyright leakage detection, comprising 50 copyrighted concepts, each with 5 images. For each concept, we have 5 videos created using the image+prompt video generation model and the prompt-only video generation model. Following that, we develop an AI toolset based on a contrastive retrieval framework that formulates copyright leakage detection as a video-to-image retrieval problem by matching aggregated video frame embeddings against a database of copyrighted image embeddings. Our method uses a single similarity threshold and retrieves the most similar copyrighted reference as supporting evidence. We conducted experiments showing strong retrieval and detection performance, achieving 99.6\% detection accuracy with only a single false negative. These results show the effectiveness of the retrieval-based method for scalable and explainable copyright leakage detection in AI-generated videos. Data can be accessed publicly from https://zenodo.org/records/21386117 and the source code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/Shaif95/video-cp-Leakage.
evidence_items.title: Copyright Leakage Detection in AI Generated Videos

evidence_items.summary: Patients admitted to pediatric ICU and cardiac ICU often require intensive perioperative support and frequent chest radiography to monitor support devices, extravascular lung water, and body-wall edema. Radiographic interpretation and analysis is often difficult due to superimposed anatomic and iatrogenic structures that obscure clinically relevant signals. While deep learning can provide decision support, translation to pediatric radiographs is still limited by high device burden and scarcity of pediatric datasets with clinically grounded device annotations. To address this gap, we first introduce PediaDeviceSeg-1K, a curated dataset of 1,000 anterior-posterior radiographs of pediatric CICU patients with clinically grounded, fine-grained annotations of common ICU devices. To our best knowledge, this is the first publicly available pediatric CICU CXR resource with clinically grounded device annotations for device-focused benchmarking. Building on PediaDeviceSeg-1K, we further present PCXR-Copilot, a device-aware pipeline that outputs lung and device masks, optional device-suppressed views, and edema-related visualization maps and scalar indices. The full pipeline has been integrated and runs in real time within the TWIST platform at Boston Children's Hospital, demonstrating feasibility for real-world clinical deployment.
evidence_items.title: PCXR-Copilot: Device-aware pediatric chest radiographic analysis with segmentation, suppression, and edema-related cues

evidence_items.summary: Natural language messages often contain quasi-identifiers that are weak in isolation but can jointly reveal an individual's private attributes. We call such a jointly revealing set of cues a quasi-evidence group. Existing privacy benchmarks focus on explicit identifiers, attribute inference, or task-driven disclosures, leaving inference from quasi-evidence groups largely unmeasured. In practice, whether exposing such a quasi-evidence group violates privacy also depends on sender-specified disclosure policies. We introduce QuasiLeak-Bench, a benchmark for policy-conditioned quasi-evidence group recovery, which evaluates whether detectors recover complete quasi-evidence groups and flag the disclosures the given policy prohibits. To obtain reliable ground truth at scale, a reverse-construction pipeline first selects weak quasi-identifiers, composes them into quasi-evidence groups verified to jointly reveal a target attribute, and generates documents around this evidence, followed by automated quality control. Experiments show that existing privacy detectors transfer poorly to QuasiLeak-Bench, and locally deployable LLM-based detectors fall far behind proprietary models, mainly because they miss most quasi-evidence groups altogether. However, a 4B model fine-tuned on our training split surpasses the strongest prompted model on held-out documents, showing that the task is learnable.
evidence_items.title: QuasiLeak-Bench: Evaluating LLM-Based Privacy Detectors on Policy-Conditioned Quasi-Evidence Group Recovery

evidence_items.summary: Memory systems for persistent personal agents must move beyond isolated memories, maintaining both personal memory about whom they serve and procedural memory about how to act. Crucially, in harness-based personal assistance, procedures or skills are inherently user-conditioned: personal context determines which procedures apply, how they are instantiated, and when they should change. Existing benchmarks typically emphasize either personal or procedural memory, leaving their interaction underexplored. We introduce PraxisMemBench, a harness-based benchmark for persistent personal assistance across daily-life and work trajectories, where personal and procedural memory evolve together and later tasks depend on both. Experiments show that maintaining two memory types separately is insufficient, with completion dropping from single-type to interdependent dependencies (84.6% to 77.9%). More broadly, across existing methods, relation-related failures increase from early to late sessions as interaction history grows (59.8% to 72.9%), revealing a continual-maintenance challenge: writing correct memories is not enough if their evolving content and organization cannot be preserved for later retrieval. To address this, we propose PraxisMem, which uses privileged joint-state supervision to internalize the ability to maintain memory content and organization into the memory manager, with location-aware GRPO and dynamic residual-routed OPSD. PraxisMem reaches 40.78% overall Session Success Rate, compared with 20.60% for Claude Code's native memory. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/QMMMS/PraxisMemBench.
evidence_items.title: Memorizing Who, Knowing How: Benchmarking Personal and Procedural Memory for Persistent Assistants

evidence_items.summary: Real-world image super-resolution aims to recover high-quality images from complex and unknown real-world degradations. However, existing generative Real-ISR methods largely inherit the dense latent representations and quadratic-cost global modeling paradigm developed for high-resolution image synthesis, causing computation, memory usage, and inference latency to scale unfavorably with resolution and thus limiting practical deployment. We argue that the key bottleneck lies not in insufficient restoration priors, but in excessive token redundancy and costly token interactions during high-resolution restoration. Motivated by this observation, we revisit Real-ISR from the perspectives of compact latent representation and linear-complexity modeling, and propose SANA-SR, an efficient one-step restoration framework. Specifically, SANA-SR employs a deep compression autoencoder with a 32x compression ratio to drastically reduce latent tokens while preserving restoration-relevant structures and textures. On top of this compact latent space, we introduce a linear-attention DiT with LoRA fine-tuning, enabling efficient high-resolution restoration with linear-complexity token mixing. Extensive experiments on all benchmark datasets demonstrate that SANA-SR achieves highly competitive and often superior quantitative performance against existing methods, while restoring clearer and more realistic textures. Moreover, after pruning, the deployed model runs in 0.019s with 407.95G MACs and 344M parameters, highlighting its strong potential for practical mobile deployment.
evidence_items.title: Efficient One-Step Diffusion Restoration Model with Compact Token Compression and Linear Attention

evidence_items.summary: Assuming that neither source data nor source model parameters are accessible, black-box domain adaptation (BBDA) represents a highly practical yet challenging setting, where transferable knowledge is limited to the predictions of a black-box source model. Existing approaches exploit such knowledge via pseudo-label refinement or by leveraging vision-language models (ViLs), but they often fail to reconcile the inherent discrepancy between task-specific knowledge from black-box models and language-aligned semantic priors of ViLs, resulting in suboptimal integration and degraded adaptation performance. To address this challenge, we propose adaptive Dual-Teacher Distillation with Subnetwork Rectification (DDSR), a framework that explicitly reconciles these complementary yet inconsistent knowledge sources. DDSR employs an adaptive prediction fusion strategy to integrate predictions from the black-box source model and a ViL, generating reliable pseudo-labels for the target domain. A subnetwork-based regularization mechanism mitigates overfitting to noisy supervision by enforcing output consistency and gradient divergency. Furthermore, progressively improved target predictions iteratively refine both pseudo-labels and ViL prompts, enhancing semantic alignment. Finally, class-wise prototypes are used to further optimize target predictions via self-training. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that DDSR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including those with access to source data or source model parameters.
evidence_items.title: Adaptive Dual-Teacher Distillation with Subnetwork Rectification for Bridging Semantic Gaps in Black-Box Domain Adaptation

evidence_items.summary: Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification typically involves large-scale data and computationally intensive training, which limits the practical deployment of deep learning models in real-world remote sensing tasks. This study introduces SpectralTrain, a universal, architecture-agnostic training framework that enhances learning efficiency by integrating curriculum learning (CL) with principal component analysis (PCA)-based spectral downsampling. By gradually introducing spectral complexity while preserving essential information, SpectralTrain enables efficient learning of spectral -- spatial patterns at significantly reduced computational costs. The framework is independent of specific architectures, optimizers, or loss functions and is compatible with both classical and state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets -- Indian Pines, Salinas-A, and the newly introduced CloudPatch-7 -- demonstrate strong generalization across spatial scales, spectral characteristics, and application domains. The results indicate consistent reductions in training time by 2-7x speedups with small-to-moderate accuracy deltas depending on backbone. Its application to cloud classification further reveals potential in climate-related remote sensing, emphasizing training strategy optimization as an effective complement to architectural design in HSI models. Code is available at https://github.com/mh-zhou/SpectralTrain.
evidence_items.title: SpectralTrain: A Universal Framework for Hyperspectral Image Classification

evidence_items.summary: Most engineering problems involve complex multi-step derivations through checkable intermediate quantities. Grading only the final answer misjudges LLMs, crediting correct answers reached through flawed steps and penalizing wrong answers built on mostly sound ones. Yet, existing benchmarks such as SuperGPQA and EEE-Bench score only final answers, and step-level ones such as TPS-CalcBench rely on LLM judges or human graders, or cover a single domain. We therefore introduce EngTrace, a symbolic benchmark for verifiable process evaluation of engineering reasoning. Its 150 expert-certified templates, spanning five branches, 15 domains, and 42 areas, generate each problem with a gold reasoning trace, so that every intermediate quantity is known exactly. We design and validate an evaluator that checks final answers, coverage of the gold trace's intermediate quantities (milestones), and displayed arithmetic, mostly without an LLM judge. Across 11 LLMs, final answers barely separate the strongest models, while their derivations differ. Wrong answers still state about half of the gold milestones, and domain experts trace most wrong answers to calculation slips, with conceptual errors rarer on easy problems than on harder ones. Overall, as LLMs near the final-answer ceiling, checking derivations, as EngTrace does, reveals differences that final answers miss.
evidence_items.title: EngTrace: A Symbolic Benchmark for Verifiable Process Evaluation of Engineering Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Audio-visual segmentation (AVS) plays a critical role in multimodal machine learning by effectively integrating audio and visual cues to precisely segment objects or regions within visual scenes. Recent AVS methods have demonstrated significant improvements. However, they overlook the inherent frequency-domain contradictions between audio and visual modalities--the substantial noise often present in audio high-frequency signals vs. the structurally rich details in visual high-frequency signals. Ignoring these differences can result in suboptimal performance. In this paper, we rethink the AVS task from a deeper perspective by reformulating AVS task as a frequency-domain decomposition and recomposition problem. To this end, we introduce a novel Frequency-Aware Audio-Visual Segmentation (FAVS) framework consisting of two key modules: Frequency-Domain Enhanced Decomposer (FDED) module and Synergistic Cross-Modal Consistency (SCMC) module. FDED module employs a residual-based iterative frequency decomposition to discriminate modality-specific semantics and structural features, and SCMC module leverages a mixture-of-experts architecture to reinforce semantic consistency and modality-specific feature preservation through dynamic expert routing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our FAVS framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on three benchmark datasets, and abundant qualitative visualizations further verify the effectiveness of the proposed FDED and SCMC modules. The project repository is available at https://github.com/happylife-pk/FAVS.
evidence_items.title: Frequency-Domain Decomposition and Recomposition for Robust Audio-Visual Segmentation

evidence_items.summary: We study how well LLMs can determine whether two programs are functionally equivalent. This is an important problem because benchmarking code equivalence helps assess LLM capability in tasks such as code rewriting and translation. To this end, we introduce CETBench - Code Equivalence with Transformations Benchmark - built from a repository of programs that may solve the same or different tasks. Each dataset instance is created by sampling a program pair and applying a random sequence of predefined code transformations, yielding either equivalent or non-equivalent pairs. Our analysis shows that even simple transformations cause a significant performance drop in state-of-the-art LLMs on code-equivalence checking. These challenges are further amplified in the cross-lingual setting when comparing programs written in different languages. To remedy this, we present a simple fine-tuning-based approach to boost LLM performance on the transformed pairs of programs. Our approach for dataset generation is generic, supporting cross-lingual equivalence checking, the generation of program pairs with varying difficulty levels, and the application of diverse transformations. In our experiments, we perform ablations over the difficulty level of original programs, as well as the kind of transformations used in generating pairs for equivalence checking. Our analysis presents deep insights into the working of LLMs for the task of code-equivalence, and points to the fact that they may still be far from what could be termed as a semantic understanding of the underlying code.
evidence_items.title: LLMs are Brittle to Simple Code Transformations: Introducing CETBench - A Benchmark for Code-Equivalence Checking

evidence_items.summary: Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long-horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for evaluating how foundation-model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP-100, a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP-Easy and EP-Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation-model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons. https://winniechen2002.github.io/Agent-bench-website/

evidence_items.summary: Scaling laws suggest that increasing model size, training data, and compute generally yields monotonic performance improvements. While this often holds at the aggregate level, we present systematic evidence that vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit inverse scaling at the subtask level: specific question categories on which larger models perform worse than smaller counterparts within the same model family. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families across eight multimodal benchmarks (nine evaluation splits), answering 29,386 questions per model, 558,334 model-question evaluations in total. Using per-question pairwise analysis across all model pairs in each family, we identify 375 subtask-model-pair combinations exhibiting inverse scaling, spanning 4,342 unique queries where a smaller model answers correctly but a larger model fails, and we find that these patterns replicate across independently developed architectures. We identify 13 subtask-dataset pairs that show inverse scaling across multiple families, consistent with the phenomenon being task-driven rather than model-specific. The most affected domains in our study include multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge, with accuracy gaps exceeding 20 percentage points in several cases, while diagram understanding appears comparatively resistant. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing model size uniformly improves multimodal capabilities and suggest that model selection should be task-aware.
evidence_items.title: On the Limits of Scale: Inverse Scaling in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Robotic value models assess task execution from visual observations and instructions, providing feedback for policy learning and execution monitoring. However, existing evaluations cover only selected aspects of execution understanding, leaving the reliability of value feedback insufficiently tested. We introduce RoboValue, a fine-grained sim-and-real benchmark for unified evaluation of robotic value models. Its framework evaluates four complementary capability dimensions through shared interfaces: task-state understanding, temporal progress monitoring, failure and recovery reasoning, and value consistency. Diagnostic trajectories and instruction variations test whether value judgments accurately reflect task requirements and changes throughout execution. RoboValue-Dataset covers 15 simulation and 20 real-world manipulation tasks, providing expert demonstrations for training and annotated trajectories for fine-grained evaluation. We evaluate representative robotic value models in zero-shot and one-shot settings under standard conditions and separate shifts in robot embodiment and environment. Our results reveal errors in fine-grained instruction grounding, history-dependent progress tracking, and recovery assessment, even in models with strong outcome and forward-progress scores. The same semantic subtask can also receive substantially different value gains across valid execution orders. These findings identify concrete targets for value supervision, while the dataset and public leaderboard support continued assessment of feedback reliability. The website is available at https://robovalue-benchmark.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: RoboValue: A Fine-Grained Sim-and-Real Benchmark for Unified Evaluation of Robotic Value Models

evidence_items.summary: Harness-side learning methods such as reflection and prompt evolution let an LLM agent improve from outcome feedback without updating its weights. In finance the natural feedback is a market or policy outcome, and such an outcome is a useful reward only when the documents the agent reads carry learnable information about it. We report a verified benchmark for outcome-guided reading of Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) minutes, built on Cieslak and Vissing-Jorgensen's study of the "Fed put," the Federal Reserve's tendency to ease policy after poor stock-market performance. The benchmark contains 1,197 equity-market passages from the minutes of 200 meetings (2000-2024), fixed chronological splits, an audited reconstruction of the authors' automated phrase-and-direction method, and the authors' human-coded tone counts, which we recover from their published figures. Screening two candidate rewards with frozen readers (fixed models and instructions) gives opposite answers. The equity return that preceded a meeting is learnable from the minutes. A frozen embedding recovers it with an out-of-sample R^2 of 0.50, and tone labels from a frozen LLM reach 0.49, against 0.32 for a linear readout of the reconstructed phrase-and-direction counts. The next change in the policy rate shows no detectable signal. In a test specified before estimation, no text representation beats a baseline without text. A pilot with a frozen LLM reader exposes a credit-assignment problem. One crisis meeting accounts for 79% of the pilot's feedback error, although the reader labels all of its passages negative, the correct direction. An LLM reflector that rewrites the reader's instructions from outcome residuals would therefore be pushed to change labels whose direction is already right. We release the environment, comparators, and a validation-gated adaptation protocol. We have not yet run the adaptive comparisons. Also available on SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=7626078.
evidence_items.title: Which Outcome Should Teach an LLM Reader? A Verified FOMC Benchmark and Reward-Design Evidence for Outcome-Guided Agents in Finance

evidence_items.summary: Background Identifying individuals on parole or probation can help inform care pathways and ensure continuity of care in health care systems. However, this sensitive justice-related information is often absent from structured electronic health record fields and is instead documented in narrative clinical notes. Developing automated parole and probation detection (PPD) systems typically requires expert-annotated clinical data, but manual annotation is costly, time-consuming, and constrained by data sparsity and privacy concerns. Objective This study aimed to develop and evaluate a synthetic-only training paradigm for PPD from clinical text that eliminates the need for expert-annotated training data while maintaining strong performance and cross-domain transfer to real-world data. Methods We developed Synth-PPD, a synthetic dataset comprising 7579 labeled clinical notes generated using large language models (LLMs), redundancy filtering, and automated quality evaluation. Dataset quality was assessed through human review of 1517 synthetic notes by 2 annotators. The primary outcome was the macro–F1-score for PPD. We evaluated Synth-PPD across unsupervised and supervised learning settings using LLMs, traditional machine learning models, and transformer encoders. Performance was assessed on 293 expert-annotated real-world clinical notes from the US Department of Veterans Affairs. Results Synth-PPD achieved 90.05% human-LLM alignment. In the unsupervised setting, Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct with chain-of-thought prompting and few-shot examples from Synth-PPD achieved a macro–F1-score of 87.22%, outperforming both the corresponding zero-shot model (80.10%) and the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; P<.001 for all comparisons).
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Generated Synthetic Data for Parole and Probation Detection in Clinical Notes: Development and Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: Log parsing turns free-text log lines into event templates and is the first step of most log-mining pipelines, yet parser behavior on mobile-platform logs remains poorly characterized. We present ABRLogParser, a multi-parser benchmark that expands the ABRLog Android bug-report dataset by applying thirteen classical parsers to its eight regular-expression block types: 342 files, 14 devices, 32.0 million log lines. Every (file, parser) pair yields a released structured output and template summary, and each parser is characterized by content (how aggressively it abstracts lines into templates) and by execution (coverage, failure modes, runtime). Abstraction spans a factor of 906 across parsers and throughput about fiftyfold; parsers carrying the LogPAI server-log defaults degenerate into near-identity transforms on Android; and we map where each one breaks down on large inputs. The corpus has no ground-truth templates, so the artifact is a substrate for parser comparison, not an accuracy benchmark.
evidence_items.title: A Multi-Parser Benchmark over Android Bug-Report Logs

evidence_items.summary: Perturbation prediction models - which forecast transcriptional responses to gene inactivation - are increasingly proposed as in silico surrogates for genome-scale drug discovery screens. Yet, rigorous evaluation of whether these models genuinely generalize beyond their training distribution has been lacking. Existing benchmarks rely predominantly on random train-test splits, obscuring systematic failure modes that only emerge under realistic out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. Here we introduce EL-PERTURB (Extrapolative Learning for PERTURBation Prediction), a benchmarking framework that stress-tests 20 perturbation prediction models spanning six architecture classes on both essential gene and genome-wide Perturb-seq screens, using a novel stratified OOD splitting strategy that partitions train and test sets into functionally distinct regions of transcriptional space. We find that model performance degrades substantially under OOD conditions, and that architectural complexity - including single-cell foundation model embeddings - confers no reliable advantage over well-tuned simpler baselines. EL-PERTURB establishes a rigorous benchmark for perturbation effect prediction across a gradient of generalization difficulty, providing a guide for building models that can genuinely serve as surrogates for wet-lab screening.
evidence_items.title: Genetic Perturbation Prediction Models Fail Out-of-Distribution: A Rigorous Benchmark and Systematic Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Modals such as may and must can take on different senses depending on discourse context, alternating between root interpretations (e.g., permission, obligation) and epistemic interpretations (e.g., knowledge, belief). While modals are known to be notoriously difficult for children to acquire, limited research exists on whether language models (LMs) can reliably distinguish between different modal senses. We evaluate seven LMs that vary in architecture, size, and training data type using vector-based similarity and surprisal measures across four datasets. Specifically, we investigate whether LMs can leverage contextual information to disambiguate modal senses and whether their performance reflects the distribution of modal senses in their training data. We show that larger LMs trained on diverse text successfully leverage additional contextual information when available. In the absence of context, they tend to favor the dominant sense based on corpus statistics. Smaller developmentally plausible LMs, including those trained on child-directed language (CDL), fail to show consistent sensitivity to modal sense distinctions and do not benefit from context to the same degree.
evidence_items.title: Modal Sense Disambiguation in Language Models: The Role of Context, Training Domain, and Input Frequency

evidence_items.summary: To prepare for future outbreaks, researchers need to know what studies have been done and what data they use. Mapping a large literature by hand is slow, while large language models alone can misstate or conflate sources. We present EpiLens, a lightweight, open-source retrieval-augmented generation package that applies a fixed retrieval template and output schema to every paper in a corpus and links outputs to source passages. We build a corpus of 2,297 papers from the sources of a multi-pathogen parameter study and evaluate EpiLens's paper-classification workflow against 214 manually labelled papers. Without task-specific training data, the classifier matches or exceeds the tested supervised and zero-shot baselines across four tasks. The study's early extraction sheets cite published sources for 327 estimates. We link each estimate to a cited document or to corpus studies included by a review. Then, we use the classifier's labels to compare the papers associated with different parameters and pathogens. EpiLens labels more papers linked to reproduction numbers than fatality risks as model-based (54% versus 22%, compared with 62% versus 24% in the manual labels). The gap is consistent with the frequent use of transmission models to estimate reproduction numbers and persists within each of five pathogens compared. Beyond the contrast between parameters, the model-based share of papers linked to incubation-period estimates differs by pathogen: 55% for SARS-CoV-2 versus 6% for mpox.
evidence_items.title: EpiLens: Lightweight RAG for Epidemiological Knowledge Acquisition

evidence_items.summary: Video-Language Models (VLMs) excel at visual recognition but struggle with causal reasoning. Current evaluations are flawed: multiple-choice QA allows shortcuts, and open-ended QA lacks robust automatic evaluation. We introduce Causal Chain Generation (CCG), a novel task where models have to generate the sequence of intermediate events connecting a cause and an effect. This structured setup demands genuine reasoning and enables reliable automatic scoring. We accompany this task with two complementary metrics: SODA-Embedding, which measures the semantic matching of a generated chain against a reference, and Causal-QA, which probes the chain's causal coherence by asking whether it contains the specific causal facts needed to reconstruct the narrative. We provide two test sets: SF20K-CC, a manually annotated diagnostic on 20 short films, and CMD-CC, a movie clip benchmark derived from audio descriptions. Our analysis reveals that state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with narrative causality understanding, frequently hallucinating or omitting key events. To address this, we fine-tune VLMs with GRPO using a composite reward that combines a format reward, SODA-Embedding, and Causal-QA accuracy, demonstrating substantial improvements over strong baselines.
evidence_items.title: From Cause to Effect: Generating Intermediate Event Chains in Videos

evidence_items.summary: This study proposes a supervised Natural Language Processing approach based on BERTimbau to classify public expenditure liquidation records according to the descriptive sufficiency of their content. The research is grounded on the premise that generic, vague, or overly document-dependent descriptions reduce transparency and hinder institutional and social oversight of public spending. A labeled dataset of 600 records was constructed by random sampling with artificial class balancing from a corpus of 4,083 permanent equipment liquidation records from the State Executive Branch of Mato Grosso, Brazil, for fiscal year 2025, with labeling validated by two independent auditors via Cohen’s Kappa (κ = 0.900). Three supervised strategies were evaluated under stratified 10-fold cross-validation: TF-IDF + SVM (baseline), BERTimbau Feature-Based, and BERTimbau Fine-Tuning. The results demonstrate that both BERTimbau configurations outperformed the baseline with medium-to-large effect sizes, significant for Feature-Based, with Fine-Tuning achieving macro-F1 of 92.66% and accuracy of 92.67%, confirming the feasibility of contextualized Portuguese-language models for supporting preventive, risk-focused governmental auditing.
evidence_items.title: Classification of Descriptive Sufficiency in Public Expenditure Liquidation Records

evidence_items.summary: Deliverable D4.3 of the ENTRACK project (Work Package 4). The report presents Local Planner, a municipal-scale energy system modelling tool developed within ENTRACK to support local authorities in assessing the impacts of energy and climate policies. Building on E3-Modelling's CompactPRIMES model, Local Planner addresses key gaps in existing approaches to municipality-level energy modelling, such as sectoral coverage and integration, simulation resolution, computational tractability, data availability, behavioural considerations and ease of use by non-experts. The tool comprises three interconnected modules that estimate sectoral energy service demand, allocate demand across technologies by simulating consumer choices, and simulate at high resolution the operation of renewable energy sources and storage to quantify self-consumption potentials in energy communities and grid infeed. The report describes the tool's architecture and modelling approach, its key enabling capabilities, and the data collection and calibration process (calibration year 2022) for the ENTRACK pilot regions of Ripollès (Spain) and Ponte de Sor (Portugal), covering macroeconomic, demographic, energy, technology cost and price datasets. Lead beneficiary: E3-Modelling. Version 1.0, January 2026. Dissemination level: Public.
