evidence_items.summary: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. Evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, Ψ_0, ω-HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot) and on held-out human egocentric video, from zero-shot inference to few-shot and full-data post-training. Scaling human pre-training data improves performance on both human and robot evaluations. After distillation, our model supports real-time, minute-long rollouts, enabling live VR interaction. Applications in policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world-action modeling further demonstrate the model's utility for embodied decision-making.
evidence_items.title: Ropedia W0: Scaling Loco-Manipulation World Models across Embodiments with Human Experience

evidence_items.summary: A guardrail classifier is reported as if unsafe were a property of text. It is not: it is a property of a policy, and the policy enters the model through its labels. We exploit an accident of an industrial deployment in which the same ~53k prompts were labelled twice, under two operational definitions ("is this a request for harmful content?" and "would a moderator block this?"), and used to train ten guardrail arms sharing architecture, codebase and optimiser family, at two model scales. First, the guardrail's own training corpus already contained the benchmarks: JailbreakBench-benign is 88% and OR-Bench-hard 82% present in the training pools, two over-refusal benchmarks, the kind a guardrail reports to argue it does not over-block. Everything below is decontaminated. Second, safety benchmarks stratify sharply by how much of their score is decided by the label definition rather than by the model: with architecture and optimiser fixed, the range across the ten arms is 0.99 on HarmBench-copyright and 0.043 on WildGuard-benign, a 23x spread. Third, a benchmark score can be moved across its entire range by 0.03% of the parameters. Across these arms HarmBench-copyright spans 0-100 and OR-Bench-hard over-refusal 3.4-56.4%, and the four arms whose last supervision signal carries a given policy occupy one extreme of both (exact rank p=0.005, or 0.04-0.14 at worst), at unchanged detection capability. For a distilled student the teacher's soft labels do this even when every hard label carries the other policy, so teacher provenance is an unrecorded confound in any released checkpoint. Fourth, validation accuracy on the one split that grades all twenty arms tracks agreement with the annotator's policy (rho=+0.74), not detection capability (rho=+0.34). We argue that guardrail evaluations should report contamination, a seed floor and the definition they were graded against as first-class variables.
evidence_items.title: Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On

evidence_items.summary: Recent works show that LLMs can generate kernels with strong performance on server GPUs. Edge deployment presents distinct challenges because the hardware is heterogeneous, the software stacks are fragmented, and the resource budgets are tight. LLM kernel generation across diverse edge backends has yet to be studied systematically. We introduce EdgeKernelBench, which combines a unified IR deployment framework with a hierarchical benchmark for edge workloads. The unified IR captures reusable computation, scheduling, and memory decisions and connects to each target backend through a compiler interface. The benchmark spans progressively larger program scopes, from individual operators to compact model graphs, across representative edge application domains. We instantiate the design with TVM as a reference compiler and validate it across heterogeneous edge backends. With a single generation attempt, the best model achieves 64.5% Correct@1 but only 25.5% Fast@1.0. This gap shows that functional correctness does not consistently translate into performance gains. We therefore introduce the Layered Edge Kernel Agent (LEKA), which organizes optimization through a layered IR. On the agent evaluation subset, LEKA achieves 43.5% Fast@1.0, compared with 13.0% for direct generation and 26.1% for Claude Code. LEKA and Claude Code use the same base model and optimization budget. Together, EdgeKernelBench and LEKA support unified evaluation and layered optimization of kernels generated by LLMs across edge backends.
evidence_items.title: EdgeKernelBench: Unified LLM-Driven Kernel Generation for Edge Backends

evidence_items.summary: Harness evolution automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, offering a way to improve agentic systems without updating model weights. The agent harness is iteratively optimized to achieve higher performance on the search set. But how much of this gain reflects benchmark-specific overfitting or additional inference-time compute, and how much may generalize beyond the search set? In this work, we introduce Harness-Delta Attribution (HDA), an evaluation protocol that dissects an evolution gain into artifact-driven overfitting, gains explained by test-time scaling, and the remainder, which gives an upper bound on residual generalizable improvement. We apply HDA to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks. In 21 of these settings that show statistically significant search-set gains, we find that a large share of the improvement is explained by overfitting or test-time scaling. Specifically, among these 21 settings, overfitting and test-time scaling account for 54% and 14% of the gain on average; their combined share exceeds 50% in 14 settings. The residual and held-out transfer vary substantially across tasks, models, and frameworks. Importantly, search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks, and provide limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts. Moreover, validation-based signals are insufficient to prevent overfitting. These results motivate attribution-aware evaluation in future harness evolution research.
evidence_items.title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution

evidence_items.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from privileged information (PI) without a separate teacher model. However, prior work largely treats PI as a fixed design choice, leaving the effects of its content and construction poorly understood. This challenge is particularly important in multi-turn agentic settings, where trajectories contain actions, observations, and reasoning that can be transformed into PI in many ways. We systematically evaluate 16 PI configurations across three multi-turn agentic benchmarks and three student models that vary in scale and reasoning mode. We find that PI effectiveness depends on its content, generation source, and the student model. Information-dense trajectories and PI produced by more capable generators generally yield larger gains, whereas thinking models benefit less consistently. To assess PI before training, we compare PI utility with two KL-based metrics: sampled-token reverse KL (D) and error-step KL contrast (Δd^{-}_{err}). The KL-based metrics track post-training performance more consistently than PI utility, which can be distorted by information leakage. Empirically, selecting each task's PI by Δd^{-}_{err} also improves post-training performance over random selection, most when the PI candidates differ widely. Finally, effective PI remains beneficial when combined with GRPO, allowing the combined objective to outperform a strong GRPO baseline. Overall, our results provide practical guidance for constructing and evaluating PI in OPSD training.
evidence_items.title: Predicting Privileged Information Effectiveness for On-Policy Self-Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Agentic capabilities are increasingly important for modern LLMs, yet remain difficult to evaluate during pretraining. Existing approaches typically rely on static trajectory-derived tasks or likelihood-based proxies, which are lightweight but provide limited visibility into how base models behave in interactive environments. We introduce ASAP (Agent Scaffold Adaptation for Pretraining Evaluation), a lightweight framework for eliciting and evaluating agentic behavior from pretrained base models on end-to-end tasks. Rather than converting base models into chat-style agents, ASAP preserves the completion interface and adapts existing agent scaffolds through structured trajectory continuation, short reference prefixes, and minimal recovery mechanisms. Across software-engineering and deep-research benchmarks, ASAP yields discriminative end-to-end performance across base models and pretraining checkpoints. Beyond aggregate scores, ASAP exposes model-generated execution trajectories, enabling analysis of exploration, editing, testing, recovery, and task completion across training stages. These trajectories provide a behavioral view of how agent-relevant capabilities change during pretraining and how execution patterns differ after post-training. Our results suggest that end-to-end agent evaluation can complement conventional pretraining benchmarks by providing a practical diagnostic of interactive model behavior.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Agentic Capabilities Before Post-Training: An End-to-End Approach

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled them to act as autonomous agents, creating and editing 3D models via code or direct software manipulation. In practical workflows, these models must infer object shapes, materials, spatial layouts, and lighting from diverse references while strictly following instructions to reconstruct, modify, or design 3D content. However, existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of such open-ended requests across real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce BlenderWorld, the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to evaluating frontier models on realistic 3D creation tasks. BlenderWorld comprises 223 tasks spanning architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization, driven by text, image, video, and structured specification inputs. To rigorously assess these complex deliverables, we establish a unified evaluation protocol: we render the submitted Blender projects from multiple viewpoints and evaluate them against 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics alongside holistic visual quality scores. Benchmarking thirteen frontier models reveals that GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest overall fused score of 79.9, followed by Opus-5 (73.0) and GPT-5.6-Sol (67.7). Ultimately, our findings reveal a critical bottleneck: while current models can parse broad instructions, they still profoundly struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence and accurate structural reproduction in Blender, leaving substantial headroom for future 3D-native agentics.
evidence_items.title: BlenderWorld: Benchmarking Visual Agents for 3D Creation from Real-World References

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are demonstrating increasingly strong offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities in the real world. Current benchmarks mostly evaluate agents in isolation against static targets. Real cyber operations, however, are dynamic and coupled: security postures constantly change as attackers and defenders adapt to each other in real time. Static benchmarks quickly saturate and miss an agent's ability to attack and defend simultaneously under live pressure. To address this gap, we present CyberArena, a dynamic, symmetric adversarial benchmark built around multi-round attack-and-defense combat. In isolated sandboxes, two agents compete under identical rules, acting concurrently as both attackers and defenders over continuously changing services. This converts static targets into evolving, semi-open challenges, directly testing an agent's speed and precision in discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. To sustain the benchmark's longevity, an automated agentic pipeline continuously generates, reviews, and validates new environments. Furthermore, because pairwise contests are notoriously hard to quantify, we introduce a dynamical model that maps match dynamics into unified, multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities. Evaluating 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches, CyberArena separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling. The trajectories read like a fight rather than an exam: defenders patch one hole and miss the next and certify repairs on stale evidence, while capable agents think a move ahead, planting backdoors for later rounds and, in one case, writing their own packet sniffer to watch the opponent. Beyond a benchmark, CyberArena serves as an adaptable, scalable experimental platform for future research on cybersecurity agents.
evidence_items.title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon, semi-verifiable agentic tasks often rely on rubric-based evaluation, but the evidence needed to assess these tasks can be spread across the environment state and the execution trace. A judge may overlook this evidence or accept unsupported claims, including an agent's own reports of success. When rubric verdicts serve as reinforcement-learning rewards, such errors can reinforce undesirable behavior. We introduce Sauron, an evidence-first agentic verifier that investigates both state and trace and relies on a claim only after independently validating it against its source. Bounded queries and joint investigation of related criteria reduce context use and redundant work, and each verdict carries an auditable receipt of its supporting evidence. Across 2,586 human-labeled criteria from 100 personal-assistant episodes, Sauron achieves the highest F1 of five verifiers on all eight backbones tested while costing less than Gandalf, the strongest baseline. With GPT-5.6 Sol, it reaches 0.96 F1 versus Gandalf's 0.92 at 23% lower cost, with a wider margin on process criteria. On a paired fault-injection suite covering 13 families, several of which simulate reward hacking, Sauron detects 97% of injected failures while flagging only 2% of clean controls, outperforming baselines even when they are given the full trace. On TRAIL, a benchmark for detecting and localizing real agent errors, Sauron leads both Gandalf and TRAIL's own judge on all three quality metrics.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-First Agentic Verification

evidence_items.summary: Intelligent question answering for textile standards requires accurate domain understanding, clause retrieval, and evidence-grounded generation, yet general-purpose large language models often lack sufficient domain adaptation and factual support. This study proposes a textile-standard question-answering framework that integrates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning with multidimensional retrieval-augmented generation (MDRAG). Based on 7017 domestic and international textile standards, we constructed a structured knowledge resource containing 121,166 annotated domain elements and a task-specific dataset of 2000 question–answer pairs. Qwen3.5-9B-Base, Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct, and GLM-4-9B were evaluated under three primary settings: Baseline, Baseline+LoRA, and Baseline+LoRA+MDRAG. A separate comparison with conventional RAG was conducted to assess the additional benefit of multidimensional retrieval over single-path retrieval. Among the primary settings, Qwen3.5-9B-Base with LoRA+MDRAG achieved the highest overall performance, with a cosine similarity of 0.624, a BLEU score of 0.283, and an expert-based overall score of 24.4. These findings support the use of lightweight domain adaptation together with multidimensional structured knowledge retrieval for textile-standard question answering.
evidence_items.title: A Textile Standardization Large Language Model Integrating LoRA Fine-Tuning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) can render structured questionnaire variables as natural-language profiles, but their value in mental-health screening cannot be judged from a single fixed-threshold score. We evaluated LLM prompt conditions in a cross-questionnaire benchmark for predicting screen-positive status on the Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) among undergraduates. The intended application was an offline methodological benchmark using previously collected questionnaire data, not a shorter alternative to direct SDS administration. Methods De-identified records were assigned to Development (n=1,951), Test (n=2,186), and Holdout (n=2,258) grade cohorts. We evaluated logistic regression, XGBoost, and 12 model-prompt conditions at the fixed 0.5 threshold and at thresholds selected only in Development-validation. We also examined paired bootstrap differences, ranking stability, scale correlations, grouped ablations, cohort shift, calibration intercepts and slopes, alternative expected calibration error specifications, representative repeated calls at temperatures 0 and 0.1, sex-stratified performance, and per-1,000 screening scenarios. Results At the fixed 0.5 threshold on Test, GPT E1, Gemini E2, and XGBoost achieved macro-F1 values of 0.732, 0.730, and 0.674. At Development-derived thresholds of 0.38, 0.50, and 0.174, the corresponding macro-F1 values were 0.702, 0.730, and 0.660. At the Development-selected specificity target, XGBoost achieved a Test macro-F1 of 0.738. Pairwise intervals showed no clear fixed-0.5 macro-F1 difference among the three highest-ranked LLM conditions. XGBoost yielded the lowest Brier scores. The combined-sample Spearman correlation between SDS and SAS was 0.60. Together with the ablation results, this correlation indicated predictive information distributed across overlapping questionnaire groups rather than dependence on a single measured group.
evidence_items.title: SDS screen-positive prediction from structured questionnaires in university students: a comparative evaluation of large language model prompting strategies

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into clinical decision support, ranging from documentation aids to triage and patient communication. However, their behavior in ethically ambiguous medical situations is poorly characterized. Variability in how different LLMs balance approval of against refusal of a proposed action could materially shape the recommendations clinicians receive, yet no widely shared benchmark systematically quantifies this variability across contemporary model families. Objective This study aimed to develop a standardized case-based audit set of medical ethics dilemmas and quantify variation in recommendation direction, model-reported confidence, within-model stability, and between-model agreement across 5 selected contemporary LLMs. Methods We constructed 60 original medical ethics dilemmas spanning 4 domains. Three researchers independently annotated case difficulty and ethical principles before reaching consensus. Five primary models—GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, full-size DeepSeek-R1, and Meta Llama-3-8B-Instruct—were each evaluated 3 times per case using a fixed prompt and temperature 0. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B was evaluated separately as an exploratory small-model comparator. The primary outcome was the binary yes or no answer; model-reported confidence and reason were also collected. Model differences were assessed using a case-clustered generalized estimating equation (GEE), and between-model agreement and within-model stability were summarized. Results Of 900 planned primary panel outputs, 897 (99.7%) had valid binary answers. Trial-level yes rates were 44.4% (80/180) for DeepSeek-R1, 42.4% (75/177) for Claude Sonnet 4.5, 38.9% (70/180) for GPT-5, 38.9% (70/180) for Gemini 2.5 Pro, and 16.7% (30/180) for Llama-3-8B. The overall model effect was significant (Wald χ24=23.34; P<.001); after Holm adjustment, only comparisons involving Llama-3-8B were significant.
evidence_items.title: Variation in Medical Ethics Recommendations Across Large Language Models: Case-Based Audit Study

evidence_items.summary: Brazilian public-safety agencies release structured crime statistics but withhold the free-text narrative field of police reports, which is rich in modus operandi and contextual information, because it contains personal data protected by the Brazilian General Data Protection Law (LGPD). We address this deadlock for robbery reports with a fully local (on-premise) two-stage anonymization pipeline: a deterministic regular-expression stage for structured personally identifiable information (PII) and a pluggable semantic layer (dedicated NER, local LLMs served by Ollama, union and chained hybrids, and Microsoft Presidio as a system baseline). We contribute (i) an expert-annotated gold standard of 996 robbery narratives, released with the source code; (ii) an entity-level evaluation protocol whose headline metric is safety recall (how much PII actually did not leak), complemented by a re-identification-criticality analysis and bootstrap confidence intervals; and (iii) an empirical benchmark of nine engine configurations quantifying the safety–utility trade-off. The union of spaCy and qwen3:8b over the regex stage reaches the highest macro safety recall (0.986, 95% CI [0.972; 0.994]; micro 0.973) and is the most conservative (highest-recall) option, while qwen3:8b alone gives the best overall balance (safety recall 0.966, precision 0.80, micro-F1 0.826, text retention 96%) and is our recommendation for general use. In this configuration, direct identifiers (names, documents, phones, e-mails) are removed at 99–100%, with residual leakage concentrated in location quasi-identifiers. Safety recall measures PII removal, not residual reidentification risk: these figures bound leakage rather than certify anonymity. We recommend qwen3:8b for general supervised anonymization, and the union when leakage must be minimized, and discuss conditions for replication across Brazilian police forces.
evidence_items.title: Local Anonymization of Free-Text Robbery Police Reports in Brazilian Portuguese: a Safety-Recall-Oriented Multi-Model Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Lithium–sulfur cycle life is limited by dissolved LiyS q x polysulfides whose speciation remains disputed. We benchmark the complete matrix (y = 0–2, q = 0 to −2, x = 1–8) in the gas phase, tetraglyme and dimethyl sulfoxide: 248 M06-2X/SMD thermochemistries, 132 refined by single-point CCSD. The convex hull, S8 → Li2S6 → Li2S4 → Li2S3 → Li2S2 → Li2S, is identical in both solvents, and every exergonic long-chain comproportionation delivers Li2S6. QTAIM analysis of the CCSD densities separates covalent S–S from electrostatic Li–S bonding, transferably between solvents. Solvation makes S 2–x the dominant lithium-free 1 charge state and places both legs of the shuttle on that branch. Infrared and Raman spectra of prepared solutions test the vibrational predictions and track the chain-length distribution through one band envelope. The open dataset is a calibrated reference for force-field, machine-learned and continuum battery models.
evidence_items.title: Lithium Polysulfide Speciation in Lithium–Sulfur Batteries: A First-Principles Benchmark of Thermodynamics, Bonding, and Solvent Control

evidence_items.summary: Financial derivatives occupy a core position in modern asset allocation, but the traditional option pricing framework, particularly the Black-Scholes (B-S) model, faces unprecedented challenges when applied to the highly volatile cryptocurrency market. The B-S assumption of constant volatility and continuous price paths fundamentally fails to capture the volatility smile, heavy-tailed distributions, and intermittent crashes inherent in digital assets. Furthermore, structural frictions such as liquidity fragmentation render the crypto ecosystem an incomplete market. This paper systematically reviews the mathematical transition from the B-S framework to high-order stochastic processes, specifically the Heston and Jump-Diffusion models. Most importantly, we contribute to the existing literature by providing a rigorous empirical evaluation using out-of-sample high-frequency options data from Deribit. Our empirical results quantitatively confirm the theoretical limitations of traditional pricing: while the Heston model reduces the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) by approximately 45%, the Stochastic Volatility with Jumps (SVJ) model demonstrates absolute superiority in pricing tail risks. Specifically, the SVJ framework decreases the valuation error for deep out-of-the-money (OTM) options by over 72% compared to the baseline B-S model. Ultimately, this study emphasizes that structurally integrating both continuous volatility clustering and discrete market shocks is mathematically indispensable for robust risk management in decentralized financial markets.
evidence_items.title: Valuation Engines Under Market Incompleteness: An Empirical Benchmark of High-Order Option Pricing in Digital Asset Markets

evidence_items.summary: Automatic auscultation is usually evaluated on the ICBHI 2017 database, where published scores depend on the split and the metric adopted. This work measures what a deployable model reaches under a fixed protocol: the official split, five seeds, patient-level bootstrap intervals, and an equivalence margin fixed in advance. Six configurations are compared, a compact convolutional neural network (CNN) trained from scratch, a closed-form continuous-time (CfC) recurrent network, and two pretrained models, MobileNetV3 on ImageNet and PANNs CNN6 on AudioSet. The compact CNN (556 500 parameters) obtains an ICBHI score of 0.460±0.017 and a binary area under the curve (AUC) of 0.572, with a patient-level interval of [0.515,0.630]. No pretrained configuration discriminates detectably better, and equivalence within the margin holds only between the CNN and its 8-bit integer (INT8) version. That level needs its baselines: a classifier that always predicts Normal scores 0.500, above every trained configuration, and an audio-free indicator of the recording device reaches an AUC of 0.582. The discrimination of the CNN ranges from 0.627 on the most represented device to 0.468 on the least, and the CfC stays at chance, which irregular event timing does not change. Quantized to INT8 with the classifier in floating point, the CNN occupies 0.58 MB and runs in 30.4 ms per cycle on a Raspberry Pi 5 without thermal throttling. Replacing the official score by a per-class macro average raises the figure by 0.121 to 0.183 on the same predictions.
evidence_items.title: A Reproducible Benchmark of Compact, Pretrained, and Continuous-Time Models for Respiratory Sound Classification at the Edge

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Individual‐tree segmentation from three‐dimensional forest point clouds underpins forest inventory, biomass estimation and ecosystem monitoring, but remains challenging in structurally complex stands, where vertical heterogeneity and point‐density degradation weaken the robustness of centre‐offset‐based instance grouping. We present TreeSegAgent, an extensible framework for forest point‐cloud analysis, whose core segmentation component is a multi‐anchor framework for tree segmentation (MA‐TreeSeg). MA‐TreeSeg stabilizes instance formation through two modules. First, a multi‐anchor (three‐vertical‐anchor) structural grouping module within an enhanced PointGroup‐style instance segmentation network, explicitly encoding tree vertical structure to improve grouping stability under sparse canopy conditions and to better recover low‐stature and understory trees. Second, we incorporate segment anything model (SAM)‐driven trunk constraint module. SAM is applied on two‐dimensional projections to identify trunk regions and generate trunk candidates, which are then employed as spatial hard constraints to regularize centre‐offset predictions and suppress clustering drift under canopy overlap. To support reproducible ecological workflow, TreeSegAgent further provides a task‐driven agent for automated, specification‐driven orchestration of common point‐cloud operations (e.g. instance segmentation, DEM generation and height‐based filtering) across datasets. Across multiple forest point‐cloud benchmarks, our method yields more spatially coherent individual‐tree instances and improved robustness to density variation, offering an extensible solution for large‐scale forest point‐cloud analysis.
evidence_items.title:
