evidence_items.summary: Clams represent an important part of the marine benthic community and are food sources for invertebrates (worms, amphipods), fish, and mammals. The purpose of this study was to examine the contamination and health status of feral Mya arenaria clam populations from the Saint-Lawrence river and Saguenay fjord at sites of anthropogenic pollution (harbors), a high residency beluga whale area and a reference site under no direct contact of pollution. Intertidal clams were collected for nanoplastics (NPs), dibutyl phthalate (DBP), metal contamination and health status assessments. Health status consisted of the evaluation of oxidative stress, protein aggregation, esterase, and carbonic anhydrase at the biochemical level, followed by morphological assessments (shell mass, condition factor, growth index) and resistance to air emersion. The data revealed that clams collected from polluted sites had elevated levels of NPs, DBP, Cd, Ce, Fe, Cu, Sn and Zn compared to the reference site. Surprisingly, the beluga high residency area site was also contaminated by these contaminants (with the exception of Cd), especially for Sn, NPs and DBP. These clams contained elevated levels of peroxidase activity, protein aggregation, esterase, (mantle) carbonic anhydrase and accumulated lipids. The clams displayed at least at one polluted or whale residency site, decreased condition factor, shell mass ratio, air survival time and increased growth index. Cluster analysis revealed that the above contaminants were strongly associated with carbonic anhydrase, esterase, peroxidase and protein aggregation changes but less so with morphological changes. In conclusion, feral clam populations are contaminated by plastic compounds, including the plasticizer DBP and Sn, contributing to reduced shell mass.
evidence_items.title: Contamination Profile and Health Status of Mya arenaria in the St-Lawrence-Saguenay Marine Park

evidence_items.summary: Using the UrbanSound8K dataset as a representative case, this study investigates how lightweight acoustic models can be trained with limited labeled data in resource-constrained environments. Because conventional knowledge distillation confines knowledge transfer to a single target dataset, it leaves the rich prior knowledge in external audio sources largely unused. We therefore propose Cross-DATA, a framework that treats a large-scale, general audio dataset such as FSD50K as an auxiliary knowledge source and integrates a newly designed Cross-data Attention Distillation mechanism. With mixed data batches as input, a powerful teacher model establishes inter-feature correlation patterns that the compact student network is encouraged to reproduce. In this way, the teacher's generic acoustic representations and discriminative capabilities can be transferred beyond the distribution of the target data, rather than being reduced to data augmentation or feature imitation. Experiments on UrbanSound8K show that the resulting student model surpasses traditional single-dataset distillation approaches in classification accuracy while using only about 4% of the teacher model's parameters and computational cost. Cross-DATA consequently alleviates the representational capacity deficit of lightweight models in small-data scenarios.
evidence_items.title: Cross-DATA: Cross-Data Attention Distillation for Lightweight Sound Classification with Limited Data

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents two related benchmark studies of AI-enabled wireless power transfer (WPT) for FR3 (7–24 GHz) ultra-massive MIMO (UM-MIMO) 6G base stations. Study 1 benchmarks time-slotted WPT scheduling across multiple IoT devices, comparing naive, sustainability-aware, round-robin and proportional-fair policies with a learned time-to-depletion predictor. Across 80 randomized 15-device populations, naive battery-priority scheduling saved none of the 238 physically sustainable devices, sustainability awareness raised the save rate to 23.5%, and a proportional-fair policy weighted by harvesting surplus performed best (51.7%), ahead of the learned predictor (42.4%). Study 2 asks whether an array should share its aperture between communication and WPT by partitioning its elements (power-splitting) or by alternating between the two functions in time (time-switching) under time-varying battery and queue demand. Power-splitting yielded shorter communication queues at every tested distance, and at 5 m, adaptive power-splitting avoided battery depletion in all 40 trials, whereas fixed allocation depleted the battery in every trial; adaptivity provided no such benefit under time-switching. Together, the studies indicate that the aperture-sharing architecture sets the achievable ceiling and the scheduling policy determines how close a deployment comes to it, so the architecture decision should be made first.
evidence_items.title: AI-Enabled Wireless Power Transfer for FR3 Ultra-Massive MIMO 6G Base Stations: A Multi-Device Scheduling and Aperture-Sharing Benchmark

organizations: UCL Institute of Finance & Technology, University College London, London WC1E 6BT, UK
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can propose financial transactions, but model output should not itself grant execution authority. We develop Authority–Inference Separation (AIS), in which an independent control plane evaluates a typed financial action intent (FAI) against institutional mandate, policy, current state, human approvals, and exact economic terms before issuing single-use authority. We specify the threat and control boundaries, instantiate AIS across four financial domains, and test fixed fixtures, a separate external-policy-gateway baseline, mechanism ablations, two small open-weight models, and an Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) contract. In 36 fixed attack fixtures, AIS accepted no unauthorized effect, compared with 36 for direct execution and 20 for prompt policy. A gateway without execution-bound authorization accepted all 20 targeted post-decision attacks. Both models followed all eight injected counterparty substitutions; the independent gate prevented unsafe execution but authorized only six of 16 legitimate requests, exposing an availability cost. The EVM prototype rejected replay, revocation, stale-policy, and call-mutation attempts. These are conformance tests, not field estimates. AIS combines established security mechanisms around financial authority and replayable evidence. A ledger can enforce granted authority and record settlement, while mandate legitimacy, delivery, and accounting require complementary governance and evidence.
evidence_items.title: Authority–Inference Separation in Agentic Finance: Intent-Bound Control, EVM Enforcement, and Replayable Assurance

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Manual creation of a surgery residency call schedule is a labor-intensive process that adds to the administrative burden of a chief resident while often producing suboptimal fairness and work distribution. While commercial scheduling software exists, many programs struggle with inflexibility, high costs, and an inability to accommodate program-specific constraints. Methods We developed a scheduling software platform using AI-assisted development tools (Codex, Claude Code), both commercially available agentic coding environments. The system applies a rule-based, weekend-first assignment hierarchy with randomized tie-breaking under a search budget fixed in advance, then performs iterative weekday assignment, accommodating vacation requests and discrete call-shift swapping. The validation roster modeled a single general surgery residency program: 55 residents (32 categorical and 2 preliminary general surgery residents spanning PGY 1 through PGY 6; 20 off-service rotators from other programs; and 1 fellow) distributed across 10 call pools. Three prespecified call-related ACGME constraints were enforced (at least 4 days off per 28-day period, call no more frequently than every third night averaged over 4 weeks, and no consecutive 24-hour call). The 80-hour weekly maximum and the 24-hour period free of all clinical and educational responsibility were not evaluated, as both depend on activity the call calendar does not capture. We evaluated the system with 100 independent full-year runs (July 1 to June 30), each generated end-to-end across all call pools and months under an independently randomized vacation distribution. Compliance and fairness were evaluated at the level of the individual call-pool month (service-month), the unit at which a monthly schedule is produced; fairness and workload metrics were computed across the program’s in-program surgery residents. Results We generated 12,000 service-month schedules over 100 independent full-year runs.
evidence_items.title: Generating ACGME-constraint-aware surgery residency call schedule software with the assistance of agentic coding large language models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used within everyday applications where their responses have significant downstream impacts. For responsible deployment of such systems, we desire insight into how much we can trust their individual outputs. A popular approach for estimating LLM confidence is to train probes on the hidden states of the LLM's tokens to predict the correctness of the model's output. These probes typically read hidden states from tokens that are already in the model's vocabulary. In this work, we introduce a new approach to confidence probes that learn a new readout token and utilize its hidden states to train the probe. We show that our learned readout approach ScratchProbe outperforms its existing-token counterpart on a variety of datasets and LLMs. We also extend our method to a multi-token approach which we show provides further performance improvements. Finally, since the learned readout changes only the position a probe reads from, any existing probe can adopt it. Applied to a state-of-the-art probe, it improves AUROC on every backbone, in domain and out of domain.
evidence_items.title: Learned Readout Tokens for Extracting Large Language Model Confidence

evidence_items.summary: Although large language models support a wide range of tasks, hallucinations remain a major obstacle to user trust. When a model generates an answer, both its internal processing and final output vary with the question. Internal states are often expected to offer richer signals for hallucination detection. However, studies using these states typically report their standalone discrimination performance, while output-side comparisons often use simple baselines with weaker modeling capacity. We integrate output-side information available at inference time into a combined baseline and compare detection performance before and after adding hidden states under identical data splits and evaluation rules. Experiments cover open-ended generation and constrained multiple-choice tasks across different models. Adding hidden states improves AUROC by approximately 0.004 and 0.039 on the two tasks, respectively. Hidden states thus provide additional predictive information, but strong standalone detection performance can still yield only limited additional gains.
evidence_items.title: Detecting Errors in Large Language Model Responses: The Incremental Predictive Value of Hidden States

evidence_items.summary: Watermarking has emerged as a key tool for identifying text generated by large language models (LLMs), with current schemes embedding statistical signals into the generation process to enable later detection. In this work, we identify a shared weakness across a broad class of popular LLM watermarking methods, including KGW (and its variants), GumbelSoft, DipMark, ITS, and SynthID. We show that these schemes exhibit a fundamental link between their detection scores and the token probability shifts they introduce during generation. This link, which we call score-ratio alignment, allows an attacker with only black-box query access to the model--and no knowledge of secret keys or model weights--to produce text that evades detection while remaining fluent and natural. We prove that the resulting attack is optimal across all covered watermark families, and show that the weakness is intrinsic: any watermark designed to maximize statistical detection power necessarily induces the very structure that attackers can exploit. We evaluate our attack on seven popular generative LLM watermarking schemes, three LLMs, and tasks, which reduce detection rates to at most 0.05 across all settings while preserving text quality. Our findings show that current watermarking methods can be reliably defeated under realistic attack conditions, highlighting the need for fundamentally different watermarking designs that decouple detection scores from token probability shifts.
evidence_items.title: A Unified Attack Framework against Statistical Generative Watermarks for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Empathetic interaction involves two distinguishable capacities: representing another person's emotional state (cognitive empathy) and generating an appropriate response to that state (affective empathy). We apply this distinction to examine how emotion-related information is internally organized, selectively attended to, and carried through response generation in Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct across 10 emotion categories from the EmpatheticDialogues dataset. Layer-wise linear probing revealed a broad middle-layer region of peak emotion-category decodability, with the layer-11 L2 probe achieving 63.6% held-out accuracy against a 10% chance level and a 54.6% TF-IDF lexical baseline. During response generation, emotion-related user tokens received 1.89 times as much attention per token as other utterance tokens, concentrated across layers 10-15. Target-emotion alignment then decreased from a mean cosine similarity of 0.239 for input representations to 0.125 for generated responses, with positive drift in 77% of examples and the largest shifts for angry and furious. Emotion-category representation, attention allocation, and response-level alignment therefore emerge as distinguishable components of model processing that can be analyzed through a functional cognitive-affective empathy framework. These findings provide a foundation for monitoring emotion representations during generation and leveraging models'existing affective structure to support more naturally empathetic responses without relying on external prompting or explicit emotion conditioning.
evidence_items.title: From Encoding to Generation: Towards Empathetic Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Pretrained Vision-Language Models (PVLMs) achieve strong zero-shot recognition but often suffer performance degradation under target-domain shift. Unsupervised adaptation provides a practical way to improve target-domain performance without labeled data, but it remains challenging because pseudo-labels generated by the model can be unreliable and no labeled validation set is available for model selection or early stopping. We propose a simple framework for unsupervised PVLM adaptation that combines progressive margin-based subset selection with cascaded consistency learning. The subset selection strategy constructs a class-balanced pseudo-labeled set using prediction margins and gradually expands it during training, enabling adaptation to start from reliable supervision anchors before incorporating broader target-domain data. Cascaded consistency learning further exploits unlabeled samples by using temporally smoothed teacher predictions on weakly augmented views to supervise student predictions on strongly augmented views, with confidence filtering to reduce the influence of uncertain pseudo-labels. To preserve the pretrained embedding structure, the framework updates only normalization parameters in the visual encoder and class prototypes initialized from text prompts. Experiments across multiple recognition benchmarks with both CLIP and SigLIP backbones show consistent improvements over zero-shot baselines and competitive performance against recent unsupervised PVLM adaptation methods. These results suggest that progressive pseudo-label selection and teacher-guided consistency provide an effective and lightweight strategy for adapting PVLM classifiers without labeled target data.
evidence_items.title: Progressive Subset Selection and Cascaded Consistency for Unsupervised Vision-Language Model Adaptation

evidence_items.summary:
This study investigates the micro-level structural differences in online review affect between social media and e-commerce platforms, exploring the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive consumers to selectively express polarised reviews across these media.
 
 
 
 Utilising large language model-driven aspect-based sentiment analysis, this study quantifies an initial dataset of 65,493 smartphone online reviews from TikTok, Bilibili, Jingdong and Suning to identify aspect-level affective differences. To explain the observed differences, Study 2 draws on uses and gratifications theory and conducts a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment, using wireless headphones as the focal product and TikTok and Taobao as the platforms, to examine how media environments moderate the translation of consumption experiences into review intentions.
 
 
 
 Affective differences extend to specific cognitive attributes, with social media platforms exhibiting a significantly more negative and heterogeneous affective landscape, whereas e-commerce platforms demonstrate overwhelming positivity. These differences are driven by a dual-pathway mechanism. Social media platforms primarily activate self-enhancement motivation, which facilitates the translation of negative experiences into negative reviews while weakening the translation of positive experiences into positive reviews. Conversely, e-commerce platforms primarily activate economic motivation, which facilitates the translation of positive experiences into positive reviews while reducing the likelihood of negative experiences translating into negative reviews.
 
 
 
 This study extends the investigation of review affect from within-medium comparisons to cross-media analysis. By shifting from macro-level indicators to micro-level attribute evidence, this study reveals a more comprehensive picture of cross-media affective bias. By extending the application of uses and gratifications theory from content consumption to content production, it offers a novel mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon.
evidence_items.title: Cross-media affective differences in online reviews: aspect-level evidence and a dual-pathway mechanism
Empirical Evaluation of Automatic Speech Act Classification: From Logistic Regression to GPT-4o

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into educational technologies for personalized support, creating opportunities for real-time learner modeling from dialogue. This study evaluates whether GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash can infer three Felder-Silverman Learning Style Model dimensions (Active-Reflective, Sensing-Intuitive, and Sequential-Global) from short, task-focused student-AI problem-solving dialogues. Using questionnaire-derived Index of Learning Styles labels from 153 undergraduate participants, we compared deterministic zero-shot and few-shot prompting under five-fold cross-validation. Although accuracy and support-weighted F1 were moderate for Sensing-Intuitive and Sequential-Global, majority-class baselines, macro-F1, balanced accuracy, and per-class recall showed that performance was often driven by dominant-label prediction rather than reliable recognition of both classes. The models substantially under-identified Intuitive and Global learners; few-shot prompting produced mixed effects and sometimes amplified majority-class bias. Active-Reflective classification remained unstable across models. These findings indicate that LLM-generated learner-style labels should be treated as uncertain, bias-prone signals rather than stable learner profiles, and that dialogue-based personalization systems require bias-aware evaluation and uncertainty-sensitive design.
evidence_items.title: Bias and Reliability in Learning-Style Inference from Student--AI Dialogues: An Evaluation of GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) are emerging as a promising paradigm for code generation, offering the potential for fast, parallel decoding. However, generating complex programs remains challenging, as their interdependent components must maintain consistent interfaces, data flows, and shared assumptions. Aggressive parallel decoding can compromise these dependencies and undermine program correctness, while conservative decoding sacrifices efficiency. To address this trade-off, we propose planning program decomposition before implementation to coordinate interdependent units during parallel generation. We introduce Self-Decomposing Diffusion for Code (SDDC), a novel framework that decomposes complex programs and implements their units in parallel, entirely through diffusion. SDDC first generates a contract specifying the program's decomposition and inter-unit dependencies, then uses it to guide coordinated parallel implementation. Across five benchmarks and two 7B diffusion backbones, SDDC substantially improves the accuracy--latency trade-off, raising pass@1 by up to 31.1 percentage points while decoding 7.5--13.7$\times$ faster than the base models, and outperforming a fine-tuning baseline by up to 23.5 points with lower latency.
evidence_items.title: Self-Decomposing Diffusion for Code Generation

evidence_items.summary: Healthcare providers lose substantial revenue to systematic payer underpayments and claim denials, yet identifying the recurring, correctable patterns behind them remains largely manual and does not scale to hospital claim volumes. We present Pattern Intelligence, a deployed system that discovers such patterns without supervision by clustering claims on their adjudication behaviour rather than their identity. Each claim is embedded in a 130-dimensional vector combining per-line expected-versus-actual payment ratios, claim adjustment reason (CARC) codes, denial and payment signals, and service composition. Payer and contract identity are deliberately excluded from the distance metric - we show they dominate the geometry and collapse clusters into trivial per-payer groups - and are reintroduced only as a post-hoc segmentation (by contract and visit type) that keeps every surfaced pattern coherent and actionable. We cluster with HDBSCAN, recover structure from the noise set via second-pass sub-clustering, and gate low-confidence memberships. A large language model translates each centroid into an analyst-ready description of dominant procedures, adjustment reasons, and failure mode. We report a recurring finding: roughly one-third to one-half of high-dollar denials, depending on tenant and segmentation, form an irreducible long tail that no density-clustering configuration or representation we tried groups - a domain property, we argue, rather than a modeling deficiency. We evaluate validity through cluster-coherence analysis and quantify impact with a recoverable-opportunity ($) metric on two production tenants (approx. 10K and 157K claims) within a six-tenant deployment. Rather than a new algorithm, the contribution is a problem formulation, a representation-design insight, and empirical findings from production.
evidence_items.title: Pattern Intelligence: Unsupervised, LLM-Interpreted Discovery of Systematic Underpayment and Denial Patterns in Healthcare Revenue Cycle Management

evidence_items.summary: Over the years, Uniform Resource Locator (URL) Phishing has been a threat to online security because their scams exploit trust in a misleading URL to trick unsuspecting users into disclosing their username or passwords and other personal information. Not only that, but it is also crucial to identify these malicious URLs and ensure online platforms and users are protected. The ISCXURL2016 data was utilized for the purpose of analyzing the performance of different Machine Learning (ML) models in differentiating phishing and legitimate URLs in this paper. A wide range of classifiers were explored including the classic classifiers as well as more advanced ensemble classifiers. The results of the experiments indicate that ensemble-based boosting models can be more beneficial for URL phishing detection. HistGradientBoost achieved the highest accuracy of 98.47%, followed closely by LightGBM and XGBoost that both outperformed the accuracy of 98%. The other classifiers, RandomForest and ExtraTrees, also performed well with accuracy above 97% and traditional classifiers such as Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) showed the poorest performance with an accuracy of 67.75%. The results show that the boosting-based ensembles provide a suitable negation of the complex and non-linear structure of phishing URLs. Along with empirical evaluation, it offers a Properties & Positioning viewpoint as well as the importance of the ML-based phishing detection in the broader context of cybersecurity issues. Moreover, it discusses the future directions, with Federated Learning (FL) in the context of decentralized and privacy-preserving collaboration and Large Language Models (LLM) in the context of semantic reasoning and flexibility. These insights together will provide the building blocks for more intelligent, adaptive and trustworthy phishing organizations.
evidence_items.title: Trustworthy Phishing URL Detection Using Machine Learning: Performance Analysis and Future Directions

evidence_items.summary: Fracture detection on musculoskeletal radiographs remains challenging, particularly when findings are subtle or visible on only one projection. This retrospective two-centre multi-reader diagnostic performance study evaluated an artificial intelligence system at the level of the complete radiographic examination and compared its performance with seven anonymized readers. Radiographic examinations from AGEL Šternberk Hospital and AGEL Vítkovice Hospital, acquired between 15 December 2025 and 25 January 2026, were retrospectively analysed. The primary endpoint was study-level fracture positivity, defined as at least one positive image within an examination; the same aggregation rule was applied to AI and reader assessments. Examinations of the spine, ribs, and hemithorax were excluded because these anatomies were outside the supported scope. The cohort comprised 526 examinations, including 101 fracture-positive and 425 fracture-negative studies. Sensitivity was 0.911 (95% CI, 0.839–0.952), specificity 0.899 (0.866–0.924), PPV 0.681 (0.599–0.754), NPV 0.977 (0.957–0.988), and accuracy 0.901 (0.873–0.924). Mean reader sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and accuracy were 0.853, 0.853, 0.598, 0.961, and 0.853, respectively. The AI showed higher point estimates than the mean of the seven readers across all principal diagnostic metrics. These findings support prospective evaluation of AI as a second-reader or workflow-support tool for fracture detection, particularly in examinations containing subtle or easily overlooked findings.
evidence_items.title: Study-Level Diagnostic Performance of Artificial Intelligence for Fracture Detection on Musculoskeletal Radiographs: A Retrospective Multi-Reader Study

evidence_items.summary:
The rapid emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot applications has transformed digital information access, yet the theoretical understanding of how users evaluate new AI tools during early adoption remains limited. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model and Expectation Confirmation Theory, the study aims to address a conceptual gap regarding mixed sentiment and explore how demographic factors, such as gender, shape user experience during early adoption.
 
 
 
 A mixed-methods approach was used to analyze 1,000 Google Play Store reviews. Reviews were categorized by sentiment: positive, negative, mixed (both positive and negative statements) or neutral. Gender predictions were also made from usernames to explore demographic differences in sentiment.
 
 
 
 Of the 1,000 reviews, 487 were mixed reviews (48.7%), 373 were negative reviews (37.3%), 139 were positive reviews (13.9%) and one was neutral (0.1%), indicating that mixed and negative sentiment predominated. Users were mostly satisfied with DeepSeek’s usability and output quality, but criticized its performance and stability issues. Female users gave more negative reviews than male users (p < 0.05).
 
 
 
 The analysis was conducted on a stratified sample of 1,000 “most relevant” Google Play reviews from a short early adoption period, which may not accurately represent later user experiences or experiences on other platforms. Only reviews from phone users were included, and the neutral sentiment category contained too few cases for comparison. Gender inference was based on usernames and reflects predicted rather than self-identified gender. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as indicative of early user perceptions rather than long-term attitudes.
 
 
 
 The findings indicate that infrastructure reliability is the primary determinant of early user satisfaction. Transparent communication about service limitations is recommended prior to large-scale deployment. For policymakers, the equity implications of performance-unstable free AI services warrant attention, particularly for users with limited access to alternatives.
 
 
 
 The mixed-methods analysis of early DeepSeek user reviews, which distinguishes between mixed sentiment and positive and negative feedback, and incorporates a gender-based comparison, provides timely insight into user expectations and challenges during early adoption, supporting the development of more user-centered and stable AI systems.
evidence_items.title: User experience and early adoption of an artificial intelligence application: a mixed-methods sentiment analysis of DeepSeek reviews on Google Play

evidence_items.summary:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW
Midurethral sling (MUS) surgery is the standard procedure for stress urinary incontinence, offering favorable long-term outcomes. Despite its success, postoperative voiding dysfunction - manifesting as urinary retention, elevated post-void residuals (PVRs), slow or weak stream, hesitancy, or the need for prolonged catheterization - remains a clinically significant complication that is difficult to predict using traditional risk stratification. Conventional methods, including history, physical examination, PVR measurement, and selective urodynamics, provide limited individualized predictive power and fail to integrate the complex interplay of patient, anatomical, and surgical factors.


RECENT FINDINGS
Artificial intelligence and machine learning offer a promising approach to addressing this gap by analyzing multidimensional datasets to forecast individualized risk and guide perioperative management. While artificial intelligence applications in pelvic floor surgery have demonstrated utility in predicting general surgical outcomes, validated models specifically targeting post-MUS voiding dysfunction are lacking. Development of such predictive tools will require high-quality multicenter datasets, careful algorithm selection, and validation.


SUMMARY
Integrating artificial intelligence into clinical practice has the potential to enhance preoperative counseling, support shared decision-making, optimize surgical planning, and ultimately improve patient outcomes. This perspective highlights the unmet need for predictive modeling of voiding dysfunction after MUS, outlines the promise of artificial intelligence, and emphasizes the importance of responsible implementation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence-based prediction of postoperative voiding dysfunction following midurethral sling.

evidence_items.summary:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human resource management (HRM), yet the cognitive and psychological factors associated with human resource (HR) professionals’ intentions to use AI remain incompletely understood. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and appraisal perspectives, this study examines the relative associations of Cognitive Evaluation, AI-Use Anxiety, AI-Related Job Insecurity, organizational AI use across HR functions, and AI Knowledge with behavioral intention to use AI. It also explores whether AI Knowledge moderates these relationships.
 
 
 
 Survey data were collected from 285 HR professionals. Confirmatory factor analyses assessed the measurement structure of the study constructs, followed by hierarchical moderated regression analyses examining their unique associations with behavioral intention and the exploratory moderating role of AI Knowledge.
 
 
 
 Cognitive Evaluation, reflecting perceived usefulness and ease of use, showed the strongest unique association with behavioral intention to use AI. AI-Use Anxiety demonstrated a smaller negative association, whereas AI-Related Job Insecurity, AI Use Across HR Functions, and AI Knowledge did not explain significant unique variance once the competing predictors were considered simultaneously. The comprehensive model explained 66.8% of the variance in behavioral intention. The exploratory interaction analyses provided no clear evidence that AI Knowledge systematically moderated the relationships examined.
 
 
 
 Organizations implementing AI in HR should address both employees’ evaluations of the technology and apprehension surrounding its use. Implementation strategies should demonstrate the practical usefulness and usability of AI through role-specific examples, hands-on training, and opportunities to experiment with AI tools in realistic HR contexts. Organizations should also recognize AI-use anxiety as a distinct potential barrier by providing accessible support, low-risk opportunities for familiarization, and clear communication throughout implementation. These strategies may help create conditions that support employees’ willingness to use AI.
 
 
 
 This study extends research on AI use intentions by examining cognitive, emotional, knowledge-related, and organizational-exposure factors simultaneously rather than in isolation. The findings show that HR professionals’ intentions to use AI are most strongly associated with evaluations of its usefulness and usability, while AI-use anxiety represents a smaller but distinct negative correlate. By distinguishing AI-use anxiety from AI-related job insecurity and individual AI knowledge from organizational AI exposure, the study provides a more differentiated account of the factors associated with HR professionals’ intentions to use AI.
evidence_items.title: Beyond usefulness: cognitive and emotional correlates of AI use intentions among HR professionals

evidence_items.summary: Rerunning every governance control after every change to an artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline is expensive, so teams reuse earlier results. Reuse is safe only if each control's declared dependencies cover everything that can change its outcome, and only if the release gate checks that reused evidence describes the candidate being released. This article makes both conditions explicit and measures how often the first fails in practice. It defines when a signed evidence record is valid for a candidate and gives sufficient conditions under which change-local re-execution reaches the same release decision as rerunning every control. A reference gate implementing these checks with Ed25519 digital signatures blocks eight of nine manipulation scenarios, against one for a gate that trusts the planner and three for a gate that only verifies signatures; a dependency the policy never declared passes every gate. A replay of 38,083 commits from 714 public Data Version Control (DVC) pipelines measures that failure mode. Reusing stage results according to declared dependencies avoids 83.4% of stage executions, but in 3.3% of commits it reuses a stage whose imported code or referenced configuration changed, and 31% of pipelines are affected. A manual audit confirms the undeclared dependency in 36 of 40 sampled events. Evaluation stages, whose outputs are the evidence, are the most exposed. Adding each stage's static import closure lowers stale reuse to 0.4% while still avoiding 81.6% of executions; sampled shadow re-execution removes far less, and rerunning everything after unexplained changes avoids only 45.3%.
evidence_items.title: Reusing Assurance Evidence in AI Pipelines: Validity Conditions, a Fail-Closed Release Gate, and a Replay of 714 Public Data Version Control Pipelines

evidence_items.summary: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.
evidence_items.title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena

evidence_items.summary: Web development involves turning UI designs into functional webpages, which can be difficult for both beginners and experienced developers due to the complexity of HTML's hierarchical structures and styles. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating source code, two major challenges persist in UI-to-HTML code generation: (1) effectively representing HTML's hierarchical structure for LLMs, and (2) bridging the gap between the visual nature of UI designs and the text-based format of HTML code. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Waffle, a new fine-tuning strategy that uses a structure-aware attention mechanism to improve LLMs' understanding of HTML's structure and a contrastive fine-tuning approach to align LLMs' understanding of UI images and HTML code. Models fine-tuned with Waffle show up to 9.00 pp (percentage point) higher HTML match, 0.0982 higher CW-SSIM, 32.99 higher CLIP, and 27.12 pp higher LLEM on our new benchmark WebSight-Test and an existing benchmark Design2Code, outperforming current fine-tuning methods.

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains supplementary computational data, MATLAB programs, and numerical results supporting the research manuscript entitled "Modelling and analysis of diphtheria transmission incorporating vaccination, asymptomatic carriage, environmental contamination, optimal control and model-based intervention efficiency", authored by Timothy Terfa Ashezua, Reuben Iortyer Gweryina, and Meshack Ogbaji, Department of Mathematics, Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University, Makurdi, Nigeria. The study formulates and analyses a deterministic nine-compartment diphtheria transmission model incorporating imperfect vaccination, breakthrough infections, asymptomatic carriage, treatment and isolation, waning immunity, and environmental contamination. The mathematical analysis investigates positivity, boundedness, disease-free and endemic equilibria, the basic reproduction number, stability, bifurcation, sensitivity, vaccination thresholds, and optimal intervention strategies. The supplementary materials include: MATLAB programs: Computational scripts for numerical simulations, sensitivity analysis, equilibrium calculations, and optimal-control investigations. Sensitivity analysis datasets: A Latin hypercube sampling dataset consisting of 5,000 samples across 27 model parameters, together with 500 bootstrap resampling index sets and partial rank correlation coefficient (PRCC) results. Numerical simulation results: Model-generated trajectories illustrating baseline transmission dynamics and the effects of vaccination, detection and treatment, sanitation, and combined interventions. Optimal-control results: State, adjoint, and control trajectories for intervention strategies involving vaccination/boosting, carrier screening, treatment/isolation, and environmental decontamination. Convergence and reproducibility data: Forward–backward sweep iteration logs, numerical convergence diagnostics, and grid-refinement comparisons.
evidence_items.title: Computational Data and MATLAB Codes for a Diphtheria Transmission Model Incorporating Vaccination, Asymptomatic Carriage, Environmental Contamination and Optimal Control

evidence_items.summary: Hate speech detection in online environments poses significant challenges due to the nuanced and evolving nature of hate speech and the complexities of real-time communication. This study evaluates whether zero-shot large language models (LLMs), including Claude, Gemini 2.0, ChatGPT-o1, and ChatGPT-4o, can support the annotation of gaming-specific hate speech. We compare individual models, a multi-model collective, and TF-IDF–Logistic Regression classifier against an operational human-majority reference on 1,178 Dota 2 chat messages. We also examine whether ChatGPT-generated messages improve the traditional classifier when used exclusively as training-time augmentation, with full-archive augmentation and SMOTE as comparators. Among the automated approaches, the four-model collective achieved the highest accuracy and macro-F1 but did not uniformly outperform the strongest individual LLMs. For the class-sensitive measures, synthetic-data composition mattered more than volume. A post-hoc qualitative analysis identified recurring disagreement patterns and model-specific difficulties. Targeted augmentation achieved higher accuracy than SMOTE. The findings show that class-aware LLM generation can provide a competitive alternative to feature-space oversampling for lightweight classifiers, while zero-shot LLMs are best positioned as complementary annotation tools under human oversight.
evidence_items.title: Improving the Hate Speech Annotation Process with Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Organizations are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to support employee performance evaluation, yet employees' perceptions of and responses to these systems within this high-stakes workplace context remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on social exchange, organizational justice, and trust theories, this study examines how employees' justice perceptions shape trust in AI-based performance evaluation systems and how trust in AI relates to broader employee–organization relationship factors, including trust in the organization, trust in managers, and affective commitment. It further investigates whether these relationships vary across gender and Eastern–Western regional contexts. Survey data from 291 employees across Eastern and Western countries were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and multigroup analysis. The findings show that distributive and procedural justice perceptions positively influence employee trust in AI across regional contexts, with distributive justice exerting the stronger effect. Trust in AI, in turn, positively influences affective commitment in both contexts. Gender differences were observed in the relationship between procedural justice perception and trust in AI within the Eastern sample but not within the Western sample. These findings contribute to research on organizational justice, trust, and AI in organizations, while also offering practical insights for fostering employee trust and supporting effective AI implementation in performance evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Employees' Justice Perceptions and Trust in AI Systems for Performance Evaluation: Uncovering the Role of Gender and Culture

evidence_items.summary: Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability through learning from their own executions. However, learning through human corrections requires teleoperators to monitor execution and intervene when policies fail, a demand that is difficult to meet as robot fleets grow. We introduce collective experience learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which deployed robots share their execution experience to improve a common policy. We realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses failure contexts from robot executions to retrieve relevant trajectory segments from the fleet's shared successful experience and uses their actions as supervision for policy updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates experience collection, policy optimization and policy distribution despite local interruptions within the robot fleet. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and FERT generally achieves higher success rates across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support collective experience as a practical basis for scalable robot learning and a path towards improving policy reliability during deployment without collecting additional expert corrective actions.
evidence_items.title: Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots

evidence_items.summary: Subword tokenization methods such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) are a core component of modern language models; yet, tokenizer capacity remains typically determined by a fixed merge budget, chosen heuristically. Since larger vocabularies increase memory usage and computational cost, selecting compact and effective token inventories is essential for efficient language modeling. We study the optimization of a BPE merge budget as a statistical model selection problem and investigate information-theoretic criteria for \emph{computing optimal merge sets} directly from corpus statistics. To further improve the merge selection in limited data conditions, we augment the BPE training corpora with synthetic texts generated from the original data, providing estimates for the unigram and bigram distributions. Experiments across multiple corpora and downstream tasks show that using a principled vocabulary selection technique reduces model size, with little degradation in performance. We further observe that synthetic data can yield better tokenizers, especially in low-resource settings.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking BPE: Merge Selection as Model Selection

evidence_items.summary: Omni-modal large language models can jointly understand video, audio, and text, yet they remain weak at temporal grounding, a capability essential for real-world audio-visual applications. To understand this limitation, we look beyond final predictions and examine the model's internal temporal evidence. We identify a temporal generation gap: the internal attention of the model localizes the target moment more accurately than the timestamps it generates. To close this gap, we propose TACG (Temporal Attention-Consistency Grounding), a post-training method that treats internal attention as a reliable temporal pivot and aligns it with both the model prediction and the ground-truth annotation through attention-consistency training. We further build a 580K-sample training dataset by reconstructing temporal QA from dense audio-visual annotations and organizing general omni-modal instruction data. Using TACG and this training dataset, we train OmniGround, a general-purpose omni-modal model with stronger temporal grounding capability, without injecting any additional temporal cues. OmniGround reaches state-of-the-art omni-modal temporal grounding, including 37.5 mIoU on LongVALE and 35.7 mIoU on UnAV-100, while staying competitive on both general audio-visual understanding and vision-only grounding.
evidence_items.title: OmniGround: Strengthening Omni-Modal Temporal Grounding via Attention-Consistency Training

evidence_items.summary: The rapid evolution of Large Language Models is fueled by massive datasets, yet this reliance poses severe privacy risks, as models can inadvertently memorize and even directly output sensitive training data. Synthetic text generation offers a promising solution to this challenge; however, existing methods struggle to reconcile rigorous privacy guarantees with high data utility. In this paper, we propose a new paradigm for private synthetic text generation: Guided Diffusion. Leveraging the unique steerability of Diffusion Language Models, we introduce novel sampling and re-masking procedures that actively guide the iterative denoising steps. These mechanisms steer the generative process to reconstruct fluent text that adheres to a target semantic distribution. We demonstrate that our framework is naturally compatible with Differential Privacy (DP): once the semantic embeddings of the private corpus are protected, the DP guarantee carries over to the generated text by post-processing. Empirically, we show that our approach generates high-quality synthetic text with precise semantic alignment. Furthermore, we validate its effectiveness in DP synthetic text generation: across two datasets and two diffusion backbones, it outperforms Private Evolution and DP-SGD-based fine-tuning in distributional fidelity and downstream utility, while generating significantly faster than Private Evolution. We further extend the framework to Data-Specific Indistinguishability (DSI), which adds a formal certificate against data poisoning and memorization at a small utility cost.
evidence_items.title: Guided Diffusion for Trustworthy Synthetic Text Generation
